questions.question: According to Adam Smith, everyday actions in a free market are motivated by ______.
questions.explanation: Adam Smith argued that in a free market people go about their everyday buying, selling and working out of self-interest, each trying to do the best for themselves. The invisible hand in option A is not the motive itself; it is his name for the way all these self-interested actions end up coordinated, as if guided, to benefit society. Market forces and pricing (options B and C) are the mechanism through which this happens, not what motivates individuals.

questions.question: Microeconomics knowledge underlines the saying that we all live in a world ______.
questions.explanation: Microeconomics starts from scarcity: our wants are unlimited but the resources to satisfy them are limited, so we must make choices. Option A (wants) is only half the story, because wants alone would not create an economic problem if resources were unlimited. Rent and riches (options C and D) have nothing to do with this basic idea.

questions.question: ______ measures the choice of building roads that Governor Ambode gave up many years ago.
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up when a choice is made, so the roads the governor did not build measure the opportunity cost of what he chose instead. Option C, 'opportunity sacrificed', sounds similar but is not the economic term. Options A and B are not measures of a forgone alternative at all.

questions.question: When resources are organised to produce the maximum output possible, it is known as ______.
questions.explanation: Efficiency means organising resources so that the maximum possible output is obtained from them, with nothing wasted. Production (option A) is simply the act of making goods, whether efficient or not. Optimality (option B) is a broader idea about the best overall outcome, and market behaviour (option D) is unrelated.

questions.question: Several rich countries are immune to scarcity.
questions.explanation: Scarcity affects every country, rich or poor, because human wants are unlimited while resources are always limited, so the statement is always false. Rich countries may have more resources, but they still have to choose between competing uses, which is exactly what scarcity means. Options A, B and D all suggest that some countries can escape scarcity at some point, which never happens.

questions.question: ______ explains why Yaba Local Government Area Council gave up some projects in order to provide what the people wants.
questions.explanation: Resource constraints mean a council has limited funds and resources, so providing some projects forces it to give others up. This is the problem of scarcity and choice in action. Elections, people's wishes and loyalty (options A, C and D) may influence which projects are chosen, but they do not explain why some must be given up.

questions.question: An economy that behaves almost as if it is guided by some power is known as ______.
questions.explanation: A free market economy works as if guided by an invisible power: without any central planner, prices coordinate the self-interested decisions of millions of buyers and sellers. Option C, perfect market economy, is not a standard term for this idea, and option D refers to markets with imperfections. A 'superpower economy' (option A) is about a country's global strength, not how its markets work.

questions.question: Which of the following cost highlights the choice that you must make relative to the alternatives given up for your academic excellence?
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative you give up when you make a choice, such as the leisure or other activities you sacrifice to achieve academic excellence. Private cost (option A) and social cost (option D) refer to who bears a cost, not to alternatives forgone. Fixed cost (option B) is a production cost that does not change with output, so it has nothing to do with choosing between alternatives.

questions.question: In any given market system, people respond to the same ______.
questions.explanation: In a market system all buyers and sellers face and respond to the same set of prices, and these prices signal what to produce and how much to buy. Market forces (option D) are demand and supply, which create those prices; people react to the price signals themselves. Commodities and regulations (options A and C) differ across people and markets.

questions.question: A typical economy has four resources, namely ______.
questions.explanation: The four factors of production are land, labour, capital and the entrepreneur (entrepreneurship), which organises the other three. Option B is a list of natural items, not the factors of production, and option C mixes unrelated categories. Since only option A is correct, option D, 'all of the above', is wrong.

questions.question: In microeconomics, ______ is interpreted as "all other things are held constant."
questions.explanation: Ceteris paribus is Latin for 'other things being equal' and is used to hold every other influence constant while we study the effect of one variable. Options B and D are misspellings, and option A is a joke version of the phrase.

questions.question: Variables classified according to whether the factors that determine them come from inside or outside the model are best described as ______ and ______ variables.
questions.explanation: Variables are classified as endogenous when they are determined within the model (for example, equilibrium price and quantity) and exogenous when they are determined outside it and simply taken as given (for example, weather or government policy). Option A, independent and dependent, describes the direction of a relationship in an equation, not where a variable's determinants come from. Options C and D mix the two classifications.

questions.question: The assumptions on which the production possibility frontier is based include the following except ______

options.a: Resources are sufficient for all production
options.d: Resources are used on just two commodities

questions.explanation: The production possibility frontier assumes resources are limited, fully employed and used to produce only two goods; it would make no sense if resources were sufficient for all production, because then there would be no scarcity and no trade-off. Options B, C and D are all standard assumptions of the frontier.

questions.question: Market failure occurs when ______.

options.a: The market operates efficiently without government intervention
options.b: The market cannot allocate resources efficiently
options.d: There is perfect competition in the market

questions.explanation: Market failure happens when the free market, left on its own, fails to allocate resources efficiently, for example because of externalities or public goods. Options A and C describe the opposite situation, where the market works well without help. Option D, perfect competition, is the case in which markets are most efficient, not where they fail.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the concept of opportunity cost in economics? ______.

options.a: The monetary value assigned to the utility derived from a commodity
options.b: The total time or money invested in producing a commodity
options.c: The value of the next best alternative that is forgone when a choice is made
options.d: The cost incurred in retraining resources to achieve optimal production

questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative you give up when you make a choice, because scarce resources used for one thing cannot be used for another. For example, the time you spend at a party is time you could have spent reading for an exam. Option B describes the total amount spent on production, which is an accounting cost rather than what is sacrificed, and option A describes the money value of utility, which is a different idea.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a capital input?
questions.explanation: Capital as a factor of production means man-made goods used to produce other goods, such as tools, machines and buildings, so a hammer is a capital input. Options A, B and C are financial assets: money, shares and bonds are claims used to buy or finance inputs, not inputs that physically take part in production.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of an intermediate product?
questions.explanation: An intermediate product is a good that is used up as an input in producing another good, and crude oil is refined into petrol, diesel and other products. Options A, C and D are normally bought by final users for their own use, so they are final goods rather than intermediate ones.

questions.question: The curve showing the different combinations of goods that an economy can produce with its given resources is known as:
questions.explanation: A production possibility curve shows the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce when it uses all its resources fully and efficiently, so it highlights scarcity, choice and opportunity cost. Option A, the indifference curve, shows combinations of goods that give a consumer equal satisfaction, not production possibilities. Option C relates to consumer choices revealed through purchases.

questions.question: In a free enterprise economy, the problems of what, how and for whom to produce are solved by :
questions.explanation: In a free enterprise economy, the questions of what, how and for whom to produce are answered by the price mechanism, the free interaction of demand and supply in markets. Prices signal what consumers want, guide firms on how to produce at least cost, and decide who can afford the output. Options A and C describe central planning bodies, which belong to a planned economy rather than a free enterprise one.

questions.question: The fundamental problem faced by an economy is one of:

options.d: Scarcity of resources and multiplicity of wants

questions.explanation: Every economy faces the basic problem that human wants are many and unlimited while the resources to satisfy them are scarce, so choices must be made. Exchange (option A) and government decisions (option B) are ways of dealing with the problem, not the problem itself, and economic welfare (option C) is a goal rather than the root problem.

questions.question: Microeconomic theory studies how a free enterprise economy determines:
questions.explanation: Microeconomics explains price determination in individual markets, and this covers the prices of goods, the prices of services and the prices of resources such as wages, rent and interest (factor pricing). Options A, B and C are each only part of the picture, so D is the complete answer.

questions.question: Which aspect of taxation involves normative economics?

options.c: The effect of the tax on incentives to work

questions.explanation: Normative economics deals with value judgements about what ought to be, and whether a tax is fair is a matter of opinion and values. The incidence of a tax (option A) and its effect on incentives to work (option C) are positive questions, because they can be checked against facts and evidence. That is why D is wrong too.

questions.question: Microeconomics deals primarily with:

options.a: Comparative statics, general equilibrium and positive economics
options.b: Comparative statics, partial equilibrium and normative economics
options.c: Dynamics, partial equilibrium and positive economics
options.d: Comparative statics, partial equilibrium and positive economics

questions.explanation: Microeconomics mainly compares equilibrium positions before and after a change (comparative statics), looks at one market at a time while holding other things constant (partial equilibrium), and explains how the economy actually works (positive economics). Option A is wrong because general equilibrium looks at all markets together, option B is wrong because the main focus is positive rather than normative, and option C is wrong because the time path of adjustment (dynamics) is not its main concern.

questions.question: Which of the following is incorrect?

options.a: Microeconomics is concerned primarily with the problem of what, how and for whom to produce
options.b: Microeconomics is concerned primarily with the economic behaviour of individual decision-making units when at equilibrium
options.c: Microeconomics is concerned primarily with the time path and processes by which one equilibrium position evolves into another
options.d: Microeconomics is concerned primarily with comparative statics rather than dynamics

questions.explanation: Statement C is the incorrect one: the time path and process by which one equilibrium moves to another is the subject of dynamics, and microeconomics is mainly concerned with comparative statics, as option D correctly says. Options A and B are also correct descriptions, since microeconomics deals with what, how and for whom to produce and with the behaviour of individual households and firms in equilibrium.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is most closely associated with general equilibrium analysis?

options.b: The equilibrium price of a factor depends on the balancing of the forces of demand and supply for that factor
options.c: The equilibrium price of a good or service depends on the balancing of the forces of demand and supply for that good or service

questions.explanation: General equilibrium analysis studies all markets together and recognises that they are interconnected, so a change in one market affects prices and quantities in others - in short, everything depends on everything else. Options B and C describe price being set by demand and supply in a single market, which is partial equilibrium analysis.

questions.question: The meaning of the word 'economic' is most closely associated with the word:
questions.explanation: Economics exists because resources are scarce relative to wants, so anything described as 'economic' involves scarcity and the need to choose. Options A, C and D (free, unlimited, unrestricted) describe the opposite situation, where there would be no economic problem to solve.

questions.question: Microeconomics studies the decision making behavior of:

options.c: The central bank in setting the money supply

questions.explanation: Microeconomics studies the decisions of individual economic units, such as a consumer, a household or a single firm. Options A and D (society or the economy as a whole) describe macroeconomics, and option C, the control of the money supply, is a macroeconomic policy question rather than individual decision making.

questions.question: A function refers to :

options.c: The demand and supply of a commodity service or resource
options.d: The relationship between one dependent variable and one or more independent variables.

questions.explanation: A function expresses the relationship between one dependent variable and one or more independent variables, for example quantity demanded depending on own price, income and tastes. Options A, B and C are particular examples where functions are used, but they do not define what a function is.

questions.question: The subject matter of economics is the study of:
questions.explanation: Economics studies how people make choices in using scarce resources to satisfy unlimited wants, so its subject matter is scarcity and choice together. Option C, scarcity alone, is only half of the idea, because it is the need to choose that scarcity creates which economics analyses. Options A and B, wealth and welfare, are older and narrower views of the subject.

questions.question: Microeconomics deals with:
questions.explanation: Microeconomics covers the pricing of products, the pricing of factors of production (wages, rent, interest and profit) and welfare economics, which asks whether resources are allocated efficiently. Since A, B and C all fall within its scope, D is the correct answer.

questions.question: A market:

options.a: Necessarily refers to a meeting place between buyers and sellers
options.b: Does not necessarily refer to a meeting place between buyers and sellers

questions.explanation: In economics, a market is any arrangement that brings buyers and sellers into contact so they can trade, whether face to face, by phone or online. So it does not have to be a physical meeting place. Option A is wrong because many markets, such as online or foreign exchange markets, have no single location, and options C and D wrongly tie a market to a particular area when its extent depends on the good being traded.

questions.question: The branch of economics that studies the behaviour of individual economic agents such as households and firms, and how they make decisions about the allocation of scarce resources, is called
questions.explanation: Microeconomics looks at the small units of the economy: individual households, consumers and firms and how they allocate scarce resources. Option C, macroeconomics, studies the economy as a whole, while A (econometrics) is the use of statistics to test economic theories.

questions.question: In microeconomics, attention is focused mainly on

options.a: The preparation of national income accounts and the balance of payments
options.b: The total output, general price level and total employment of the whole economy
options.c: Specific markets and how demand and supply determine prices, production and consumption
options.d: The control of money supply and interest rates by the central bank

questions.explanation: Microeconomics concentrates on individual markets and the way demand and supply in them fix prices, output and consumption. Options B, A and D all deal with aggregates of the whole economy or with monetary policy, which are macroeconomic matters.

questions.question: Which of the following is a microeconomic question?

options.a: Why did Nigeria's inflation rate rise last year?
options.b: What determines the price of tomatoes in Mile 12 market?
options.c: What is the national rate of unemployment in Nigeria?
options.d: How fast did Nigeria's real GDP grow this year?

questions.explanation: The price of one commodity in one market is a typical microeconomic question because it concerns an individual market. Options A, C and D concern economy-wide aggregates (the general price level, total unemployment and national output), which belong to macroeconomics.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a microeconomic issue?

options.a: Pricing decision of a bakery in Yaba
options.c: Determination of the general price level of the whole economy
options.d: Wages paid in the market for bricklayers

questions.explanation: The general price level of the whole economy is an aggregate, so it is studied in macroeconomics. Options A, B and D each refer to a single firm, a single household or a single market, which is exactly what microeconomics studies.

questions.question: Because it deals largely with how the prices of goods and factors are determined, microeconomics is also commonly called
questions.explanation: Microeconomics is often called price theory because explaining how prices of individual goods and factors are determined is at its centre. Income theory (option B) is a name associated with macroeconomics, which explains national income and employment, and A refers to the study of long-run growth of the whole economy.

questions.question: Which of the following is a role of microeconomics?

options.a: Examining how firms decide what to produce, how much to produce and at what cost
options.b: Measuring the gross domestic product of a country
options.c: Setting the target for the overall inflation rate
options.d: Recording a country's trade with the rest of the world in the balance of payments

questions.explanation: Microeconomics studies how firms decide what and how much to produce and at what cost. Options B, C and D deal with national aggregates and economy-wide policy, which belong to macroeconomics.

questions.question: An economist studies how buyers and sellers of soft drinks in Lagos adjust their purchases and output after the government introduces a N10-per-litre tax on sugary drinks. This study best illustrates which role of microeconomics?

options.a: Identifying situations where markets fail to allocate resources efficiently
options.b: Studying how different market structures affect pricing and output
options.c: Explaining how scarce resources are allocated across the whole economy
options.d: Assessing how individuals and firms respond to taxes, subsidies, price controls or regulations

questions.explanation: The study is about how people and firms react to a tax, which is the role of assessing responses to taxes, subsidies, price controls and regulations. Option A would apply if the focus were on a market that misallocates resources, and option B would require comparing markets with different numbers of sellers; neither is the focus here.

questions.question: A cement factory in Ogun State pours waste into a river used by nearby farmers, and the cost of the damage is not reflected in the price of cement. Studying such a case falls under which role of microeconomics?

options.a: Identifying situations where markets fail to allocate resources efficiently
options.b: Explaining how prices are determined in a competitive market
options.d: Understanding how consumers choose what goods to buy

questions.explanation: When the price of cement leaves out the damage done to farmers, the market is not allocating resources efficiently, which is a market failure. Option B is about normal price determination, while C and D concern consumer demand and choices, which are not the issue in this case.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT within the scope of microeconomics?

options.d: Determination of national income and aggregate employment

questions.explanation: National income and aggregate employment are totals for the whole economy, so they belong to macroeconomics. Consumer behaviour (option C), production and costs (option A) and factor pricing and distribution (option B) are all part of the scope of microeconomics.

questions.question: Which of the following falls within the scope of microeconomics?

options.a: Monetary policy and the control of inflation
options.b: Theory of the firm and market structure
options.d: Government budget deficits and national debt

questions.explanation: The theory of the firm and market structure studies how individual firms behave in different kinds of markets, so it is a core part of microeconomics. Options A, D and C are concerned with the whole economy and belong to macroeconomics.

questions.question: The part of microeconomics that explains how wages, rent, interest and profit are determined and how income is shared among the owners of factors of production is
questions.explanation: Factor pricing and distribution explains the rewards to labour, land, capital and entrepreneurship and how income is shared among them. Option C, welfare economics, judges whether resource allocation is efficient and improves well-being, and option B studies how output relates to inputs and costs.

questions.question: The manager of a bottled-water company uses estimates of demand and production costs to choose the price and output that maximise profit. This shows the relevance of microeconomics as

options.a: A tool for predicting and managing market failures
options.b: A means of understanding market structures
options.c: A guide to policy formulation and evaluation

questions.explanation: Here a firm is using demand and cost analysis to make its own business choice, which is the use of microeconomics as a decision-making tool. Option C refers to government using microeconomics to design and judge policies, and option A is about markets that misallocate resources, neither of which describes a manager setting price and output.

questions.question: The basic economic problem that arises because human wants are unlimited while the resources available to satisfy them are limited is
questions.explanation: Scarcity means that resources are limited relative to unlimited wants. Choice (option A) and opportunity cost (option D) are consequences of scarcity rather than the problem itself, and market failure (option C) is when markets allocate resources inefficiently.

questions.question: Individuals, firms and governments must make choices mainly because

options.b: Money is used as a medium of exchange
options.c: Prices of goods are usually high
options.d: Resources are scarce relative to wants

questions.explanation: Because resources are scarce compared with wants, not every want can be satisfied, so economic agents must choose among alternatives. Options B, C and A describe features of some economies, but choice would still be necessary without money, high prices or regulation as long as resources are scarce.

questions.question: The value of the next best alternative forgone when a choice is made is called
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative given up when a choice is made. Marginal cost (option B) is the extra cost of producing one more unit, sunk cost (option A) is a cost already incurred that cannot be recovered, and total cost (option C) is the whole cost of producing a given output.

questions.question: Ada has N15,000. She can buy a scientific calculator, a pair of shoes or a cinema ticket with it, and she ranks them in that order: calculator first, shoes second, cinema third. If she buys the calculator, her opportunity cost is

options.d: The shoes and the cinema ticket together

questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is only the next best alternative given up, and Ada's second choice is the pair of shoes. The calculator (option C) is what she chose, not what she gave up, and option D wrongly adds all forgone alternatives instead of taking only the next best one.

questions.question: Using all his land and labour, a farmer in Oyo State can produce either 40 bags of maize or 20 bags of cassava, with a constant rate of trade-off between them. What is the opportunity cost of producing one bag of cassava?
questions.explanation: Giving up 40 bags of maize to get 20 bags of cassava means each bag of cassava costs 40 / 20 = 2 bags of maize. Option B (0.5) is the opportunity cost of one bag of maize in terms of cassava, the inverse ratio, and options D and C use totals instead of dividing.

questions.question: On an economy's production possibility curve, point A shows 10 units of cloth and 50 units of food, while point B shows 14 units of cloth and 42 units of food. Moving from A to B, the opportunity cost of each extra unit of cloth is
questions.explanation: Moving from A to B gives 4 more units of cloth at the cost of 8 units of food, so each unit of cloth costs 8 / 4 = 2 units of food. Option D inverts the ratio, while options C and B give only the change in cloth or the total change in food rather than the cost per unit.

questions.question: An economy's production possibilities are: P (0 cloth, 100 food), Q (10 cloth, 90 food), R (20 cloth, 70 food), S (30 cloth, 40 food), T (40 cloth, 0 food). Moving from R to S, the opportunity cost of one unit of cloth is
questions.explanation: From R to S the economy gains 10 units of cloth and gives up 70 - 40 = 30 units of food, so one unit of cloth costs 30 / 10 = 3 units of food. Option B (2) is the cost between Q and R, option C (1) is between P and Q, and option A (4) is between S and T; the rising figures show increasing opportunity cost.

questions.question: A point lying inside (below) an economy's production possibility curve indicates that

options.a: The economy has experienced economic growth
options.b: Some resources are unemployed or used inefficiently
options.c: The output combination cannot be attained with present resources
options.d: The economy is producing efficiently with all resources fully employed

questions.explanation: A point inside the PPC means the economy could produce more of at least one good without producing less of the other, so resources are idle or wasted. Option C describes a point outside the curve, option D describes a point on the curve, and growth (option A) is shown by the curve itself shifting outward.

questions.question: A combination of goods that lies outside (beyond) an economy's production possibility curve is

options.b: Unattainable with the present resources and technology

questions.explanation: Points beyond the PPC need more resources or better technology than the economy currently has, so they are unattainable for now. Options D and A describe points inside the curve, and option C describes points on the curve.

questions.question: A production possibility curve is usually concave to the origin (bowed outward) because

options.a: Opportunity cost is constant along the curve
options.b: Resources are equally suited to producing both goods
options.c: Opportunity cost increases as more of one good is produced
options.d: Marginal utility diminishes as more of a good is consumed

questions.explanation: As an economy shifts more resources into one good, it must use resources less suited to it, so each extra unit costs more of the other good; this increasing opportunity cost bows the curve outward. Options A and B would give a straight-line PPC, and option D is about consumer satisfaction, not production.

questions.question: Which of the following would shift Nigeria's production possibility curve outward?

options.a: A change in consumers' tastes towards imported goods
options.b: A reduction in unemployment of existing resources
options.c: An improvement in technology used in production
options.d: A rise in the price of one of the goods

questions.explanation: Better technology (or more resources) raises the maximum output the economy can produce, so the whole PPC shifts outward. Option B moves the economy from a point inside the curve towards the curve without shifting it, and options A and D change what is demanded, not what can be produced.

questions.question: In economics, the phrase ceteris paribus means

options.d: All variables change at the same time

questions.explanation: Ceteris paribus means other things remain equal, so the economist changes one variable and holds all other influences constant. Option D is the opposite of the assumption, and options C and B refer to the time period and to small changes, which are different ideas.

questions.question: "If the price of garri rises, the quantity of garri demanded will fall, assuming consumers' income, tastes and the prices of other goods remain unchanged." The assumption at the end of this statement is known as the
questions.explanation: Holding income, tastes and other prices unchanged so the effect of the price of garri alone can be seen is the ceteris paribus (other things being equal) assumption. Option B, rationality, is about consumers knowing what they want and maximising satisfaction, and option D, laissez-faire, is a policy of non-interference by government.

questions.question: Which of the following is a positive economic statement?

options.a: It is unfair that petrol prices are so high
options.b: Federal universities should charge lower school fees
options.c: The government ought to raise the minimum wage
options.d: An increase in the minimum wage will raise unemployment among unskilled workers

questions.explanation: A positive statement describes what is or what will happen and can be tested against facts, as with the claim about the effect of the minimum wage on unemployment. Options C, A and B contain value judgements ("ought", "unfair", "should"), so they are normative.

questions.question: Which of the following is a normative economic statement?

options.a: A tax on cigarettes will reduce the quantity of cigarettes sold
options.b: Nigeria's inflation rate was higher in 2024 than in 2020
options.c: A fall in the price of rice will increase the quantity of rice demanded
options.d: The government should provide free healthcare for children under five

questions.explanation: A normative statement expresses a value judgement about what ought to be, and the word "should" signals this. Options C, B and A are positive statements because each can be checked against evidence, whether or not it turns out to be true.

questions.question: The type of economic analysis that studies an equilibrium position at a given point in time, without considering the process of change, is
questions.explanation: Static analysis looks at one equilibrium as if frozen at a moment in time. Comparative static analysis (option D) compares two equilibria, and dynamic analysis (option A) traces the path of change over time; general equilibrium (option C) concerns the interdependence of all markets, not the treatment of time.

questions.question: Comparing the old equilibrium price and quantity of a good with the new equilibrium after a change in demand, without tracing the path between them, is called
questions.explanation: Comparative static analysis compares two equilibrium positions, before and after a change, without studying how the economy moves from one to the other. Static analysis (option D) looks at only one equilibrium, and dynamic analysis (option A) is the one that traces the time path of adjustment.

questions.question: After a ban on rice imports, an economist traces month by month how the price of local rice changes until it settles at a new equilibrium. This is an example of
questions.explanation: Tracing the time path of adjustment, period by period, from one equilibrium to another is dynamic analysis. Comparative statics (option B) would only compare the starting and final equilibria, and normative analysis (option A) involves value judgements about what ought to be.

questions.question: Analysis of a single market in isolation, assuming that conditions in all other markets remain unchanged, is called
questions.explanation: Partial equilibrium analysis studies one market on its own and uses the ceteris paribus assumption to hold other markets constant. General equilibrium analysis (option B) instead studies all markets together and the links between them, and dynamic analysis (option D) is about the time path of change.

questions.question: The approach that studies the simultaneous determination of prices and quantities in all markets, taking account of their interdependence, is
questions.explanation: General equilibrium analysis considers all markets at once and how a change in one affects the others. Partial equilibrium analysis (option A) looks at only one market and ignores these feedback effects, while options C and B describe how time is treated rather than how many markets are studied.

questions.question: An analyst studies how a new tax on bread affects the price and quantity of bread only, ignoring any effects on the markets for flour, butter and tea. The analyst is using
questions.explanation: Looking at the bread market alone while ignoring its links with related markets is partial equilibrium analysis. General equilibrium analysis (option D) would trace the effects on flour, butter, tea and other markets as well.

questions.question: The main difference between partial and general equilibrium analysis is that partial equilibrium analysis

options.a: Ignores the feedback effects between markets, while general equilibrium analysis takes them into account
options.b: Is normative, while general equilibrium analysis is positive
options.c: Deals with the long run only, while general equilibrium analysis deals with the short run only
options.d: Studies all markets at once, while general equilibrium analysis studies one market

questions.explanation: Partial equilibrium analysis isolates one market and assumes other markets are unaffected, while general equilibrium analysis allows for the interdependence and feedback among all markets. Option D reverses the two approaches, and options C and B confuse them with the time period and with positive versus normative economics.

questions.question: The system by which prices, set by the free interaction of demand and supply, guide the allocation of resources in an economy is called the
questions.explanation: The price mechanism lets prices formed by demand and supply signal to buyers and sellers how resources should be used. A command system (option D) relies on government directives instead of prices, and market failure (option A) describes cases where markets do not allocate resources efficiently.

questions.question: An economist compares how a single electricity distribution company in an area sets its tariff with how many sellers of sachet water in the same area set their prices. This study mainly concerns

options.a: How different market structures affect pricing and output decisions
options.b: How the general price level is determined

questions.explanation: Comparing a single seller with many sellers is a comparison of market structures and their effect on prices and output. Option D is about responses to subsidies, which are not involved, and option B is a macroeconomic question about the whole economy.

questions.question: The basic microeconomic concept that measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded or supplied to a change in one of its determinants, such as price, is
questions.explanation: Elasticity measures how strongly quantity demanded or supplied responds to a change in price, income or another determinant. Utility (option D) is the satisfaction from consumption, and profit maximisation (option B) is the assumed goal of the firm.

questions.question: When is a consumer said to be rational?

options.b: He knows the prices of goods and services

questions.explanation: A rational consumer knows what he wants and has full knowledge of the prices of goods and services and of his own income, so both B and C apply. Option A is the opposite of rationality, since a rational consumer seeks to maximize satisfaction, not dissatisfaction. Choosing B or C alone leaves out one part of the consumer's knowledge.

questions.question: When a commodity is said to have utility, it means?
questions.explanation: Utility is the want-satisfying power of a commodity, so saying a commodity has utility means it can give satisfaction. Option C goes too far, because utility does not require maximum satisfaction. Option B is not enough on its own, since being consumable does not guarantee satisfaction.

questions.question: Given that the marginal utilities of two goods Z and Y are MUz and MUy respectively, and their prices are Pz and Py, if MUz/Pz is less than MUy/Py, a rational consumer will buy ______.

options.a: More of Z and less of Y
options.b: More of Y and less of Z
options.c: Both Z and Y in equal amounts
options.d: The same amount of money on both Z and Y

questions.explanation: When MUz/Pz is less than MUy/Py, the last naira spent on Y gives more satisfaction than the last naira spent on Z, so the consumer should buy more Y and less Z. As he does, MUy falls and MUz rises (diminishing marginal utility) until MUz/Pz = MUy/Py. Option A is the reverse, and options C and D ignore the condition for equilibrium.

questions.question: When total utility increases, marginal utility is ______.
questions.explanation: Total utility rises as long as each extra unit adds something positive, so marginal utility is positive, and by the law of diminishing marginal utility it is falling as consumption increases. Option C, zero, is the point where total utility reaches its peak, not where it is rising. Negative marginal utility (options A and B) makes total utility fall.

questions.question: When a consumer begins consuming a good, total utility typically: ______
questions.explanation: The first units of a good give the highest marginal utility, so when a consumer starts consuming a good, total utility rises quickly. As more units are consumed, marginal utility diminishes and total utility rises more and more slowly until it peaks at the saturation point. Option D describes what happens later in consumption, not at the start, and options A and B would need marginal utility to be negative or zero from the first unit.

questions.question: The typical shape of the total utility curve is: ______
questions.explanation: Total utility rises at first as more units are consumed, flattens out at the saturation point where marginal utility is zero, and then falls once marginal utility turns negative. That gives a curve that slopes upward and then bends downward. Option A ignores the rising portion, and options C and D are not shapes used to describe total utility.

questions.question: Which of the following is correct? ______

options.c: AU is constant when MU > AU

questions.explanation: Average utility is pulled up whenever the extra unit adds more than the current average, so AU rises when MU > AU, is at its maximum when MU = AU, and falls when MU < AU. Options A and B state these relationships the wrong way round, and option C is wrong because AU cannot stay constant while MU is above it.

questions.question: The cardinalist approach assumes that utility is: ______.
questions.explanation: The cardinal approach assumes utility can be measured in numbers, using imaginary units called utils, so we can say one unit gives 10 utils and another 6 utils. Option A, ranking, describes the ordinal approach, which only orders bundles as preferred, indifferent or less preferred without measuring how much. Option C does not describe either approach.

questions.question: When total utility increases at a decreasing rate, marginal utility is: ______
questions.explanation: Marginal utility is the extra satisfaction from one more unit, so it measures how fast total utility is rising. If total utility is increasing at a decreasing rate, each extra unit adds less than the one before, which means marginal utility is diminishing. Option B would make total utility rise faster and faster, and option D would make total utility fall.

questions.question: When marginal utility is negative, total utility: ______
questions.explanation: Marginal utility is the change in total utility from one more unit, so a negative marginal utility means the extra unit actually reduces total satisfaction and total utility is falling. This happens after the saturation point. Option D, maximum total utility, occurs where marginal utility is zero, not negative.

questions.question: Total utility reaches its maximum when marginal utility is: ______
questions.explanation: Total utility keeps rising as long as each extra unit adds positive satisfaction, and starts falling once marginal utility turns negative. It therefore reaches its maximum, the saturation point, where marginal utility is zero. Option A means total utility is still rising, and option C means it is already falling.

questions.question: Average utility is defined as: ______
questions.explanation: Average utility is total utility divided by the number of units consumed, AU = TU / Q. For example, if 4 units give 40 utils in total, average utility is 40 / 4 = 10 utils. Option A, TU x Q, has no economic meaning, and options C and D use marginal utility instead of total utility.

questions.question: If a consumer continues consumption beyond the saturation point, total utility: ______
questions.explanation: At the saturation point marginal utility is zero and total utility is at its maximum. Consuming beyond it gives negative marginal utility, as each extra unit causes discomfort, so total utility decreases. Option B describes the saturation point itself, not what happens beyond it, and option A would need marginal utility to be high and positive.

questions.question: The cardinal theorists of consumer behaviour postulate consumer equilibrium is achieved when: ______.

options.a: Indifference curve is tangent to the budget line
options.b: MU per unit of price is equal to zero
options.c: MU per unit of price is equal across goods
options.d: MU of every good is equal, whatever its price

questions.explanation: Cardinal theorists say a consumer buying several goods is in equilibrium when the marginal utility per naira spent is the same for every good, MUx/Px = MUy/Py. If one good gave more utility per naira, the consumer could do better by shifting spending towards it. Option D ignores prices: equal MUs only give equilibrium if the goods also cost the same. Option A is the ordinal (indifference curve) condition, and option B is wrong because MU per naira is generally positive at equilibrium, not zero.

questions.question: The want-satisfying power of a commodity is called:
questions.explanation: Utility is the power of a commodity to satisfy a human want. Option A, satisfaction, is the result a consumer gets from using the good, not the power of the good itself, and option D, marginal utility, is only the extra utility from one more unit.

questions.question: Utility is the concept which is:
questions.explanation: Utility is subjective because it depends on each person's tastes and feelings, so the same good can give very different satisfaction to different people. Option A is wrong because utility cannot be observed like weight or price; it exists in the mind of the consumer.

questions.question: Change in utility resulting from one unit change in consumption is called:
questions.explanation: Marginal utility is the change in total utility from consuming one more unit of a good: MU = change in TU / change in Q. Option A, total utility, is the overall satisfaction from all units consumed, and option B is not the standard name used in economics.

questions.question: Saturation point is the point where:
questions.explanation: The saturation point is where the consumer has had so much of a good that one more unit adds no satisfaction at all, so MU = 0 and total utility is at its maximum. Option A is wrong because TU is at its highest, not zero, at this point, and option C describes the stage before saturation.

questions.question: Measurable utility is the postulate of:
questions.explanation: The idea that utility can be measured in cardinal units such as utils comes from the neo-classical economists, especially Alfred Marshall, whose approach is known as the cardinal utility theory. Option B is wrong because the ordinalists argued that utility can only be ranked, not measured.

questions.question: Which of the following is Gossen's first law:
questions.explanation: Gossen's first law is the law of diminishing marginal utility: as a person consumes more units of a good, the extra satisfaction from each additional unit falls. Option B, the law of equi-marginal utility (MUx/Px = MUy/Py), is known as Gossen's second law.

questions.question: Which of the following is a cardinalist approach to demand analysis:
questions.explanation: Marshallian utility analysis assumes utility can be measured in cardinal numbers (utils), so it is the cardinalist approach. Option B, indifference curve analysis, is ordinal because it only ranks combinations of goods, and option C, revealed preference, is based on observed choices rather than measured utility.

questions.question: A consumer finds that MUx/Px > MUy/Py. What should the consumer do to attain equilibrium?

options.a: Buy less of X and more of Y until MUx/Px = MUy/Py
options.b: Buy more of X and less of Y until MUx/Px = MUy/Py
options.c: Buy more of both X and Y until their marginal utilities are equal
options.d: Keep the same purchases, since the consumer is already in equilibrium

questions.explanation: The last naira spent on X gives more utility than the last naira spent on Y, so switching spending towards X raises total utility. As more X is bought its marginal utility falls, and as less Y is bought MUy rises, by the law of diminishing marginal utility, until MUx/Px = MUy/Py. Option A moves in the wrong direction, and option D is wrong because equilibrium requires the two ratios to be equal.

questions.question: In consumer theory, utility refers to

options.a: The satisfaction a consumer derives from consuming a good or service
options.b: The usefulness of a good as judged by society's moral standards
options.c: The quantity of a good bought at a given price
options.d: The price a consumer pays for a good

questions.explanation: Utility is the satisfaction, happiness or benefit a person gets from consuming a good or service. It is not the price paid (option D) or the quantity bought (option C), and it has no moral meaning (option B): even a harmful good can yield utility to the person who wants it.

questions.question: The two approaches to the study of consumer behaviour are the
questions.explanation: Consumer behaviour is analysed by the cardinal approach, which measures utility in numbers, and the ordinal approach, which only ranks preferences. The other pairs are real economic distinctions, but they describe types of statements (option D), treatment of time (option C) or the number of markets studied (option A).

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an assumption of the cardinal utility theory?

options.a: Utility can be measured in utils

questions.explanation: Diminishing marginal rate of substitution belongs to the ordinal (indifference curve) approach, not the cardinal approach. Rationality (option D), measurable utility in utils (option A) and constant marginal utility of money (option C) are all assumptions of cardinal utility theory, along with diminishing marginal utility.

questions.question: Which of the following is an assumption of the cardinal utility theory?

options.b: Indifference curves are convex to the origin
options.c: Utility can only be ranked, not measured

questions.explanation: Cardinal theory assumes that the more a consumer has of a good, the less an extra unit adds, which is diminishing marginal utility. Options C and B are features of the ordinal approach, and option D contradicts the cardinal assumption that the marginal utility of money is constant.

questions.question: The cardinal assumption that each additional N1 gives the consumer the same level of satisfaction is known as
questions.explanation: Constant marginal utility of money means every extra naira is worth the same satisfaction to the consumer. Diminishing marginal utility (option C) refers to goods consumed, not money, and cardinality (option A) is the assumption that utility can be measured in utils.

questions.question: In the cardinal approach, the assumption of constant marginal utility of money is important because it

options.a: Guarantees that total utility always rises
options.b: Allows money to serve as a stable measuring rod of utility
options.c: Ensures that consumers can rank but not measure utility
options.d: Makes the demand curve slope upward

questions.explanation: If each naira always carries the same satisfaction, the amount of money a consumer is willing to pay can be used as a fixed yardstick for utility. Option A is wrong because total utility can fall once marginal utility is negative, option D is wrong because the demand curve slopes downward, and option C describes the ordinal approach.

questions.question: The theory of consumer behaviour (the axiom of utility maximisation) assumes that the consumer

options.a: Is rational and has full knowledge of available commodities, their prices and his or her income
options.b: Aims to minimise spending regardless of satisfaction
options.c: Can influence the market price by the amount he or she buys
options.d: Has unlimited income to spend on all goods

questions.explanation: Utility maximisation assumes a rational consumer who knows the available goods, their prices and his or her own income. Option D contradicts the basic idea of a limited budget, option C contradicts the assumption that prices are given, and option B reverses the goal of maximising satisfaction.

questions.question: Marginal utility is best defined as

options.a: The extra utility obtained from consuming one additional unit of a commodity
options.b: The total satisfaction obtained from all units consumed
options.c: The satisfaction obtained from the first unit only
options.d: Total utility divided by the number of units consumed

questions.explanation: Marginal means extra, so marginal utility is the additional utility from one more unit, measured as the change in total utility divided by the change in quantity. Option B is total utility, and option D is average utility, which is a different measure.

questions.question: "Holding taste constant, as a person's consumption of a commodity increases, each additional unit yields less and less utility." This statement is the
questions.explanation: The law of diminishing marginal utility says that each extra unit of a commodity adds less satisfaction than the one before. The law of demand (option C) relates price to quantity demanded, the equi-marginal law (option D) is about allocating income across goods, and diminishing returns (option A) concerns production.

questions.question: After a long walk in the sun, a student drinks sachets of water one after the other. The first sachet gives great relief, the second gives less, and the fourth gives very little extra satisfaction. This illustrates

options.d: The law of diminishing marginal utility

questions.explanation: Each additional sachet adds less satisfaction than the one before, which is the law of diminishing marginal utility. Option B refers to money, not water, consumer surplus (option C) compares willingness to pay with price paid, and the equi-marginal law (option A) involves choosing between two or more goods.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a condition for the law of diminishing marginal utility to hold?

options.c: There must be a long time gap between the consumption of successive units

questions.explanation: The law requires that units be consumed one after another without a significant time gap, so a long gap is the opposite of a condition. Identical units (option B), rational consumers (option A) and continuous consumption (option D) are genuine conditions for the law to hold.

questions.question: Chidi eats a plate of amala at 8 a.m. and a second identical plate at 7 p.m., and enjoys the second as much as the first. The law of diminishing marginal utility fails here mainly because which condition is not met?

options.b: Consumption must be continuous, without a significant time gap
options.c: Utility must be measurable in utils
options.d: The marginal utility of money must be constant

questions.explanation: The two plates were eaten eleven hours apart, so consumption was not continuous and Chidi's appetite returned. Option A is met because the plates are identical, and options D and C are assumptions of cardinal theory that do not explain why the second plate was equally satisfying.

questions.question: When marginal utility is positive but falling, total utility
questions.explanation: Each extra unit still adds something to total utility, but less than before, so total utility rises more and more slowly. Total utility is at its maximum (option C) only when marginal utility is zero, and it decreases (option D) only when marginal utility is negative.

questions.question: If a consumer keeps consuming a good after marginal utility becomes negative, total utility will
questions.explanation: A negative marginal utility means each extra unit reduces satisfaction, so total utility declines. Total utility rises (options C and B) only when marginal utility is positive, and it is at its maximum (option A) when marginal utility is zero.

questions.question: The point on the total utility curve where total utility is highest and marginal utility is zero is called the
questions.explanation: The bliss or saturation point shows the highest level of satisfaction, beyond which further consumption gives negative marginal utility. The break-even and shutdown points (options B and D) belong to the theory of the firm, and the consumer's equilibrium (option A) is where marginal utility equals price, not where it is zero.

questions.question: Under the cardinal approach, with marginal utility measured in naira, a consumer buying a single good X is in equilibrium when
questions.explanation: With utility measured in money, the consumer keeps buying until the satisfaction from the last unit just equals its price, so MUx = Px. Option D (MUx = 0) is the bliss point, which a consumer paying a positive price would not reach, and option A means the consumer can still gain by buying more.

questions.question: Under the cardinal approach, a consumer who spends all income on two goods X and Y is in equilibrium when

options.a: MUx x Px = MUy x Py

questions.explanation: Equilibrium requires that the marginal utility from each good be proportional to its price, so the last naira spent on X gives the same utility as the last naira spent on Y. Option D ignores prices, and options B and A combine utility and price in the wrong way.

questions.question: The principle that a consumer maximises utility by allocating income so that the last naira spent on each good yields the same marginal utility is the
questions.explanation: The law of equi-marginal utility says income is best allocated when marginal utility per naira is equal across all goods. The law of diminishing marginal utility (option D) is about one good's extra units giving less satisfaction; it helps the adjustment but is not the allocation rule itself.

questions.question: If MUx/Px > MUy/Py, the consumer can increase total utility by

options.a: Buying more of X and less of Y
options.b: Buying more of Y and less of X
options.c: Buying more of both X and Y

questions.explanation: A higher MUx/Px means the last naira spent on X gives more satisfaction than the last naira spent on Y, so money should be moved from Y to X. Option B would widen the gap, option C is not possible because income is already fully spent, and option D ignores the gain available.

questions.question: When a consumer with MUx/Px > MUy/Py buys more X and less Y, the ratios move towards equality because

options.a: The law of diminishing marginal utility lowers MUx and raises MUy
options.b: The prices of X and Y adjust to the consumer's purchases
options.c: The marginal utility of money rises as more X is bought
options.d: Total utility from X falls to zero

questions.explanation: By the law of diminishing marginal utility, consuming more X lowers MUx and consuming less Y raises MUy, so the ratios approach each other until equilibrium is restored. Option B is wrong because prices are given to the consumer, and option C contradicts the assumption of constant marginal utility of money.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an assumption of the cardinal analysis of the equilibrium of a consumer buying two goods?

options.a: The consumer spends all of his or her disposable income on the two products
options.b: The market prices Px and Py are given
options.c: The consumer can change the market prices of X and Y by his or her purchases
options.d: The consumer buys only two products, X and Y

questions.explanation: In the analysis the consumer is a price taker, so he or she cannot influence the prices of X and Y. Options D, B and A are the stated assumptions: two goods, given prices and full spending of disposable income.

questions.question: In the cardinal approach, the demand curve slopes downward because

options.a: The marginal utility of money falls as the price falls
options.b: Total utility falls as consumption rises
options.c: The consumer's income rises when the price falls
options.d: Marginal utility falls as consumption rises, so the price the consumer is willing to pay for extra units falls

questions.explanation: The demand curve is the marginal utility curve measured in money: as each extra unit gives less satisfaction, the consumer will pay less for it, so a lower price is needed to sell more. Option B is wrong because total utility keeps rising as long as marginal utility is positive, and option A contradicts the assumption that the marginal utility of money is constant.

questions.question: In the cardinal approach, the consumer's demand curve is derived from the

options.c: Marginal utility curve measured in money terms

questions.explanation: The demand curve comes from the marginal utility curve once marginal utility is expressed in naira, because the consumer buys an extra unit only if its price does not exceed its marginal utility. The total utility curve (option A) shows overall satisfaction, not the value of each extra unit, and the PPC (option D) is about production.

questions.question: Consumer surplus is the difference between

options.a: What a consumer is willing to pay for a good and what the consumer actually pays
options.b: The price of a good and its cost of production
options.d: The consumer's income and total spending

questions.explanation: Consumer surplus is the extra benefit a consumer enjoys because he or she would have paid more than the market price. Option B is the seller's margin, not the buyer's gain, and option D is savings, which has nothing to do with willingness to pay.

questions.question: On a demand (or marginal utility in money) diagram, consumer surplus is shown by the area

options.a: Below the price line up to the quantity bought
options.b: Below the demand curve and above the price line
options.c: Above the demand curve and below the price line

questions.explanation: Consumer surplus is the area under the demand curve (what the consumer is willing to pay) minus what is actually paid, which leaves the area between the demand curve and the price line. Option A is the amount actually spent, and option D is the total willingness to pay before subtracting spending.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a feature of the traditional theory of demand?

options.a: It examines demand in only one market
options.b: It focuses only on the demand of final consumers
options.c: It starts with an examination of consumer behaviour
options.d: It concentrates on the demand for investment goods

questions.explanation: The traditional theory of demand neglects the demand for investment goods, so concentrating on it is not one of its features. Focusing on final consumers (option B), studying one market at a time (option A) and starting from consumer behaviour (option C) are its genuine features.

questions.question: Tola's total utility (in utils) from sticks of suya is: (units, TU) = 1, 10; 2, 18; 3, 24; 4, 28; 5, 30; 6, 30; 7, 28. What is the marginal utility of the 3rd stick?
questions.explanation: Marginal utility of the 3rd stick is the change in total utility: 24 - 18 = 6 utils. Option A is total utility at 3 sticks, option B is either the MU of the 2nd stick or the average utility 24 / 3, and option C is the MU of the 4th stick.

questions.question: Tola's total utility (in utils) from sticks of suya is: (units, TU) = 1, 10; 2, 18; 3, 24; 4, 28; 5, 30; 6, 30; 7, 28. Marginal utility becomes zero at which stick?
questions.explanation: Total utility is 30 at both 5 and 6 sticks, so the 6th stick adds 30 - 30 = 0 utils. The 5th stick (option C) still adds 2 utils, and the 7th stick (option B) has negative marginal utility of -2.

questions.question: Tola's total utility (in utils) from sticks of suya is: (units, TU) = 1, 10; 2, 18; 3, 24; 4, 28; 5, 30; 6, 30; 7, 28. What is the marginal utility of the 7th stick?
questions.explanation: The 7th stick changes total utility from 30 to 28, so its marginal utility is 28 - 30 = -2 utils, showing that consumption has gone past the bliss point. Option D is total utility, option A is the MU of the 6th stick, and option B drops the negative sign.

questions.question: The marginal utilities of the first four oranges a consumer eats are 12, 9, 6 and 3 utils respectively. What is the total utility from the four oranges?
questions.explanation: Total utility is the sum of the marginal utilities of all units consumed: 12 + 9 + 6 + 3 = 30 utils. Option C is only the MU of the 4th orange, option B is only the MU of the first, and option A leaves out the last orange.

questions.question: When a consumer increases consumption of a drink from 4 to 7 bottles, total utility rises from 40 utils to 52 utils. Using MU = change in TU / change in quantity, the marginal utility per bottle over this range is
questions.explanation: MU = change in TU / change in quantity = (52 - 40) / (7 - 4) = 12 / 3 = 4 utils per bottle. Option A forgets to divide by the change in quantity, and option B is average utility (52 / 7), not marginal utility.

questions.question: Bisi's marginal utility, measured in naira, from successive bananas is N100, N80, N60, N40 and N20. If a banana costs N60 and she buys a unit only when its marginal utility is at least equal to its price, how many bananas will she buy?
questions.explanation: She buys each banana whose marginal utility is at least N60, which are the 1st (N100), 2nd (N80) and 3rd (N60); at the 3rd banana MU = P, so she is in equilibrium. Option B stops one unit early, and options D and A include bananas worth less to her than their price.

questions.question: Bisi's marginal utility, measured in naira, from successive bananas is N100, N80, N60, N40 and N20, and she buys a unit only when its marginal utility is at least equal to its price. If the price of a banana falls from N60 to N40, her quantity demanded rises from 3 to
questions.explanation: At N40 she also buys the 4th banana, whose marginal utility is exactly N40, so quantity demanded rises to 4; this is how a falling MU curve gives a downward-sloping demand curve. Option D includes the 5th banana, which is worth only N20 to her, and option C ignores the price fall.

questions.question: Bisi's marginal utility, measured in naira, from successive bananas is N100, N80, N60, N40 and N20. At a price of N40 she buys 4 bananas. Taking consumer surplus as total willingness to pay minus the amount actually paid, her consumer surplus is
questions.explanation: Her total willingness to pay for 4 bananas is 100 + 80 + 60 + 40 = N280 and she actually pays 4 x 40 = N160, so consumer surplus is 280 - 160 = N120. Option D is total willingness to pay and option A is total spending, neither of which is the surplus.

questions.question: A student is willing to pay up to N5,000 for a used scientific calculator but buys it at Yaba market for N3,500. Her consumer surplus is
questions.explanation: Consumer surplus is willingness to pay minus the price actually paid: 5,000 - 3,500 = N1,500. Option B is the price paid, option A is her maximum willingness to pay, and option D wrongly adds the two.

questions.question: A consumer's marginal utility, measured in naira, from the Qth plate of jollof rice is MU = 1000 - 100Q. If a plate costs N600, how many plates will the consumer buy in equilibrium?
questions.explanation: Equilibrium for one good is where MU = P, so 1000 - 100Q = 600, giving 100Q = 400 and Q = 4. Option B uses 600 / 100, option A is where MU would fall to zero (the bliss point), and option D adds a plate worth only N500, less than its price.

questions.question: A consumer's marginal utility, measured in naira, from the Qth plate of jollof rice is MU = 1000 - 100Q, and the consumer buys 4 plates at N600 each. Treating plates as whole units and consumer surplus as total willingness to pay minus total amount paid, the consumer surplus is
questions.explanation: Willingness to pay for plates 1 to 4 is 900 + 800 + 700 + 600 = N3,000, and the amount paid is 4 x 600 = N2,400, so consumer surplus is 3,000 - 2,400 = N600. Option D is total willingness to pay, option B is total spending, and option C is only the surplus on the first plate (900 - 600).

questions.question: For a consumer, the last unit of X bought gives 30 utils and costs N10, while the last unit of Y bought gives 40 utils and costs N20. To increase total utility with the same income, the consumer should

options.a: Buy more Y and less X
options.c: Make no change because MUy > MUx
options.d: Buy more X and less Y

questions.explanation: MUx/Px = 30 / 10 = 3 utils per naira while MUy/Py = 40 / 20 = 2 utils per naira, so a naira moved from Y to X adds satisfaction. Option A and option C compare marginal utilities without dividing by prices, which is the common mistake.

questions.question: At a consumer's present purchases, MUx = 24 utils, Px = N8 and MUy = 36 utils. For the consumer to be in equilibrium, the price of Y must be
questions.explanation: Equilibrium requires MUx/Px = MUy/Py, so 24 / 8 = 36 / Py, giving 3 = 36 / Py and Py = N12. Option C wrongly assumes the prices must be equal, option B inverts the utilities (24 x 8 / 36), and option A divides MUy by Px (36 / 8).

questions.question: A consumer in equilibrium buys X at N10 and Y at N4. If the marginal utility of the last unit of X is 50 utils, the marginal utility of the last unit of Y must be
questions.explanation: In equilibrium MUx/Px = MUy/Py, so 50 / 10 = MUy / 4, giving MUy = 5 x 4 = 20 utils. Option D multiplies by the wrong price ratio (50 x 10 / 4), option A ignores prices, and option C is only the MU per naira of X.

questions.question: The equi-marginal condition extends to three goods as MUx/Px = MUy/Py = MUz/Pz. A consumer in equilibrium pays N2 for X, N4 for Y and N6 for Z. If MUx = 10 utils, what is MUz?
questions.explanation: MUx/Px = 10 / 2 = 5 utils per naira, so MUz = 5 x 6 = 30 utils (and MUy = 5 x 4 = 20 utils). Option C is MUy, option B wrongly sets marginal utilities equal, and option A multiplies MUx by Pz without dividing by Px.

questions.question: In the cardinal approach, a consumer of a single good X is in equilibrium when MUx = Px x MUm, where MUm is the constant marginal utility of money. If MUm = 2 utils per naira and Px = N15, the marginal utility of the last unit of X bought is
questions.explanation: Using the stated condition, MUx = Px x MUm = 15 x 2 = 30 utils. Option C divides instead of multiplying, option D adds the two figures, and option B ignores the marginal utility of money.

questions.question: Emeka has N20 to spend on X (price N4) and Y (price N2). His marginal utilities (in utils) for successive units are: X: 40, 32, 24, 16, 8; Y: 24, 20, 16, 12, 8, 4. To maximise utility while spending all N20, how many units of X should he buy?
questions.explanation: MU per naira for X is 10, 8, 6, 4, 2 and for Y is 12, 10, 8, 6, 4, 2; the ratios are equal at 6 when he buys 3 X and 4 Y, which costs 3 x 4 + 4 x 2 = N20. Option A (2 X with 6 Y) and option B (4 X with 2 Y) also cost N20 but give only 156 utils instead of 168, and option D (5 X) leaves no money for Y.

questions.question: Emeka has N20 to spend on X (price N4) and Y (price N2). His marginal utilities (in utils) for successive units are: X: 40, 32, 24, 16, 8; Y: 24, 20, 16, 12, 8, 4. In his utility-maximising equilibrium, how many units of Y does he buy?
questions.explanation: At 3 X and 4 Y, MUx/Px = 24 / 4 = 6 and MUy/Py = 12 / 2 = 6, and spending is 12 + 8 = N20, so both conditions hold. Option A (3 Y) leaves N2 unspent, option D (6 Y) forces him down to 2 X and lower total utility, and option B (5 Y) together with 3 X would cost N22, more than his income.

questions.question: Emeka has N20 to spend on X (price N4) and Y (price N2). His marginal utilities (in utils) for successive units are: X: 40, 32, 24, 16, 8; Y: 24, 20, 16, 12, 8, 4. What is his total utility at the utility-maximising combination?
questions.explanation: At equilibrium he buys 3 X and 4 Y, so total utility is (40 + 32 + 24) + (24 + 20 + 16 + 12) = 96 + 72 = 168 utils. Option D (156) is the total for the other affordable combinations such as 2 X and 6 Y, option C counts only the utility from X, and option A adds only the MUs of the last units bought (24 + 12).

questions.question: Emeka has N20 to spend on X (price N4) and Y (price N2). His marginal utilities (in utils) for successive units are: X: 40, 32, 24, 16, 8; Y: 24, 20, 16, 12, 8, 4. If Emeka buys 2 units of X and 6 units of Y (spending all N20), what should he do to raise his total utility?

options.a: Buy more X and less Y
options.b: Buy more Y and less X

questions.explanation: At 2 X and 6 Y, MUx/Px = 32 / 4 = 8 while MUy/Py = 4 / 2 = 2, so a naira spent on X gives far more satisfaction; he should switch spending from Y to X until the ratios are equal. Option B widens the gap, and option D is impossible because his income is already fully spent.

questions.question: Which of the following total utility schedules, for units 1, 2, 3 and 4 of a good, shows diminishing marginal utility throughout?
questions.explanation: For 10, 18, 24, 28 the marginal utilities are 10, 8, 6 and 4, which fall steadily, as the law of diminishing marginal utility predicts. Option C has constant MU of 10, option B has rising MU (10, 11, 12, 13), and option D has MU of 10, 8, 12, 10, which does not fall throughout.

questions.question: Under the cardinal utility approach, utility is assumed to be

options.a: shown only by the slope of the budget line
options.b: independent of the quantity of the good consumed
options.c: capable only of being ranked in order of preference
options.d: measurable in absolute units such as utils

questions.explanation: Cardinal utility treats satisfaction as something that can be counted, for example 20 utils from one plate of rice. Option C is the ordinal assumption, option A confuses utility with the price ratio, and option B contradicts the idea that utility changes as more of a good is consumed.

questions.question: The optimum point of a utility-maximizing consumer is ______.

options.a: One attainable on low indifference curve
options.b: One unattainable on high indifference curve
options.c: One attainable on high indifference curve
options.d: One unattainable on low indifference curve

questions.explanation: A utility-maximizing consumer reaches equilibrium at the point on the highest indifference curve that can be attained, where the budget line just touches (is tangent to) an indifference curve. Option B is wrong because points on higher curves beyond the budget line cannot be afforded. Option A gives an attainable point on a lower curve, which leaves the consumer less satisfied than he could be.

questions.question: In the ordinal approach to the theory of consumer behaviour, which among the following are objective factors.
questions.explanation: In the ordinal approach, price and income are objective factors because they are external facts that can be measured and are the same for anyone checking them; together they fix the budget line. Taste and preferences (in options A, B and C) are subjective, since they exist in the consumer's own mind and are shown by indifference curves.

questions.question: One of the following is not a property of an indifference curve.

options.a: It slopes downward from left to the right
options.b: It gives the same level of satisfaction at all points on the curve
options.c: It has no shape for some commodities
options.d: Two indifference curves do not intersect

questions.explanation: Every indifference curve has a definite shape: it slopes downward, is convex to the origin, and two curves never cross. Saying it has no shape for some commodities is not a property. Options A, B and D are all genuine properties of indifference curves.

questions.question: Which approach to the theory of consumer adopts the concept of indifference curve?

options.a: Both the ordinal and the cardinal approaches

questions.explanation: The ordinalist approach uses indifference curves, because it only needs consumers to rank bundles of goods, not measure satisfaction in utils. The cardinalist approach (option B) measures utility in numbers and uses total and marginal utility instead. So option A is wrong, and option D, marginalist, is not the approach associated with indifference curves.

questions.question: If she spends all of her income on lemons and tangerines, Isabella can just afford 30 lemons and 8 tangerines per day. She could also use her entire budget to buy 6 lemons and 14 tangerines per day. The price of lemons is N6 each. How much is Isabella's income per day? ______.
questions.explanation: Both bundles cost the whole income, so 30L + 8T = 6L + 14T, which gives 24L = 6T, so one tangerine costs 4 lemons. With lemons at N6, a tangerine costs N24, and income = 30(6) + 8(24) = 180 + 192 = N372; check: 6(6) + 14(24) = 36 + 336 = N372. Option C, N180, counts only the 30 lemons and leaves out the tangerines.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the price consumption curve for a straight-line demand curve extended to both axes? ______.
questions.explanation: Along a straight-line demand curve, demand is elastic on the upper part, unit elastic at the midpoint and inelastic on the lower part. As price falls in the elastic range spending on the good rises, so less money is left for other goods and the price consumption curve falls; at unit elasticity it is flat, and in the inelastic range spending on the good falls, so the curve rises. Options A and B would only hold if demand were elastic or inelastic all the way along, and option D reverses the order.

questions.question: Which property of preferences means "more is always better"?
questions.explanation: Monotonicity is the property that more of a good is always better than less, so a bundle with more of at least one good and no less of the other is preferred. Option A, convexity, is about preferring balanced bundles and gives indifference curves their bowed shape. Option C, transitivity, is about consistency in ranking, and option D, completeness, means the consumer can compare any two bundles.

questions.question: If a consumer gives up some quantity of one good to gain more of another while staying equally satisfied, the indifference curve must be: ______.
questions.explanation: To stay equally satisfied, a consumer who gets more of one good must give up some of the other, so as one quantity rises the other falls. That inverse relationship makes the indifference curve slope downward from left to right. An upward-sloping curve (option B) would mean more of both goods gives the same satisfaction, which goes against more being better, and horizontal or vertical curves (options C and D) would mean one good adds nothing to satisfaction.

questions.question: As a consumer substitutes one good for another, they are willing to give up less and less of the second good. This implies that indifference curves are: ______.
questions.explanation: When a consumer is willing to give up less and less of one good for each extra unit of the other, the marginal rate of substitution is diminishing. A diminishing MRS makes the indifference curve flatter as you move down it, which means it is convex to the origin. Option A, a straight line, would mean a constant MRS (perfect substitutes), and option B, concave, would mean an increasing MRS.

questions.question: If two indifference curves were to cross, it would violate: ______.
questions.explanation: If two indifference curves crossed, the bundle at the crossing point would give the same satisfaction as bundles on both curves, so all those bundles would have to be equally good. But one curve lies above the other elsewhere, so some bundle would be both preferred and equally preferred at the same time, which breaks transitivity of preferences. Option A, the law of demand, and option D, the income effect, are about responses to price and income changes, not the shape of the preference map, and option C, diminishing marginal utility, belongs to the cardinal approach.
