questions.question: Indifference curves typically do not touch the axes because: ______

options.c: One good alone gives maximum satisfaction

questions.explanation: Indifference curves are normally drawn without touching the axes because the consumer is assumed to consume some of both goods, preferring a mix to a bundle of only one good. A point on an axis would mean consuming none of one good. Option C says the opposite of this assumption, and options A and D have nothing to do with the shape of the indifference map.

questions.question: The ordinalist approach to utility focuses on: ______.
questions.explanation: The ordinal approach holds that satisfaction cannot be measured in numbers, but a consumer can rank bundles in order of preference, and indifference curves are built on that ranking. Options A and C describe the cardinal approach, which measures utility in utils and works with total and marginal utility schedules. Option D is wrong because the budget line only shows what the consumer can afford, not how preferences are treated.

questions.question: ______ is a popular analytical tool among the ordinal theorists of consumer behaviour.
questions.explanation: Ordinal theorists rank preferences instead of measuring utility, and the indifference curve is their main tool for showing those rankings. Options A, C and D, the marginal utility schedule, the law of diminishing marginal utility and the total utility curve, are all tools of the cardinal approach, which assumes utility can be measured in utils.

questions.question: Which of the following is a property of an indifference curve?

options.c: Sloping upward from left to right

questions.explanation: Indifference curves are normally convex to the origin, because the marginal rate of substitution diminishes as the consumer moves along the curve. Option C is wrong because indifference curves slope downward, and option D is wrong because two indifference curves can never intersect.

questions.question: A movement from one point to another along an indifference curve makes the satisfaction:
questions.explanation: Every point on an indifference curve gives the consumer the same level of satisfaction, which is why he is indifferent between them. So moving along the curve leaves satisfaction unchanged. Options A and B describe moving to a higher or lower indifference curve.

questions.question: As moving from left to right through an indifference curve, the MRS of X for Y
questions.explanation: As the consumer moves down the indifference curve, getting more X and less Y, he is willing to give up fewer units of Y for each extra unit of X. So the marginal rate of substitution of X for Y diminishes. Option A would mean a concave curve, and option B a straight-line indifference curve.

questions.question: With good X measured on the horizontal axis and good Y on the vertical axis, a horizontal indifference curve indicates that:

options.c: X and Y are perfect substitutes
options.d: X and Y are perfect complements

questions.explanation: A horizontal indifference curve means the consumer stays equally satisfied whatever amount of X he has, as long as Y is unchanged. Good X therefore adds nothing to satisfaction, so it is a neuter. Option B would give a vertical indifference curve, and option C gives a downward-sloping straight line.

questions.question: On a budget line for goods X and Y, if the price of Y alone changes, the X intercept will:
questions.explanation: The X intercept of the budget line is M / Px, the most X the consumer can buy with all his income. It depends only on income and the price of X, so a change in the price of Y alone leaves it unchanged, and the budget line pivots around it. Option D is wrong because a parallel shift happens only when income changes with prices constant.

questions.question: The approach to consumer behaviour which assumes that a consumer can rank bundles of goods in order of preference, but cannot measure satisfaction in absolute units, is called the
questions.explanation: The ordinal approach only requires the consumer to say which bundle she prefers, or that she is indifferent, without attaching numbers to satisfaction. Options A, D and C all belong to the cardinal tradition, which assumes utility can be measured in units such as utils.

questions.question: The main difference between the cardinal and the ordinal approaches to consumer behaviour is that

options.a: ordinal analysis assumes the consumer has unlimited income
options.b: ordinal analysis measures satisfaction in numbers, while cardinal analysis only ranks bundles
options.c: cardinal analysis ignores prices, while ordinal analysis uses prices
options.d: cardinal analysis measures satisfaction in numbers, while ordinal analysis only ranks bundles

questions.explanation: Cardinal theory assumes utility can be quantified, while ordinal theory only needs the consumer to order bundles by preference. Option B reverses the two approaches, option C is false because both use prices, and option A is wrong because ordinal theory uses a budget constraint.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an assumption of the ordinal (indifference curve) theory of consumer behaviour?

options.c: Satisfaction can be measured in utils
options.d: More of a good is preferred to less (non-satiation)

questions.explanation: Ordinal theory deliberately drops the idea that satisfaction can be measured in utils; that is the cardinal assumption. Completeness (B), transitivity (A) and non-satiation (D) are all core assumptions of ordinal theory.

questions.question: The assumption that, for any two bundles A and B, a consumer can always say that she prefers A to B, prefers B to A, or is indifferent between them is called
questions.explanation: Completeness means the consumer is able to compare and rank any pair of bundles. Transitivity (C) is about consistency across three or more bundles, non-satiation (B) means more is preferred to less, and option D describes the shape of indifference curves.

questions.question: Chidi prefers jollof rice to fried rice, and fried rice to ofada rice. For his preferences to be consistent, he must also prefer jollof rice to ofada rice. This requirement is the assumption of
questions.explanation: Transitivity says that if A is preferred to B and B to C, then A must be preferred to C, exactly as with Chidi's rice choices. Completeness (A) only says he can compare any two bundles, non-satiation (C) says more is better, and convexity (B) is about the shape of indifference curves.

questions.question: In ordinal utility theory, the assumption that a consumer always prefers more of a good to less, other things being equal, is known as
questions.explanation: Non-satiation (more is better) means extra units of a good never make the consumer worse off. Completeness (C) and transitivity (B) are about ranking bundles, while diminishing marginal utility (A) is a cardinal idea about utils falling with consumption.

questions.question: A curve showing all combinations of two goods that give a consumer the same level of satisfaction is called
questions.explanation: Every point on an indifference curve gives equal satisfaction, so the consumer is indifferent between them. A budget line (B) shows affordable bundles, a price consumption curve (D) joins equilibrium points as price changes, and an Engel curve (A) relates income to quantity demanded.

questions.question: A set of indifference curves for a consumer, each curve representing a different level of satisfaction, is called
questions.explanation: An indifference map is the whole family of indifference curves, with curves further from the origin showing higher satisfaction. A budget set (C) is the set of affordable bundles, an income consumption curve (D) traces equilibria as income changes, and a demand schedule (B) is a price-quantity table.

questions.question: Indifference curves slope downward from left to right because

options.a: the consumer's income rises as we move along the curve
options.b: to keep satisfaction unchanged, more of one good must be matched by less of the other, given that more is preferred to less
options.c: the prices of both goods fall as we move along the curve
options.d: the marginal rate of substitution rises as more of X is consumed

questions.explanation: If the consumer gets more X and more is always better, she can only stay equally satisfied by giving up some Y, which gives the negative slope. Option D is wrong because MRS falls, not rises, and options C and A are wrong because prices and income do not appear on an indifference curve.

questions.question: An indifference curve is normally convex to the origin because of

options.a: an increasing marginal rate of substitution
options.c: a diminishing marginal rate of substitution
options.d: a constant marginal rate of substitution

questions.explanation: Convexity means the curve becomes flatter as we move down it, which is what a falling MRS of X for Y produces. An increasing MRS (A) would make the curve concave, a constant MRS (D) gives a straight line, and transitivity (B) explains why curves do not cross, not their shape.

questions.question: Two indifference curves of the same consumer cannot intersect because an intersection would

options.a: make the marginal rate of substitution diminish
options.b: mean that the budget line has become vertical
options.c: imply that the same bundle gives two different levels of satisfaction, violating transitivity and non-satiation
options.d: imply that the consumer is in equilibrium at the crossing point

questions.explanation: At a crossing point one bundle would lie on two curves representing different satisfaction levels, which leads to contradictory rankings. Option B is irrelevant because budget lines are separate from preferences, option A describes convexity, and option D confuses an intersection of two indifference curves with tangency to a budget line.

questions.question: A bundle on a higher indifference curve is preferred to a bundle on a lower one because

options.a: the consumer's income is lower on higher curves
options.b: the MRS is constant on higher curves
options.c: bundles on a higher curve always cost less
options.d: a higher curve contains bundles with more of at least one good and no less of the other

questions.explanation: Given non-satiation, moving out to a higher curve means getting more goods, so satisfaction is greater. Option C is wrong because higher curves usually need more spending, option B is not true in general, and option A reverses the link between income and attainable curves.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a property of normal indifference curves?

options.a: They are convex to the origin
options.b: They may intersect when the consumer's tastes are strong
options.c: They slope downward from left to right
options.d: A higher curve represents a higher level of satisfaction

questions.explanation: Indifference curves of one consumer never intersect, because that would break consistent ranking of bundles. Downward slope (C), convexity (A) and higher curves meaning more satisfaction (D) are all standard properties.

questions.question: The rate at which a consumer is willing to give up units of good Y to obtain one more unit of good X while remaining on the same indifference curve is the

options.d: marginal rate of substitution of X for Y

questions.explanation: The marginal rate of substitution measures the consumer's willingness to trade one good for another at constant satisfaction. The marginal rate of transformation (C) is about production, the price ratio (A) is the market rate of exchange shown by the budget line, and marginal utility (B) is the extra satisfaction from one good alone.

questions.question: The marginal rate of substitution of X for Y (MRSxy) is equal to
questions.explanation: Along an indifference curve the utility gained from extra X must equal the utility lost from less Y, so MRSxy = MUx/MUy. Option D is the inverse, giving MRSyx, while options C and A are not ratios of marginal utilities at all.

questions.question: As a consumer moves down an indifference curve, acquiring more X and less Y, MRSxy falls because

options.a: the more X she has relative to Y, the less Y she is willing to give up for an extra unit of X
options.b: the price of X falls as she buys more of it
options.c: X becomes an inferior good at high quantities
options.d: her money income rises as she consumes more X

questions.explanation: When X becomes plentiful and Y scarce, each additional X is worth less to her in terms of Y, so she gives up fewer units of Y for it. Options B and D bring in prices and income, which do not change along an indifference curve, and option C confuses tastes with the income effect.

questions.question: If two goods are perfect substitutes for a consumer, her indifference curves are

options.a: straight downward-sloping lines with a constant MRS
options.b: convex to the origin with a diminishing MRS

questions.explanation: Perfect substitutes are always traded at the same rate, so the MRS is constant and each indifference curve is a straight line. L-shaped curves (D) describe perfect complements, option B describes ordinary goods, and horizontal lines (C) would mean X gives no satisfaction.

questions.question: Bisi regards a 75cl bottle of one brand of table water as exactly as good as a 75cl bottle of another brand, and always swaps them one-for-one. Her indifference curves between the two brands are

options.b: convex curves with a diminishing MRS
options.c: straight lines with a constant MRS of 1

questions.explanation: Since she will always give up one bottle of one brand for one of the other, the two brands are perfect substitutes and the MRS is fixed at 1, giving straight-line indifference curves. L-shaped curves (D) are for goods used in fixed proportions, option B applies to imperfect substitutes, and vertical lines (A) would mean she does not value one brand at all.

questions.question: Goods that are consumed only in fixed proportions, such as left shoes and right shoes, have indifference curves that are
questions.explanation: Extra left shoes add nothing without matching right shoes, so each indifference curve has a corner at the fixed ratio and is L-shaped. Straight lines (B) describe perfect substitutes, while upward-sloping (D) or concave (C) curves break the usual assumptions about preferences.

questions.question: A line showing all combinations of two goods that a consumer can buy when she spends all her income at given prices is called
questions.explanation: The budget line (price line) marks the boundary of what the consumer can afford with her income at given prices. An indifference curve (A) shows equal satisfaction, the income consumption curve (D) traces equilibria as income changes, and the production possibility frontier (B) belongs to production, not consumer theory.

questions.question: If a consumer's money income rises while the prices of both goods remain unchanged, her budget line will

options.a: shift inward parallel to the original line
options.b: shift outward parallel to the original line
options.d: rotate outward about the vertical intercept

questions.explanation: With prices fixed the slope -Px/Py does not change, and higher income raises both intercepts, so the line moves out parallel. A rotation (D) happens when only one price changes, an inward shift (A) follows a fall in income, and a steeper line (C) needs a rise in Px relative to Py.

questions.question: With good X on the horizontal axis, a fall in the price of X, with income and the price of Y unchanged, causes the budget line to

options.a: rotate outward along the Y-axis, keeping the same X-intercept
options.d: rotate outward along the X-axis, keeping the same Y-intercept

questions.explanation: The maximum amount of Y (M/Py) is unchanged, but the maximum amount of X (M/Px) rises, so the line pivots outward on the X-axis and becomes flatter. A parallel shift (C) needs an income change, option B describes a rise in Px, and option A describes a fall in Py.

questions.question: If a consumer's money income and the prices of both goods all double at the same time, her budget line will
questions.explanation: Both intercepts M/Px and M/Py, and the slope -Px/Py, are unchanged when M, Px and Py are multiplied by the same number. Options C and A would need real income to change, and option B would need the price ratio to change.

questions.question: In indifference curve analysis, a consumer maximising satisfaction (with an interior solution) is in equilibrium where
questions.explanation: At equilibrium the rate at which she is willing to swap Y for X (MRSxy) equals the rate at which the market lets her swap them (Px/Py). Option D inverts the price ratio, option C ignores prices, and option A is a statement about prices, not about the consumer's choice.

questions.question: Graphically, the consumer's equilibrium in ordinal analysis occurs

options.a: where the budget line is tangent to the highest attainable indifference curve
options.b: where the budget line meets the X-axis
options.c: on the highest indifference curve in the map, whatever the budget
options.d: where an indifference curve cuts the budget line from above

questions.explanation: The best affordable bundle is on the highest indifference curve the budget line can reach, which it just touches at a tangency point. A point where a curve cuts the line (D) can be improved upon, option C ignores the budget constraint, and the X-intercept (B) is only optimal in special corner cases.

questions.question: A consumer is spending all her income on goods X and Y, but at her current bundle MRSxy is greater than Px/Py. To raise her satisfaction she should

options.b: buy more X and less Y
options.c: buy more Y and less X
options.d: make no change, since all income is already spent

questions.explanation: MRSxy > Px/Py means she values an extra unit of X, in terms of Y, more than the market charges for it, so swapping some Y for X moves her to a higher indifference curve. Option C moves her in the wrong direction, option D ignores the tangency condition, and option A would leave income unspent.

questions.question: The locus of consumer equilibrium points traced out as the price of good X changes, with money income and the price of Y held constant, is the
questions.explanation: The price consumption curve joins the tangency points that result as the budget line rotates when Px changes. The income consumption curve (C) comes from income changes, the Engel curve (B) plots income against quantity, and a budget line (A) is a single affordability constraint.

questions.question: The locus of consumer equilibrium points traced out as money income changes, with the prices of both goods held constant, is the
questions.explanation: The income consumption curve joins the tangency points formed as the budget line shifts in parallel when income changes. The price consumption curve (D) comes from a price change, the demand curve (B) relates price to quantity, and the indifference map (A) shows preferences only.

questions.question: In indifference curve analysis, the individual's demand curve for good X is derived from the
questions.explanation: Each point on the price consumption curve pairs a price of X with the quantity chosen, which gives the demand curve. The income consumption curve (C) gives the Engel curve (A) instead, and the indifference map (D) alone has no prices in it.

questions.question: A curve showing the relationship between a consumer's income and the quantity of a good she demands, with prices held constant, is called
questions.explanation: The Engel curve plots income against quantity demanded and is derived from the income consumption curve. A demand curve (B) plots price against quantity, the price consumption curve (D) shows equilibria as price changes, and an indifference curve (A) shows equal satisfaction.

questions.question: For an inferior good, the Engel curve is

options.a: negatively sloped, since quantity demanded falls as income rises
options.d: positively sloped, since quantity demanded rises as income rises

questions.explanation: An inferior good is bought less as income rises, so its Engel curve slopes downward. Option D describes a normal good, option C would mean quantity never responds to income, and option B confuses income with price on the vertical axis.

questions.question: With X on the horizontal axis, the income consumption curve bends back towards the Y-axis as income rises. This shows that

options.a: X is a necessity with positive income elasticity

questions.explanation: A curve bending towards the Y-axis means less X is bought at higher incomes, which is the definition of an inferior good, while Y is still rising and so normal. Option C gets the goods the wrong way round, and options D and A are both normal goods whose consumption rises with income.

questions.question: Ngozi has N2,000 a week to spend on boli (X) at N100 each and packs of groundnut (Y) at N50 each. What is the maximum quantity of boli she can buy?
questions.explanation: Spending all N2,000 on boli gives M/Px = 2,000/100 = 20, the X-intercept of her budget line. Option B divides by the price of groundnut instead, option D divides by the sum of both prices, and option A is just the price ratio Px/Py.

questions.question: A student has N3,600 to spend on bread (X) at N120 per loaf and sachets of milk (Y) at N90 each. With Y on the vertical axis, what is the vertical intercept of the budget line?
questions.explanation: The vertical intercept is the most Y she can buy, M/Py = 3,600/90 = 40. Option B uses the price of bread (3,600/120 = 30), option A divides by both prices added together, and option C is only the price ratio 120/90.

questions.question: A consumer with an income of N1,500 buys X at N150 and Y at N50. With Y on the vertical axis, the slope of her budget line is
questions.explanation: The slope is -Px/Py = -150/50 = -3, meaning one more unit of X costs her 3 units of Y. Option D inverts the price ratio, while options A and C are the Y-intercept (30) and X-intercept (10) mistaken for the slope.

questions.question: Ngozi's income is N2,000, the price of X is N100 and the price of Y is N50. Which equation describes her budget line with Y on the vertical axis?
questions.explanation: From 100X + 50Y = 2,000, dividing by 50 gives Y = 40 - 2X, so the intercept is M/Py = 40 and the slope is -Px/Py = -2. Option C uses the X-intercept as the vertical intercept, while options B and D invert the price ratio.

questions.question: A consumer has income N2,000; Px = N100 and Py = N50. If her income rises to N3,000 with prices unchanged, the new maximum quantity of X she can buy is
questions.explanation: The new X-intercept is 3,000/100 = 30, and since prices have not changed the budget line shifts out parallel. Option B is the old intercept, option A is the new Y-intercept (3,000/50), and option D is the old Y-intercept.

questions.question: With income N2,000, Px = N100 and Py = N50, the price of X falls to N50. What are the new X-intercept and Y-intercept of the budget line?
questions.explanation: The new X-intercept is 2,000/50 = 40, while the Y-intercept stays at 2,000/50 = 40 because Py and income are unchanged; the line rotates outward on the X-axis. Option B is the original line, and options A and C wrongly change the Y-intercept.

questions.question: Emeka has N2,000 and buys 12 units of X at N100 each and 15 units of Y at N50 each. How much of his income is left unspent?
questions.explanation: The bundle costs 12 x 100 + 15 x 50 = 1,200 + 750 = N1,950, so N50 is left and the bundle lies just inside the budget line. Option A assumes it is on the line, option D is the cost of the bundle rather than what is left, and option C comes from an arithmetic slip.

questions.question: A consumer's budget line cuts the X-axis at 25 units and the Y-axis at 50 units. If the price of Y is N40, what is the price of X?
questions.explanation: Income is 50 x N40 = N2,000 (the Y-intercept times Py), and since the X-intercept is M/Px, Px = 2,000/25 = N80. Option D assumes the two prices are equal, option C inverts the ratio of intercepts, and option B confuses the Y-intercept with a price.

questions.question: With income N2,000, Px = N100 and Py = N50, the price of X rises to N200. With Y on the vertical axis, the slope of the new budget line is
questions.explanation: The new slope is -Px/Py = -200/50 = -4, steeper than the original -2, because X is now dearer relative to Y. Option D ignores the price change, option C inverts the price ratio, and option A has no basis in the figures.

questions.question: Tolu's utility function is U = XY. Her income is N1,200, the price of X is N20 and the price of Y is N30. Using MRSxy = Y/X = Px/Py and her budget constraint, how many units of X does she buy in equilibrium?
questions.explanation: Y/X = 20/30 gives 30Y = 20X, so she spends equal amounts on each good; 20X = 600 gives X = 30 (and Y = 20). Option C spends the whole income on X, option A is the quantity of Y, and option B divides income by the sum of prices.

questions.question: A consumer has U = XY, income N900, Px = N15 and Py = N45. In equilibrium (MRSxy = Y/X = Px/Py) she buys how many units of Y?
questions.explanation: With U = XY she spends half her income on each good, so 45Y = 450 and Y = 10 (while X = 30). Option B spends the whole N900 on Y, option A is the quantity of X, and option D divides income by Px + Py.

questions.question: Tolu has U = XY, income N1,200, Px = N20 and Py = N30. What is the maximum level of utility she can reach?
questions.explanation: Her equilibrium is X = 30 and Y = 20, so U = 30 x 20 = 600. Option B confuses utility with income, option A halves the correct answer, and option C adds X and Y instead of multiplying them.

questions.question: For the utility function U = XY, MRSxy = MUx/MUy = Y/X. What is MRSxy at the bundle X = 4, Y = 10?
questions.explanation: MUx = Y and MUy = X, so MRSxy = Y/X = 10/4 = 2.5: she would give up 2.5 units of Y for one more X. Option D is X/Y, the inverse, option B is the utility level XY, and option A is X + Y.

questions.question: A consumer with U = XY (so MRSxy = Y/X) has N300, buys X at N10 and Y at N20, and currently consumes 10 X and 10 Y. Which statement is correct?

options.a: MRSxy = 1 exceeds Px/Py = 0.5, so she should buy more X and less Y
options.b: MRSxy = 1 exceeds Px/Py = 0.5, so she should buy more Y and less X
options.c: MRSxy equals Px/Py, so she is already in equilibrium
options.d: MRSxy = 1 is less than Px/Py = 2, so she should buy more Y and less X

questions.explanation: MRSxy = 10/10 = 1 while Px/Py = 10/20 = 0.5, so she values X more highly than the market price ratio and gains by switching spending towards X. Option B moves the wrong way, option C ignores the gap between the two ratios, and option D inverts the price ratio.

questions.question: A consumer has U = XY, so her demand for X is X = M/(2Px). With Px = N10 and Py = N5, her income rises from N200 to N400. Along her income consumption curve, her purchase of X rises from 10 units to
questions.explanation: At M = 400, X = 400/(2 x 10) = 20, so X doubles as income doubles and X is a normal good. Option D uses M/Px and forgets that half of income goes on Y, option C assumes no change, and option B has no basis in the formula.

questions.question: A consumer has U = XY, so X = M/(2Px). Her income is N600 and Py = N10. If the price of X falls from N30 to N20, her quantity of X along the price consumption curve rises from 10 to
questions.explanation: At Px = 20, X = 600/(2 x 20) = 15, up from 600/60 = 10, which is one point on her downward-sloping demand curve. Option B is M/Px without halving, option D assumes no response, and option A is a miscalculation.

questions.question: A consumer with utility U = XY maximises utility subject to Px.X + Py.Y = M. Her demand function for X is
questions.explanation: Setting MRSxy = Y/X equal to Px/Py gives Px.X = Py.Y, so she spends half of M on X and X = M/(2Px). Option C spends all income on X, option D doubles it, and option A wrongly buys equal quantities of both goods.

questions.question: A consumer has U = XY and an income of N5,000. Whatever the prices, how much will she spend on good X in equilibrium?

options.b: It cannot be found without the prices

questions.explanation: With U = XY the tangency condition gives Px.X = Py.Y, so exactly half of income, N2,500, is spent on X whatever the prices. Option D spends all income on X, option C is a quarter of income, and option B misses that the spending share is fixed for this utility function.

questions.question: Kemi always takes one cup of tea with exactly one sachet of milk, so U = min(X, Y), where X is cups of tea and Y is sachets of milk. Her income is N1,200, tea costs N40 a cup and milk N20 a sachet. How many cups of tea does she buy?
questions.explanation: For perfect complements she buys equal quantities, so 40X + 20X = 1,200 gives X = Y = 20. Option B spends all income on tea, option D spends it all on milk, and option A halves the correct answer.

questions.question: A consumer treats brands X and Y of garri as perfect substitutes, U = X + Y. Her income is N2,000, X costs N50 a cup and Y costs N40 a cup. Her utility-maximising bundle is
questions.explanation: With perfect substitutes exchanged one-for-one she buys only the cheaper brand, so she spends N2,000 on Y at N40, getting 50 cups (utility 50). Option C buys only the dearer brand (utility 40), option B splits equally (utility 44.4), and option D gives utility 45, all lower.

questions.question: A consumer is indifferent between the bundles (X=1, Y=20), (X=2, Y=14), (X=3, Y=10) and (X=4, Y=8). What is MRSxy when moving from the third bundle to the fourth?
questions.explanation: Moving from (3, 10) to (4, 8) she gives up 2 units of Y for 1 more X, so MRSxy = 2; the values 6, 4, 2 show a diminishing MRS. Option C is the MRS for the first move, option A is for the second move, and option D is the quantity of Y in the fourth bundle.

questions.question: A consumer has U = XY, so X = M/(2Px). If Px = N25, which equation is her Engel curve for X?
questions.explanation: Substituting Px = 25 gives X = M/(2 x 25) = M/50, a straight upward-sloping line through the origin, showing X is a normal good. Option C forgets the 2, option B multiplies instead of dividing, and option D would make X fall as income rises.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: The income effect of a price increase of a normal good is to ______ of that good, and the substitution effect is to ______ of that good.

options.a: Increase quantity demanded, reduce quantity demanded
options.b: Increase quantity demanded, increase quantity demanded
options.c: Reduce quantity demanded, reduce quantity demanded
options.d: Reduce quantity demanded, increase quantity demanded

questions.explanation: For a normal good, a price rise makes the good relatively dearer, so the substitution effect reduces quantity demanded, and it also lowers real income, which reduces purchases of a normal good too. Both effects work in the same direction, which is why a normal good has a downward-sloping demand curve. Option A pairs a falling substitution effect with a rising income effect, which is the inferior-good case, while options B and D wrongly make the substitution effect raise quantity after a price rise.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: Which of the following describes the substitution effect when the price of a commodity falls? ______.
questions.explanation: The substitution effect is measured along the original indifference curve, holding real income constant. When the price of a good falls it becomes relatively cheaper, so the consumer moves down the same indifference curve towards more of that good. Option D, moving to a higher curve, is what the income effect does, and options A and B describe the wrong direction or a fall in welfare.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: Consumer surplus is the difference between ______ and ______.

options.a: Willingness to pay and market price
options.b: Market price and cost of production

questions.explanation: Consumer surplus is the gap between the most a consumer is willing to pay for a good and the price actually paid in the market. If you would pay N500 for a plate of food but the price is N350, your consumer surplus is N150. Option B describes the producer's side, and option D, revenue minus profit, gives total cost, not consumer surplus.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: Consumer surplus on a demand-supply graph is the area: ______.

options.a: Below the demand curve and above the price
options.b: Above the demand curve and below the price
options.c: Above the supply curve and below the price

questions.explanation: Consumer surplus is shown as the area below the demand curve and above the market price, up to the quantity bought. The demand curve shows what consumers are willing to pay for each unit, and the price line shows what they actually pay, so the gap between them is their surplus. Option C, the area above the supply curve and below the price, is producer surplus, and option B reverses the correct position.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: If the market price of a good increases, consumer surplus will: ______.
questions.explanation: Consumer surplus is the gap between what consumers are willing to pay and the market price. When the price rises, that gap shrinks and fewer units are bought, so consumer surplus decreases. Option D is wrong because surplus only disappears if the price rises to the highest amount any consumer would pay, not always.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: Consumer surplus is mainly used in microeconomics to measure: ______.
questions.explanation: Consumer surplus measures the benefit consumers get over and above what they pay, so it is used to measure consumer welfare, for example to judge how a tax or price change affects buyers. Options B and C are wrong because government revenue and national income are measured with different tools, and option A concerns producers, not consumers.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: The curve showing the quantity of a good that would be purchased at various income levels:
questions.explanation: An Engel curve plots the quantity of a good bought against the consumer's income. Option A, the income consumption curve, is drawn on an indifference map and joins the equilibrium combinations of two goods as income changes, so it is related but is not a direct plot of quantity against income.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: Substitution Effect is:
questions.explanation: The substitution effect always moves quantity demanded in the opposite direction to the price change: a cheaper good is always substituted for others. That is why it is described as always negative. Options B and C are wrong because, unlike the income effect, the substitution effect never changes sign.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: The demand curve for a Giffen good has:
questions.explanation: A Giffen good is an inferior good whose negative income effect is strong enough to outweigh the substitution effect, so quantity demanded rises when price rises and the demand curve slopes upward. A negative slope (option C) is the normal case under the law of demand, which Giffen goods violate.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a normal good from an inferior good?

options.a: A normal good is a necessity, while an inferior good is a luxury
options.b: Demand for a normal good falls when income rises, while demand for an inferior good rises when income rises
options.c: Demand for a normal good rises when income rises, while demand for an inferior good falls when income rises
options.d: A normal good obeys the law of demand, while an inferior good always has an upward-sloping demand curve

questions.explanation: The difference lies in how demand responds to income: buyers want more of a normal good as they get richer, but switch away from an inferior good (for example, cheaper staples) as income rises. Option B reverses the two, and option D is wrong because most inferior goods still have downward-sloping demand curves; only Giffen goods slope upward. Option A is wrong because necessities and luxuries are both normal goods.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: When the price of a normal good falls, how are its substitution effect and income effect related?

options.a: Both effects increase the quantity demanded, so the income effect reinforces the substitution effect
options.b: The income effect increases quantity demanded but the substitution effect reduces it
options.c: The substitution effect increases quantity demanded but the income effect reduces it
options.d: Both effects reduce the quantity demanded

questions.explanation: A price fall makes the good relatively cheaper, so the substitution effect raises quantity demanded; it also raises real income, and for a normal good higher real income raises demand too, so the two effects work in the same direction. Option C describes an inferior good, where the income effect works against the substitution effect. Option B is wrong because the substitution effect of a price fall always raises quantity demanded, never reduces it.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: In indifference curve analysis, the total effect of a change in the price of a good on its quantity demanded (the price effect) can be split into

options.a: a substitution effect and a scale effect
options.b: a substitution effect and an income effect
options.c: a price effect and an Engel effect
options.d: an income effect and an output effect

questions.explanation: A price change alters both relative prices and the consumer's real income, so the total change is the substitution effect plus the income effect. Options D and A borrow terms from the theory of the firm, and option C is circular because the price effect is the total being decomposed.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: The change in quantity demanded of a good that results only from a change in its relative price, with the consumer's real income held constant, is the
questions.explanation: Holding real income constant means keeping the consumer on her original indifference curve, so the only influence left is the change in relative prices, which is the substitution effect. The income effect (C) holds relative prices constant instead, the price effect (A) is the total change, and option D is not a component of the decomposition.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: The change in quantity demanded of a good that results from a change in the consumer's real income, with relative prices held constant, is the
questions.explanation: The income effect captures how a change in purchasing power alone alters consumption, shown by a parallel shift of the budget line. The substitution effect (C) holds real income constant, option B applies only to consumers who sell goods they own, and the compensating variation (A) is a sum of money, not a change in quantity.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: In the indifference curve diagram of a price fall, the substitution effect is measured as a movement

options.b: along the price consumption curve from the old to the new equilibrium
options.c: along the new, higher indifference curve

questions.explanation: The substitution effect rotates the budget line around the original indifference curve to the new price slope, so it is a movement along that curve from E0 to E1. Options C and D point to the higher curve and the parallel shift between budget lines, which belong to the income effect, and option B is the total price effect from E0 to E2.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: In the decomposition of a price change, the income effect is shown by

options.a: a movement along the original indifference curve
options.b: a parallel shift of the budget line from the compensated line to the actual new line
options.c: a change in the slope of the indifference curves
options.d: a rotation of the budget line around the original indifference curve

questions.explanation: The income effect keeps relative prices fixed, so it is shown by a parallel shift between the compensated and the actual new budget line, moving the consumer from E1 to E2. Options D and A describe the substitution effect, and option C would mean tastes had changed.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: After the price of X falls, a hypothetical budget line is drawn parallel to the new budget line but just tangent to the original indifference curve. This line is called the
questions.explanation: The compensated budget line shows the new relative prices but with enough income taken away to leave the consumer on her original indifference curve, which isolates the substitution effect. The income consumption curve (D) and Engel curve (C) trace income changes, and the original budget line (A) has the old price slope.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: The difference between the Hicks and Slutsky approaches to separating income and substitution effects is that

options.a: Hicks applies only to normal goods, while Slutsky applies only to inferior goods
options.b: Hicks keeps the consumer on her original indifference curve, while Slutsky lets her just afford her original bundle
options.c: Slutsky keeps the consumer on her original indifference curve, while Hicks lets her just afford her original bundle
options.d: Hicks holds money income constant, while Slutsky holds the price of the good constant

questions.explanation: Hicks compensates so that the original level of satisfaction (utility) is kept, while Slutsky compensates so that the original bundle is just affordable at the new prices (constant purchasing power). Option C swaps the two, option D misdescribes both, and option A is false because both methods apply to any good.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: In the Slutsky approach, the compensated budget line has the new price ratio and passes through

options.b: the bundle the consumer bought before the price change
options.c: the point where the new indifference curve meets the Y-axis
options.d: the bundle the consumer buys after the price change

questions.explanation: Slutsky removes just enough income for the consumer to be able to buy her original bundle at the new prices, so the compensated line goes through that bundle. Option D is the final equilibrium, while options A and C have no role in the construction.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: After the price of X falls and the Slutsky compensation is made, the consumer generally ends up

options.a: on an indifference curve at least as high as the original one
options.b: on the new budget line without any compensation
options.c: on an indifference curve below the original one
options.d: at her original bundle in every case

questions.explanation: She can still afford her original bundle, but with the new relative prices she usually prefers to substitute towards X, reaching a slightly higher indifference curve; Hicks, by contrast, keeps her exactly on the original curve. Option C is impossible since the old bundle is affordable, option D ignores substitution, and option B ignores the compensation.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: The substitution effect of a fall in the price of good X, holding real income constant, always

options.a: increases the quantity demanded of X
options.b: decreases the quantity demanded of X
options.c: depends on whether X is normal or inferior
options.d: leaves the quantity demanded of X unchanged

questions.explanation: More is always consumed of the good whose relative price has fallen, so the substitution effect moves quantity in the opposite direction to the price change. Options B and D contradict this, and option C describes the income effect, whose direction does depend on the type of good.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: The substitution effect always works in the opposite direction to the price change because

options.a: the demand curve always slopes downward
options.b: indifference curves are convex to the origin
options.d: the good is always a normal good

questions.explanation: With convex indifference curves, rotating the budget line around the original curve to a flatter slope (cheaper X) must move the tangency towards more X. Option D is wrong because the result holds for inferior goods too, option C confuses money with real income, and option A is a result to be explained, not a cause.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: A good is a normal good when, for a fall in its price,

options.a: the income effect works against the substitution effect but is smaller
options.c: the income effect works against the substitution effect and is larger
options.d: the income effect reinforces the substitution effect

questions.explanation: For a normal good the rise in real income from the price fall raises consumption further, so both effects increase quantity demanded. Option A describes an inferior good that is not Giffen, option C describes a Giffen good, and option B cannot happen with convex indifference curves.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: For an inferior good, the income effect of a fall in its price

options.b: reinforces the substitution effect, raising quantity demanded
options.d: works against the substitution effect, reducing quantity demanded

questions.explanation: An inferior good is bought less as real income rises, so the income effect of a price fall is negative and offsets part of the positive substitution effect. Option B is the normal-good case, option C is false, and option A is only true of the special Giffen case.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: An inferior good that is not a Giffen good still has a downward-sloping demand curve because

options.b: the income effect is larger than the substitution effect
options.c: the substitution effect is larger than the negative income effect
options.d: both effects increase quantity demanded when price falls

questions.explanation: When the negative income effect is smaller, the substitution effect dominates and a price fall still raises quantity demanded on balance. Option B describes a Giffen good, option D describes a normal good, and option A is not what makes a good inferior.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: A good for which a fall in price leads to a fall in quantity demanded, because a strong negative income effect outweighs the substitution effect, is called
questions.explanation: A Giffen good has an upward-sloping demand curve because its negative income effect is bigger than the substitution effect. Normal (B) and luxury (A) goods have positive income effects that reinforce the substitution effect, and option D describes a shape of indifference curve, not a demand response.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a condition usually needed for a good to be a Giffen good?

options.b: The good has few close substitutes, so the substitution effect is small
options.c: Spending on the good takes a large share of the consumer's budget
options.d: The good is a luxury with a high positive income elasticity

questions.explanation: A Giffen good needs a large negative income effect and a small substitution effect, so a luxury, which has a large positive income effect, cannot be Giffen. Strong inferiority (A), a large budget share (C) and few substitutes (B) are exactly the conditions that make the negative income effect dominate.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: Which of the following statements about inferior and Giffen goods is correct?

options.a: Every inferior good is a Giffen good
options.b: Every Giffen good is inferior, but not every inferior good is a Giffen good
options.c: Giffen goods are normal goods with a strong income effect
options.d: A Giffen good has a substitution effect that raises quantity when price rises

questions.explanation: A Giffen good must have a negative income effect, so it is inferior, but most inferior goods have income effects too small to outweigh substitution. Option A reverses the relationship, option C contradicts the negative income effect, and option D is wrong because the substitution effect always moves opposite to price.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: A very poor household in a Nigerian village spends most of its income on garri. When the price of garri rises, the household cuts out meat altogether and buys more garri to avoid going hungry. For this household, garri is behaving as
questions.explanation: Quantity demanded rises with price because the large fall in real income forces the household to drop dearer foods and rely more on the cheap staple, which is the Giffen case. A normal good (A) or a luxury (B) would be bought less after a price rise, and option C would make the household switch completely towards the now relatively cheaper meat.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: The main reason the demand curve for most goods slopes downward is that

options.b: the substitution effect is always smaller than the income effect
options.c: the substitution effect always raises quantity when price falls, and for normal goods the income effect adds to it
options.d: the income effect of a price fall is always negative

questions.explanation: A price fall always makes the good relatively cheaper, raising quantity through substitution, and for normal goods the rise in real income adds to this; even for most inferior goods substitution still dominates. Option D is only true of inferior goods, option A is unrealistic, and option B would point towards the Giffen case.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: After a fall in the price of X, a consumer moves from E0 (quantity q0) to E1 (quantity q1) by the substitution effect and then to E2 (quantity q2) by the income effect. Which ordering of quantities indicates a Giffen good?
questions.explanation: In the Giffen case the negative income effect pulls quantity back past the starting point, so the final quantity q2 is below q0 even though substitution raised it to q1. Option B shows a normal good, option D shows an inferior but non-Giffen good, and option A would need a substitution effect in the wrong direction.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: After a fall in the price of X, the quantities at E0, E1 and E2 are q0, q1 and q2, with q0 < q2 < q1. Good X is

options.a: a good with a zero substitution effect
options.d: an inferior good that is not a Giffen good

questions.explanation: The substitution effect raises quantity from q0 to q1, then a negative income effect reduces it to q2, but q2 is still above q0, so demand slopes downward. A normal good (C) would have q2 beyond q1, a Giffen good (B) would have q2 below q0, and option A contradicts the rise from q0 to q1.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: After a fall in the price of X, the quantities at E0, E1 and E2 are q0, q1 and q2, with q0 < q1 < q2. This shows that X is

options.c: a good whose income effect is negative
options.d: an inferior good that is not Giffen

questions.explanation: Both moves increase quantity: substitution from q0 to q1 and income from q1 to q2, so the income effect reinforces the substitution effect, which is a normal good. Options D, B and C all involve a negative income effect, which would put q2 to the left of q1.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: Hairdressers sell haircuts. If the price of haircuts rises, with all other prices constant, a hairdresser is likely to experience

options.a: a negative income effect, because haircuts are now dearer
options.c: a substitution effect towards buying more haircuts
options.d: a positive income effect, because her income from selling haircuts rises

questions.explanation: For someone who sells a good, a rise in its price raises her income, so the endowment income effect is positive and she can buy more of all normal goods. Option A applies to ordinary buyers of haircuts, option B ignores her extra earnings, and option C is wrong because a dearer good is substituted away from.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: After the price of a good falls, the amount of income that must be taken away from the consumer to return her to her original indifference curve is the
questions.explanation: The compensating variation works with the new prices and asks how much money must be removed to leave her just as well off as before the price fall. The equivalent variation (B) works with the original prices, consumer surplus (A) is the area under the demand curve, and the substitution effect (D) is a change in quantity, not a sum of money.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: The change in income, at the original prices, that would leave a consumer just as well off as a specific fall in the price of a good is the
questions.explanation: The equivalent variation asks how much extra income, instead of the price fall, would raise her to the new indifference curve; it is found by shifting the original budget line out parallel. The compensating variation (B) is measured at the new prices back to the old curve, the income effect (D) is a quantity change, and option C is the income adjustment that keeps the old bundle affordable.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: For a fall in the price of good X, which statement correctly compares the compensating variation (CV) and the equivalent variation (EV)?

options.a: CV uses the original prices and the new indifference curve; EV uses the new prices and the original indifference curve
options.b: CV uses the new prices and the original indifference curve; EV uses the original prices and the new indifference curve
options.c: Both CV and EV are measured at the original prices along the original indifference curve
options.d: CV is a change in quantity demanded, while EV is a change in income

questions.explanation: CV shifts the new budget line back until it touches the old indifference curve, while EV shifts the old budget line out until it touches the new one. Option A swaps the two, option C would give zero for both, and option D is wrong because both are sums of money.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: The demand for suya in a Yaba neighbourhood is P = 100 - 2Q, where P is in naira per stick. If the market price is N40, consumer surplus is
questions.explanation: At P = 40, Q = (100 - 40)/2 = 30, and consumer surplus is the triangle 0.5 x 30 x (100 - 40) = N900. Option B forgets the one-half, option A is total spending (30 x 40), and option D uses the price instead of the gap between the intercept and the price.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: Funke is willing to pay N500 for her first plate of amala, N400 for the second, N300 for the third and N200 for the fourth. If a plate costs N250, her consumer surplus is
questions.explanation: She buys 3 plates, since the fourth is worth only N200, and her surplus is (500 - 250) + (400 - 250) + (300 - 250) = N450. Option C wrongly includes the fourth plate (a loss of N50), option B is her total willingness to pay for three plates, and option D is what she spends.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: Demand is P = 100 - 2Q. If the price falls from N40 to N20, by how much does consumer surplus increase?
questions.explanation: Quantity rises from 30 to 40, and consumer surplus rises from 0.5 x 30 x 60 = N900 to 0.5 x 40 x 80 = N1,600, an increase of N700. Option B is the new surplus, option C is the old surplus, and option D counts only the saving on the first 30 units (30 x 20) and leaves out the gain on the 10 extra units.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: A consumer's demand for sachet water is Q = 200 - 4P. At a price of N30 per sachet, her consumer surplus is
questions.explanation: At P = 30, Q = 80, and the demand curve meets the price axis at P = 50, so consumer surplus is 0.5 x 80 x (50 - 30) = N800. Option C forgets the one-half, option B is total spending (80 x 30), and option A uses the price 30 instead of the gap 50 - 30.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: A consumer has U = XY, income N80 and Py = N1, so her demands are X = M/(2Px) and Y = M/(2Py). The price of X falls from N4 to N1, raising her purchase of X from 10 to 40. Using the Hicks approach (compensating her back to her original utility of 400), the substitution effect on X is
questions.explanation: To keep U = 400 at the new prices she needs income M with (M/2)(M/2) = 400, so M = N40 and X = 40/2 = 20; the Hicks substitution effect is 20 - 10 = 10. Option C is the total effect, option A is the income effect, and option B is the Slutsky substitution effect, not the Hicks one.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: A consumer has U = XY, income N80 and Py = N1, so her demands are X = M/(2Px) and Y = M/(2Py). The price of X falls from N4 to N1, raising her purchase of X from 10 to 40. Using the Hicks approach (compensating her back to her original utility of 400), the income effect on X is
questions.explanation: On the compensated budget line she buys 20 units of X; restoring her full income of N80 raises this to 40, so the income effect is 40 - 20 = 20, which reinforces the substitution effect because X is normal. Option D is the substitution effect, option C is the total effect, and option A is the Slutsky income effect.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: A consumer has U = XY, income N80 and Py = N1, so her demands are X = M/(2Px) and Y = M/(2Py). The price of X falls from N4 to N1, raising her purchase of X from 10 to 40. How much income must be taken away from her at the new prices to return her to her original indifference curve (U = 400)?
questions.explanation: At the new prices she reaches U = 400 with only N40, since (40/2)(40/2) = 400, so N80 - N40 = N40 must be removed; this is the Hicks compensation, equal to the compensating variation. Option B is the Slutsky reduction (10 units x N3), option C is the Slutsky compensated income, and option D is her whole income.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: A consumer has U = XY, income N80 and Py = N1, so her demands are X = M/(2Px) and Y = M/(2Py). The price of X falls from N4 to N1, raising her purchase of X from 10 to 40. Under the Slutsky approach, what compensated income would allow her to just buy her original bundle (10 X and 40 Y) at the new prices?
questions.explanation: At the new prices the original bundle costs 10 x N1 + 40 x N1 = N50, which is the Slutsky compensated income. Option C is the Hicks compensated income, option D is the amount removed (N80 - N50), and option B is her original income.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: The price of a staple food falls. The substitution effect raises a household's weekly purchase by 4 kg, while the income effect reduces it by 6 kg. Which statement is correct?

options.a: Quantity falls by 2 kg in total, so the good is a normal good
options.b: Quantity rises by 2 kg in total, so the good is an inferior but non-Giffen good
options.c: Quantity falls by 2 kg in total, so the good is a Giffen good
options.d: Quantity rises by 10 kg in total, so the good is a normal good

questions.explanation: The total effect is +4 - 6 = -2 kg, so a price fall reduces quantity demanded, which happens only when a negative income effect outweighs the substitution effect: a Giffen good. Option D adds the effects as if both were positive, option B gets the sign wrong, and option A is impossible because a normal good has a positive income effect.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: When the price of rice falls, a consumer's total purchase rises by 10 bags. The substitution effect accounts for 6 bags. The income effect and type of good are

options.a: +16 bags; rice is a normal good
options.b: +4 bags; rice is an inferior good
options.c: +4 bags; rice is a normal good
options.d: -4 bags; rice is an inferior good

questions.explanation: Since total effect = substitution effect + income effect, the income effect is 10 - 6 = +4 bags; a positive income effect from a price fall reinforces substitution, so rice is normal. Option D gets the sign wrong, option A adds instead of subtracting, and option B pairs a positive income effect with an inferior good.

questions.topic: Income and Substitution Effects and Consumer Surplus
questions.question: When the price of good X falls, the substitution effect raises quantity demanded by 8 units and the income effect reduces it by 3 units. Which statement is correct?

options.a: Quantity rises by 5 units, and X is inferior but not a Giffen good
options.b: Quantity falls by 5 units, and X is a Giffen good
options.c: Quantity rises by 11 units, and X is a normal good
options.d: Quantity rises by 5 units, and X is a normal good

questions.explanation: The total effect is 8 - 3 = +5 units; the income effect is negative, so X is inferior, but the substitution effect dominates, so demand still slopes downward. Option C treats both effects as positive, option B gets the direction wrong, and option D ignores the negative income effect.

questions.question: When you sum up the quantity demand of a commodity by individual A, individual B, and individual C, the outcome is called ______.
questions.explanation: Market demand is the horizontal sum of all individual demands: adding what A, B and C each buy at a given price gives the market demand for that commodity. Option C, aggregate demand, is a macroeconomic idea referring to total spending on all goods and services in the whole economy, not one commodity. A demand curve (option A) is just the graph of demand, and elastic demand (option B) describes responsiveness to price.

questions.question: In microeconomics, you are always advised to work with simplistic assumptions that demand is a function of ______.
questions.explanation: To keep analysis simple, microeconomics usually treats demand for a good as a function of its own price, Qd = f(P), holding income, tastes and other prices constant (ceteris paribus). Option B, the prices of commodities in general, brings in other goods' prices, which are held constant in this simple setup. Income and taste (options A and D) are determinants too, but they are the factors we assume fixed.

questions.question: A demand schedule, when plotted on a graph, becomes ______.
questions.explanation: A demand schedule is a table of prices and the quantities demanded at each price; when those pairs are plotted on a graph and joined, the result is the demand curve. Option A, 'demand graph', is not the standard term. Option D, market demand, is the sum of individual demands, which may or may not be what the schedule shows.

questions.question: Dx = f(Px, Pz, Y, T) is also known as ______.
questions.explanation: Dx = f(Px, Pz, Y, T) is a demand function: it states that the quantity demanded of x depends on its own price, the price of other goods, income and taste. Option A only names what is being determined, not what the expression is called. Options B and C are loose terms; a demand equation would give the exact numerical form, such as Qd = 100 - 2P, rather than the general f( ) form.

questions.question: A line that expresses that all things remaining equal, demand varies inversely with price, is called ______.
questions.explanation: A demand curve shows the inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded, ceteris paribus: as price falls, quantity demanded rises. Options A and B are not the standard names, and a scatter plot (option D) only shows raw data points rather than the relationship itself.

questions.question: When we move from point A to point B, and to point C on the same demand curve, the resulting impact is called ______.
questions.explanation: Moving along the same demand curve from A to B to C is a change in quantity demanded, caused only by a change in the good's own price. Option D, a change in demand, describes a shift of the whole curve caused by things like income or tastes. Option C sounds close but is not the standard term, and option A just describes the curve's slope.

questions.question: What variable is accountable for the movement from point A, to point B, and to point C, on the same demand curve? ______.

options.a: change in price of the commodity alone
options.b: Change in prices of commodities alone
options.c: change in quantity of other commodities

questions.explanation: Movement along a single demand curve is caused only by a change in the commodity's own price, with everything else held constant. Option B brings in the prices of other commodities, which would shift the curve instead. Option C is not a determinant of the movement, and option D describes the market outcome, not the cause of the movement.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a market demand?

options.a: the quantities of commodity that is demanded at different market prices by an individual
options.b: the quantities of commodity that is demanded at given market prices by different individuals
options.c: the quantities of commodity that is demanded at each alternative prices by different individuals
options.d: the quantities of commodity that is demanded at different market prices by different individuals

questions.explanation: Market demand adds up the quantities demanded by all the different individuals in the market at each price, so a schedule for just one individual is individual demand, not market demand. Options B, C and D all describe quantities demanded by different individuals, which is exactly what market demand is.

questions.question: Effective demand describes all of the following EXCEPT ______.

options.a: A consumer's ability to pay with no willingness to buy
options.b: A consumer's willingness to buy backed by the ability to pay
options.c: A consumer's ability to pay combined with readiness to buy
options.d: A consumer's wishes backed by purchasing power

questions.explanation: Effective demand is a desire or willingness to buy that is backed by the ability to pay, so it needs both parts. Option A has the ability to pay but no willingness to buy, so it is not effective demand. Options B, C and D each combine willingness (readiness or wishes) with the ability or purchasing power to pay, which is exactly what effective demand means.

questions.question: A rightward shift in the demand curve means ______.

options.a: More quantity of a commodity demanded at a higher price
options.b: Lesser quantity of a commodity demanded at a higher price
options.c: More quantity of a commodity demanded at the same price
options.d: Lesser quantity of a commodity demanded at a lesser price

questions.explanation: A rightward shift of the demand curve is an increase in demand: consumers buy more of the commodity at the same price, because of factors like higher income or a rise in the price of a substitute. Option A mixes a shift with a price change, which is not what defines the shift. Options B and D describe less being demanded, which would be a leftward shift or a movement.

questions.question: When children refer to all noodle brands as "indomie," this is mainly due to: ______.
questions.explanation: When one brand becomes so well known that its name is used for the whole product, as with calling every noodle brand Indomie, that reflects brand dominance shaping consumers' tastes and preferences. Options B and C, the income and substitution effects, describe how quantity demanded responds to a price change, not how a brand name becomes the general name for a product. Option A, price discrimination, is about charging different prices to different buyers.

questions.question: When consumer income increases, demand for an inferior good will ______
questions.explanation: An inferior good is one people buy less of as their income rises, because they switch to better-quality alternatives. So an increase in income decreases demand for an inferior good. Option A describes a normal good, and option D confuses income effects with price elasticity.

questions.question: Frequent exposure to noodle advertisements influences children's preference mainly through: ______
questions.explanation: Advertising works mainly by making consumers aware of a product and shaping their tastes and preferences, which is one of the determinants of demand. Repeated noodle adverts make children familiar with the product and more likely to ask for it. Options A, B and D relate to income or the supply side, which adverts do not directly change.

questions.question: An increase in income leads to an increase in demand for: ______
questions.explanation: A normal good is defined as one whose demand rises when income rises, so an increase in income increases demand for normal goods. Option D, inferior goods, behave the opposite way, and option A, Giffen goods, are a special type of inferior good. Option B is wrong because it is not only Veblen goods whose demand rises with income.

questions.question: When two goods are substitutes, an increase in the price of one good will: ______.
questions.explanation: Substitutes can replace each other, so when the price of one rises, consumers switch to the other and demand for it increases. For example, if Dettol soap becomes more expensive, demand for another antiseptic soap rises. Option B describes complementary goods, and option C describes unrelated goods.

questions.question: Theory of demand examines the behaviour of the--------
questions.explanation: The theory of demand studies how consumers decide how much of a good to buy at different prices, incomes and prices of related goods. Options B, C and D (producer, firm and industry) belong to the theory of supply and production.

questions.question: Change in demand due to a change in the price of related good :
questions.explanation: Cross demand shows how the quantity demanded of one good responds to a change in the price of a related good, such as a substitute or complement. Option B, price demand, is about the good's own price, and option C, income demand, is about changes in consumer income.

questions.question: In the case of normal goods, the quantity demanded varies inversely with:
questions.explanation: For normal goods, the law of demand holds: when the price of the good rises, the quantity demanded falls, so quantity varies inversely with its own price. Option B is wrong because for a normal good quantity demanded rises when income rises, which is a direct relationship, not an inverse one.

questions.question: Which one of the following is an example of close substitutes?
questions.explanation: Tea and coffee are close substitutes because either one can satisfy the same want, so a rise in the price of one pushes people towards the other. Option C (bread and butter) and option D (car and petrol) are complements that are used together, and milk and water in option B are not normally bought as replacements for each other.

questions.question: Other things remaining the same, the quantity of a product demanded increases with a ______ in its price.
questions.explanation: By the law of demand, price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions, so quantity demanded rises when price falls, other things being equal. Option A reverses this inverse relationship, and option C is too vague to describe the law.

questions.question: A change in demand (a shift of the whole demand curve) is NOT caused by a change in:
questions.explanation: A change in the good's own price causes a movement along the demand curve (a change in quantity demanded), not a shift of the curve. Income (option A), prices of related goods (option C) and expectations (option D) are all non-price factors that shift the whole demand curve.

questions.question: In drawing an individual demand curve for a commodity, all but which of the following are kept constant?

options.c: The price of the commodity under consideration

questions.explanation: An individual demand curve shows how quantity demanded changes as the commodity's own price changes, so that price is the variable allowed to change. Money income (option A), prices of related goods (option B) and tastes (option D) are held constant, and changes in them would shift the curve.

questions.question: A fall in the price of a commodity, holding everything else constant, results in:
questions.explanation: A change in the good's own price, with everything else constant, moves the consumer along the same demand curve, so a fall in price raises quantity demanded. An increase in demand (option A) means a shift of the whole curve, which happens only when a non-price factor changes.

questions.question: When an individual's income rises, everything else remaining the same, his demand for normal goods:

options.d: Any of the above is possible

questions.explanation: A normal good is one whose demand rises as income rises, so higher income shifts its demand curve to the right. Demand falling with income (option B) describes an inferior good instead.

questions.question: When an individual's income falls, everything else remaining the same, his demand for inferior goods:
questions.explanation: For an inferior good, demand moves opposite to income, so when income falls the consumer buys more of it (for example, switching to cheaper staples). A decrease (option B) is what happens to a normal good when income falls.

questions.question: When the price of a substitute for commodity X falls, the demand for X:

options.d: Any of the above is possible

questions.explanation: When a substitute becomes cheaper, consumers switch towards it and away from X, so the demand for X falls. Option A would be true only if the price of the substitute rose.

questions.question: When both the price of a substitute and the price of a complement of X rise, the demand for X:

options.d: Any of the above is possible

questions.explanation: A rise in the price of a substitute increases the demand for X, while a rise in the price of a complement reduces it. Since the two forces push in opposite directions, the net effect depends on which is stronger, so options A, B and C are each possible.

questions.question: For a normal good, a fall in the income of the consumer, other things being equal, causes:
questions.explanation: For a normal good, demand moves in the same direction as income, so a fall in income shifts the whole demand curve to the left, which is a decrease in demand. Option A would apply only to an inferior good, and options C and D describe movements along the curve, which only own-price changes cause.

questions.question: A movement down a given demand curve shows:
questions.explanation: Moving down a given demand curve means price has fallen and quantity demanded has risen, which is called an extension of demand (an increase in quantity demanded). An increase in demand (option A) is a rightward shift of the whole curve, and a contraction (option D) is a movement up the curve.

questions.question: Which of the following results in an increase in demand for a normal good?

options.a: A fall in the prices of substitutes
options.b: An increase in the price of complementary goods
options.c: A fall in the consumer's income

questions.explanation: Each listed change lowers demand for a normal good: cheaper substitutes pull buyers away (option A), dearer complements make the good less attractive (option B), and lower income reduces what consumers buy of a normal good (option C). None of them raises demand, so D is correct.

questions.question: In economics, the relationship between the quantity of a good that consumers are willing to buy and the price of the good, other things held constant, is called the
questions.explanation: A demand curve links each possible price of a good to the quantity consumers are willing to buy, holding other influences constant. Option C shows what producers are willing to sell, not what consumers want to buy. Options A and D come from consumer theory and describe affordability and equal satisfaction, not the price-quantity relationship.

questions.question: The law of demand states that, other things being equal,

options.a: as income rises, the quantity demanded of every good rises
options.b: as the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded of it rises
options.c: as the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded of it falls
options.d: as the price of a good rises, the quantity supplied of it rises

questions.explanation: The law of demand describes an inverse relationship between a good's own price and the quantity demanded, which is why the demand curve slopes downward. Option B reverses the relationship. Option A is about income, not price, and is not true for inferior goods, while option D is the law of supply.

questions.question: In the demand function QD = D(P, I), the variable I stands for
questions.explanation: Here QD is quantity demanded, P is the good's own price and I is consumers' income. When the demand curve is drawn against price, I is held fixed. Options A, C and D are other economic variables, but none of them is what I represents in this function.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a determinant of the demand for a good?

options.c: The cost of producing the good

questions.explanation: Production cost affects how much sellers are willing to offer, so it is a determinant of supply rather than demand.
