Consumer income (option A), prices of substitutes and complements (option B) and tastes (option D) all change how much buyers want at each price, so they are genuine determinants of demand.

questions.question: Other things being equal, a fall in the price of bread will cause

options.a: a leftward shift of the demand curve for bread
options.b: a movement up along the demand curve for bread
options.c: a movement down along the demand curve for bread
options.d: a rightward shift of the demand curve for bread

questions.explanation: A change in a good's own price changes the quantity demanded and is shown as a movement along its demand curve; a lower price means moving down the curve to a larger quantity. Options D and A are shifts, which happen only when some other factor such as income or tastes changes. Option B would follow a rise in the price of bread, not a fall.

questions.question: A shift of the whole demand curve to the left or right is described in economics as a
questions.explanation: Economists reserve the phrase 'change in demand' for a shift of the entire demand curve, caused by something other than the good's own price. Option B is the movement along the curve caused by a change in the good's own price. Options D and C refer to the supply side, not to demand.

questions.question: A rightward shift of the demand curve for a good means that

options.a: consumers will buy less at each price, or pay a lower price for the same quantity
options.b: producers will sell more at each price
options.c: the price of the good has fallen, so more is bought
options.d: consumers will buy more at each price, or pay a higher price for the same quantity

questions.explanation: When demand shifts right, at the old price a larger quantity is bought, and the old quantity would now be bought even at a higher price. Option A describes a leftward shift. Option B describes an increase in supply, and option C describes a movement along an unchanged demand curve.

questions.question: Salaries of civil servants in Lagos are increased. If fresh fish is a normal good, the demand curve for fresh fish in Lagos will

options.c: stay the same, with a movement up along it

questions.explanation: For a normal good, higher income makes consumers willing to buy more at every price, so the demand curve shifts to the right. Option B is what happens to a normal good when income falls, or to an inferior good when income rises. Option C is wrong because a change in income shifts the curve; only a change in the fish's own price moves along it.

questions.question: Two goods for which an increase in the price of one leads to an increase in the quantity demanded of the other are called
questions.explanation: Substitutes can replace each other, so when one becomes dearer, buyers switch to the other and its demand rises. Complements (option B) are used together, so a price rise of one reduces demand for the other. Options C and A describe how a good responds to income or to its own price, not the link between two goods.

questions.question: Two goods for which an increase in the price of one leads to a decrease in the quantity demanded of the other are called
questions.explanation: Complements are consumed together, like cars and petrol, so a higher price for one reduces the demand for the other. Substitutes (option A) move the opposite way: a dearer good raises demand for its substitute. Independent goods (option C) have no such link at all, and normal goods (option D) are defined by their response to income.

questions.question: Which of the following pairs of goods are best described as complements?
questions.explanation: Cars and petrol are used together, so a rise in the price of petrol reduces the demand for cars, which is the mark of complements. Beef and chicken (option C), butter and margarine (option B) and tea and coffee (option D) can each replace one another, so they are substitutes.

questions.question: Suppose petrol and cars are complements. A sharp rise in the pump price of petrol in Nigeria will, other things equal,

options.a: shift the demand curve for cars to the right
options.b: shift the supply curve of cars to the right
options.c: cause a movement down along the demand curve for cars
options.d: shift the demand curve for cars to the left

questions.explanation: Because cars and petrol are used together, dearer petrol makes owning a car more costly, so fewer cars are wanted at each car price and the demand curve for cars shifts left. Option A would be the response of a substitute. Option C is wrong because the price of cars itself has not changed, and option B confuses a demand influence with a supply one.

questions.question: Rice and spaghetti are substitutes for a household. If the price of spaghetti falls, the demand curve for rice will

options.a: not move, but the quantity of rice demanded falls
options.d: not move, but the quantity of rice demanded rises

questions.explanation: With substitutes, cheaper spaghetti draws buyers away from rice, so less rice is wanted at every rice price and its demand curve shifts left. Option C would follow a rise in the price of spaghetti. Options D and A describe movements along the rice demand curve, which only a change in the price of rice itself can cause.

questions.question: A good whose demand increases when consumers' income increases, other things equal, is called a
questions.explanation: A normal good is one that people buy more of as they become richer, so its income elasticity is positive. An inferior good (option C) is bought less as income rises. A Giffen good (option A) is a special inferior good defined by its response to its own price, and a free good (option B) is one with no price at all.

questions.question: When Tunde's monthly income rose from N50,000 to N80,000, he began taking fewer bus rides and more taxi rides, even though fares did not change. For Tunde, bus rides are
questions.explanation: An inferior good is one whose demand falls as income rises, which is exactly what happened to Tunde's bus rides with fares unchanged. Option B fits taxi rides, whose demand rose with income. Option A needs quantity to rise when the good's own price rises, which did not happen here, and option C is wrong because Tunde used taxis in place of buses, which makes them substitutes.

questions.question: If incomes in a town fall, the demand curve for an inferior good will
questions.explanation: Demand for an inferior good moves opposite to income, so when incomes fall people buy more of it at each price and its demand curve shifts right. Option C is what a fall in income does to a normal good. Option A ignores that income is a determinant of demand, and option D has nothing to do with income changes.

questions.question: Which of the following is an exception to the law of demand?
questions.explanation: A Giffen good is an inferior good for which a rise in its own price leads to a rise in quantity demanded, so its demand curve slopes upward, breaking the law of demand. Normal goods (option B) obey the law of demand. Substitutes (option D) and complements (option C) describe how two goods are related, not an upward-sloping demand curve.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT usually given as an exception to the law of demand?

options.a: Goods that have many close substitutes
options.b: Goods whose high price is taken as a sign of high quality

questions.explanation: A good with many close substitutes has very elastic demand, so a rise in its price causes a large fall in quantity demanded, which strongly obeys the law of demand. Giffen goods (option D), Veblen goods bought to show off (option C) and goods where buyers judge quality by price (option B) are the usual cases where more may be bought at a higher price.

questions.question: An inferior good for which a rise in its own price causes the quantity demanded to rise is called a
questions.explanation: A Giffen good is an inferior staple whose negative income effect is so strong that it outweighs the substitution effect, so quantity demanded rises with its price. A Veblen good (option C) also can have an upward-sloping demand, but because it is prized for its high price as a status symbol, not because it is inferior. Normal and luxury goods (options A and B) are bought more as income rises and obey the law of demand.

questions.question: A wealthy Lagos businessman buys more of a designer wristwatch after its price is raised, because the high price shows off his status. This wristwatch is an example of a
questions.explanation: A Veblen good is valued partly because it is expensive, so a higher price can increase the quantity demanded by status-seeking buyers. Option D also has an upward-sloping demand, but a Giffen good is a cheap inferior staple, not a luxury item. Option A is wrong because the watch is bought more by the rich, and option C describes a link between two goods.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about Giffen goods and inferior goods is correct?

options.a: Giffen goods are normal goods with an upward-sloping demand curve
options.b: Every Giffen good is an inferior good, but not every inferior good is a Giffen good
options.c: Giffen goods and inferior goods are exactly the same thing
options.d: Every inferior good is a Giffen good, but not every Giffen good is inferior

questions.explanation: A Giffen good must be inferior, because only a negative income effect can outweigh the substitution effect; but most inferior goods have a weak income effect and still obey the law of demand. Option D reverses the relationship and option C wrongly makes them identical. Option A is wrong because a normal good's income effect reinforces the substitution effect, so it cannot be Giffen.

questions.question: Which of the following helps to explain why the demand curve for most goods slopes downward?

options.a: When a good becomes cheaper, firms are willing to produce more of it
options.b: When a good becomes cheaper, the prices of all its substitutes rise
options.c: When a good becomes cheaper, consumers switch to it from other goods (the substitution effect)
options.d: When a good becomes cheaper, consumers' money incomes rise

questions.explanation: A lower price makes a good relatively cheaper than its alternatives, so buyers substitute towards it, which raises the quantity demanded; together with the income effect this gives the downward slope. Option A describes producers and would go with a higher, not a lower, price. Option D confuses real purchasing power with money income, and option B is not something a price fall causes.

questions.question: A table showing the different quantities of a good that consumers are willing to buy at different prices, other things equal, is called a
questions.explanation: A demand schedule lists price-quantity pairs for buyers, and plotting it gives the demand curve. A supply schedule (option B) lists what sellers would offer at each price. A demand function (option A) expresses the same relationship as an equation rather than a table, and option D is not a standard demand concept.

questions.question: The demand for garri in a market is given by Qd = 100 - 4P, where P is in naira per cup. What quantity is demanded when P = N15?
questions.explanation: Substituting P = 15 gives Qd = 100 - 4(15) = 100 - 60 = 40 cups. Option D is the amount subtracted (4 x 15), not the quantity left. Option C adds instead of subtracting, and option B is the price at which quantity demanded would be zero (100/4).

questions.question: The demand function for a good is Qd = 120 - 3P. If its price rises from N10 to N15, other things equal, what happens?

options.a: Quantity demanded falls by 5 units, a movement along the demand curve
options.b: Quantity demanded falls by 15 units, a leftward shift of the demand curve
options.c: Quantity demanded falls by 15 units, a movement along the demand curve
options.d: Quantity demanded rises by 15 units, a movement along the demand curve

questions.explanation: At P = 10, Qd = 90 and at P = 15, Qd = 75, so quantity demanded falls by 3 x 5 = 15 units; because only the good's own price changed, this is a movement along the curve. Option B gets the number right but wrongly calls it a shift. Option A uses the price change instead of multiplying by the slope of 3, and option D has the wrong direction.

questions.question: The market demand curve for a good is obtained from individual demand curves by

options.a: multiplying each consumer's quantity demanded by the price
options.b: adding the prices each consumer is willing to pay for each quantity (vertical summation)
options.c: taking the average of the quantities demanded by consumers at each price
options.d: adding the quantities demanded by all consumers at each price (horizontal summation)

questions.explanation: Market demand is the total quantity all buyers want at each price, so the individual quantities are added sideways along the quantity axis. Option B adds prices, which is not how private market demand is formed. Option C gives the average buyer's quantity, not the market total, and option A gives spending, not quantity.

questions.question: At a price of N200 per bottle, Ada, Bayo and Chidi are willing to buy 5, 8 and 12 bottles of zobo per week respectively. If they are the only buyers, the market quantity demanded at N200 is
questions.explanation: Market quantity demanded at a price is the sum of individual quantities at that price: 5 + 8 + 12 = 25 bottles. Option C takes only the largest buyer. Option B is the average per buyer, and option A multiplies the price by the number of buyers, which is not a quantity.

questions.question: Two consumers are the only buyers of a good. Their demands are Qa = 20 - 2P and Qb = 30 - 3P (both positive at the prices considered). The market quantity demanded at P = 4 is
questions.explanation: At P = 4, Qa = 20 - 8 = 12 and Qb = 30 - 12 = 18, so the market quantity is 12 + 18 = 30 units. The market demand can also be written Q = 50 - 5P, which gives the same result. Options A and D are just one consumer's quantity, and option C adds only the intercepts and forgets the price terms.

questions.question: There are 100 identical buyers of a good, each with demand q = 10 - 0.5P. The market quantity demanded at P = 8 is
questions.explanation: Each buyer demands 10 - 0.5(8) = 6 units, and with 100 identical buyers the market quantity is 100 x 6 = 600 units, from market demand Q = 1000 - 50P. Option C is one buyer's quantity only. Option D ignores the price term, and option A is the amount by which the price reduces market demand (50 x 8), not the quantity bought.

questions.question: The only two buyers of a good have demands Qa = 20 - 2P and Qb = 12 - P, where quantity cannot be negative. The market quantity demanded at P = 11 is
questions.explanation: At P = 11, buyer A would want 20 - 22 = -2, which means A buys nothing, while buyer B wants 12 - 11 = 1 unit, so market demand is 0 + 1 = 1 unit. Option D wrongly adds a negative quantity. Option B assumes neither buyer is in the market, and option A drops the minus sign on A's figure.

questions.question: A large number of new students arrive on campus at the start of a session. The likely effect on the market for meals at campus canteens is

options.a: a rightward shift of the market demand curve
options.b: a leftward shift of the market demand curve
options.c: a rightward shift of the market supply curve
options.d: a movement down along the market demand curve

questions.explanation: Market demand is the sum of all individual demands, so more buyers means more is wanted at each price and the market demand curve shifts right. Option B would follow a fall in the number of buyers. Option D needs a fall in the meal price itself, and option C is about sellers, not buyers.

questions.question: The demand for a good is Qd = 200 - 5P + 0.01I, where I is income in naira. With P = N20, income rises from N50,000 to N60,000. Quantity demanded rises from

options.a: 600 to 700 units, so the good is an inferior good
options.b: 600 to 610 units, so the good is a normal good
options.c: 100 to 200 units, so the good is a normal good
options.d: 600 to 700 units, so the good is a normal good

questions.explanation: At P = 20 and I = 50,000, Qd = 200 - 100 + 500 = 600; at I = 60,000 it is 200 - 100 + 600 = 700, and since demand rises with income the good is normal. Option A has the right numbers but the wrong label, as the income coefficient is positive. Option C leaves out the income term entirely at the start, and option B multiplies the income change wrongly.

questions.question: A demand function is estimated as Qx = 300 - 4Px - 0.002I, where I is income. The negative sign on I shows that good X is
questions.explanation: A negative income coefficient means that as income rises, less of X is demanded at each price, which is the definition of an inferior good. Option B would need a positive coefficient. Option D is about an upward-sloping response to X's own price, but here the price coefficient is negative, so X obeys the law of demand, and option A is not an economic category.

questions.question: The demand for good X is Qx = 50 - 2Px + 3Py, where Py is the price of good Y. If Py rises from N10 to N14, the demand curve for X

options.a: shifts right by 12 units, because X and Y are substitutes
options.b: shifts right by 4 units, because X and Y are complements
options.c: shifts right by 8 units, because X and Y are substitutes
options.d: shifts left by 12 units, because X and Y are complements

questions.explanation: The quantity of X demanded at every Px rises by 3 x (14 - 10) = 12 units, and since a dearer Y raises the demand for X, the two goods are substitutes. Option D gets the direction and relationship wrong. Option C uses the coefficient of Px (2) instead of the coefficient of Py (3), and option B ignores the coefficient and mislabels the goods.

questions.question: The demand for good A is QA = 80 - 2PA - 4PB, where PB is the price of good B. An increase in PB will

options.a: shift the demand curve for A to the left, so A is an inferior good
options.b: shift the demand curve for A to the right, so A and B are substitutes
options.c: shift the demand curve for A to the left, so A and B are complements
options.d: cause a movement up along the demand curve for A

questions.explanation: The negative coefficient on PB means a higher price of B reduces the quantity of A demanded at every PA, a leftward shift, which happens when goods are used together as complements. Option B would need a positive coefficient. Option D needs a change in PA itself, and option A wrongly links a price of another good to the income-based idea of an inferior good.

questions.question: A successful advertising campaign makes zobo drink more popular among students. Other things equal, the market for zobo will experience

options.a: a rightward shift of the demand curve
options.b: a leftward shift of the demand curve
options.c: a leftward shift of the supply curve
options.d: a movement up along the demand curve

questions.explanation: Tastes are a determinant of demand, so when zobo becomes more popular buyers want more at every price and the demand curve shifts right. Option D is caused only by a rise in the price of zobo itself. Option C is a supply-side change, and option B would follow a loss of popularity.

questions.question: When a demand curve is drawn, economists hold constant factors such as income, tastes and the prices of related goods. This assumption is known as
questions.explanation: Ceteris paribus means 'other things being equal', and it lets the demand curve show the effect of the good's own price alone. Option D is a policy of non-interference by government. Option C is the value of the next best alternative given up, and option B relates to trade and specialisation.

questions.question: A shift in supply curve is the same as ______
questions.explanation: A shift of the supply curve is a change in supply, caused by factors other than the good's own price, such as costs of production or technology. Options A and B describe a movement along the same curve, which happens only when the good's own price changes. Option D, a change in price, causes a movement, not a shift.

questions.question: The supply curve represents a ______ relationship between quantity and price.
questions.explanation: By the law of supply, sellers offer more at higher prices, so price and quantity supplied move in the same direction and the relationship is direct. An inverse relationship (option B) describes demand, not supply.

questions.question: If the supply curve of a commodity has a positive slope, a rise in the price of the commodity results in:
questions.explanation: With an upward-sloping supply curve, a rise in the commodity's own price moves sellers up along the same curve, so quantity supplied rises. An increase in supply (option A) means a rightward shift of the curve, caused by non-price factors such as cheaper inputs.

questions.question: Which of the following causes an increase in supply?

options.a: A fall in the price of inputs
options.b: An increase in the number of producers
options.c: A decrease in the price of production substitutes

questions.explanation: Each option shifts supply to the right: cheaper inputs lower production costs (option A), more producers add to market supply (option B), and a fall in the price of a production substitute makes it more attractive to switch resources into this good (option C). Since all three raise supply, D is the best answer.

questions.question: An increase in supply means:

options.a: A movement down a given supply curve
options.b: A movement up a given supply curve
options.c: A leftward shift of the supply curve
options.d: A rightward shift of the supply curve

questions.explanation: An increase in supply means producers offer more at every price, so the whole supply curve shifts to the right. Options A and B are movements along a given curve caused by own-price changes, and option C is a decrease in supply.

questions.question: Which of the following causes a movement along a given supply curve rather than a shift of the supply curve?

options.a: A change in the number of firms in the market
options.c: A change in the price of an input used to make the good
options.d: A change in the price of the good itself

questions.explanation: A supply curve shows how quantity supplied responds to the good's own price, so a change in that price moves sellers along the curve (a change in quantity supplied). Input prices (option C), technology (option B) and the number of firms (option A) are non-price factors that change the quantity offered at every price, shifting the whole curve.

questions.question: Americans bought 15.75 billion packs of cigarettes at an average price of $5.00 per pack. The price elasticity of demand is -0.4 and the price elasticity of supply is 0.5. What linear supply curve, Q = c + dP, is consistent with these figures?
questions.explanation: From elasticity of supply = d(P/Q), we get d = 0.5 x 15.75/5 = 1.575. Then c = Q - dP = 15.75 - 1.575 x 5 = 7.875, so Q = 7.875 + 1.575P. Option A adds dP to Q instead of subtracting it, and options D and C use the elasticity itself as the slope.

questions.question: The relationship between the quantity of a good that producers are willing to sell and the price of the good, holding other factors constant, is called the
questions.explanation: A supply curve shows how much sellers are willing to offer at each price, other things held constant. Option D shows buyers' behaviour, not sellers'. Option A shows the combinations an economy can produce with its resources, and option B shows how cost varies with output, not with price.

questions.question: The law of supply states that, other things being equal,

options.a: the higher the price of a good, the smaller the quantity supplied
options.b: the higher the cost of production, the greater the quantity supplied
options.c: the higher the price of a good, the greater the quantity supplied
options.d: the higher the price of a good, the smaller the quantity demanded

questions.explanation: The law of supply describes a direct, positive relationship between price and quantity supplied, which is why the supply curve slopes upward. Option A reverses that relationship. Option D is the law of demand, and option B is wrong because higher costs reduce supply.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a reason why a supply curve slopes upward?

options.a: At higher prices, firms can expand their plants
options.b: At higher prices, firms can profitably hire extra workers or pay for overtime
options.c: At higher prices, higher-cost new firms can enter the market
options.d: At higher prices, consumers are willing to buy less

questions.explanation: Consumers buying less at higher prices is the law of demand, so it explains the slope of the demand curve, not the supply curve. Overtime and extra workers (option B), bigger plants (option A) and entry of higher-cost firms (option C) are all ways that a higher price makes more output profitable, which gives supply its upward slope.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a determinant of the supply of a good?
questions.explanation: Consumer income affects how much buyers want, so it is a determinant of demand, not supply. Wages (option C) and the cost of inputs (option A) are production costs, and technology (option D) changes how cheaply output can be produced, so all three shift the supply curve.

questions.question: Other things equal, a fall in the cost of the raw inputs used to make a good will

options.a: shift the supply curve to the left
options.b: shift the demand curve to the right
options.c: cause a movement up along the supply curve
options.d: shift the supply curve to the right

questions.explanation: Lower input costs make each unit cheaper to produce, so firms offer more at every price and the supply curve shifts right. Option A follows a rise in costs. Option C needs a change in the good's own price, and option B is wrong because input costs affect sellers, not buyers.

questions.question: A rightward shift of a supply curve means that

options.a: more is offered at each price, or the same quantity is offered at a lower price
options.b: less is offered at each price, or the same quantity is offered only at a higher price
options.c: the price of the good has risen, so more is offered
options.d: more is bought by consumers at each price

questions.explanation: After a rightward shift, at the old price producers offer a larger quantity, and they would offer the old quantity even at a lower price. Option B describes a leftward shift. Option D describes an increase in demand, and option C describes a movement along an unchanged supply curve.

questions.question: A rise in the market price of cement, other things equal, leads to

options.a: a decrease in the supply of cement, shown as a leftward shift of the supply curve
options.b: a decrease in the quantity of cement supplied, shown as a movement along the supply curve
options.c: an increase in the quantity of cement supplied, shown as a movement along the supply curve
options.d: an increase in the supply of cement, shown as a rightward shift of the supply curve

questions.explanation: A change in the good's own price changes the quantity supplied and is a movement along the supply curve, upward to a larger quantity when price rises. Option D is wrong because a shift (a change in supply) needs some other factor such as costs to change. Option A is also a shift, and option B has the wrong direction.

questions.question: Bakeries in Ibadan have to pay their workers higher wages. Other things equal, the supply curve of bread in Ibadan will

options.c: not move, but quantity supplied falls along it

questions.explanation: Higher wages raise the cost of producing each loaf, so bakers offer less bread at every price and the supply curve shifts left. Option D would follow a fall in costs. Option C is wrong because wages are not the price of bread, so they shift the curve rather than move along it, and option A has no basis in the scenario.

questions.question: A new machine that cuts the time needed to process cassava into garri is widely adopted. The likely effect is

options.a: a rightward shift of the demand curve for garri
options.b: a movement down along the supply curve of garri
options.c: a leftward shift of the supply curve of garri
options.d: a rightward shift of the supply curve of garri

questions.explanation: Better technology lowers the cost of producing each unit, so producers supply more at each price and the supply curve shifts right. Option C would follow higher costs. Option A is about buyers, and option B needs a fall in the price of garri itself.

questions.question: Several new firms enter the market for sachet water in Abuja. Other things equal, the market supply curve will

options.a: shift the market demand curve to the left
options.d: not change, since each firm's supply is unchanged

questions.explanation: Market supply is the sum of all firms' supplies, so more firms means more is offered at each price and the market supply curve shifts right. Option C would follow firms leaving. Option D forgets that adding firms adds to the horizontal sum, and option A confuses supply with demand.

questions.question: A severe drought destroys much of the maize crop in northern Nigeria. Other things equal, the effect on the maize market is

options.a: a leftward shift of the supply curve
options.b: a rightward shift of the demand curve
options.c: a rightward shift of the supply curve
options.d: a movement up along the supply curve

questions.explanation: Bad weather reduces the amount farmers can bring to market at any price, so supply shifts left. Option C would follow a good harvest. Option D is a movement caused by a rise in the maize price, not by the drought itself, and option B is a change in buyers' behaviour.

questions.question: The market supply curve is derived from individual firms' supply curves by

options.a: adding the quantities supplied by all firms at each price
options.b: taking the average quantity supplied by firms at each price
options.c: choosing the supply curve of the largest firm
options.d: adding the prices charged by all firms at each quantity

questions.explanation: Market supply at any price is the total output all firms are willing to sell at that price, so individual supply curves are added horizontally. Option D adds prices, which is not how market supply is formed. Option B gives the average firm's output, and option C ignores all the other firms.

questions.question: At a price of N500 per crate, three poultry farms are willing to supply 40, 55 and 25 crates of eggs per week. If they are the only sellers, the market quantity supplied at N500 is
questions.explanation: Market quantity supplied is the horizontal sum of the firms' quantities at that price: 40 + 55 + 25 = 120 crates. Option B is the largest farm only. Option C is the average per farm, and option A multiplies price by quantity, which gives revenue in naira, not crates.

questions.question: There are 50 identical firms in a market, each with supply qs = -10 + 2P. The market quantity supplied at P = N20 is
questions.explanation: Each firm supplies -10 + 2(20) = 30 units, so 50 firms supply 50 x 30 = 1,500 units, from market supply Qs = -500 + 100P. Option D is one firm's output only. Option B ignores the negative intercept (100 x 20), and option C just multiplies the number of firms by the price.

questions.question: Firm A's supply is qA = 2P and firm B's supply is qB = -20 + 4P for P >= 5 (B produces nothing below N5). The market quantity supplied at P = N4 is
questions.explanation: At P = 4, firm A supplies 2 x 4 = 8 units, while firm B's formula gives -4, which means B supplies nothing, so the market total is 8 + 0 = 8 units. Option A wrongly adds B's negative figure. Option D is B's negative figure alone, and option B forgets B's intercept and adds 8 + 16.

questions.question: The supply of a good is Qs = -40 + 5P. If the price rises from N20 to N30, quantity supplied
questions.explanation: At P = 20, Qs = -40 + 100 = 60 and at P = 30, Qs = -40 + 150 = 110, an increase of 50 units along the supply curve. Option D forgets the intercept of -40. Option C reverses the direction, and option A adds the price change of 10 rather than multiplying it by the slope of 5.

questions.question: A perfectly inelastic supply curve is

options.a: horizontal, with an elasticity of supply equal to infinity
options.b: vertical, with an elasticity of supply equal to zero
options.c: a straight line through the origin, with elasticity equal to one
options.d: vertical, with an elasticity of supply equal to infinity

questions.explanation: Perfectly inelastic supply means the quantity offered does not change at all when price changes, so the curve is vertical and the elasticity is zero. Option A describes perfectly elastic supply. Option D pairs the vertical shape with the wrong value, and option C describes unit-elastic supply.

questions.question: A football stadium has exactly 20,000 seats for a particular match, and no more can be added whatever the ticket price. The supply of seats for that match is
questions.explanation: Because the number of seats is fixed at 20,000 regardless of price, quantity supplied does not respond to price, which is perfectly inelastic supply with a vertical curve. Option D would mean any quantity is supplied at one price. Options A and C both require quantity supplied to respond to price.

questions.question: A perfectly elastic supply curve is

options.a: horizontal, with an elasticity of supply equal to zero
options.b: upward sloping, with an elasticity of supply equal to one
options.c: vertical, with an elasticity of supply equal to zero
options.d: horizontal, with an elasticity of supply equal to infinity

questions.explanation: With perfectly elastic supply, sellers will supply any quantity at one price but nothing below it, so the curve is horizontal and elasticity is infinite. Option C describes perfectly inelastic supply. Option A pairs the horizontal shape with the wrong value, and option B does not describe a perfectly elastic curve.

questions.question: Any straight-line supply curve that passes through the origin has a price elasticity of supply that is

options.a: greater than one at every point
options.b: equal to zero at every point
options.c: equal to one at every point
options.d: less than one at every point

questions.explanation: For a supply line through the origin, Q = dP, so elasticity = d(P/Q) = d(P/dP) = 1 at every point, whatever the slope. Option B describes a vertical supply curve. Option A fits a line that cuts the price axis, and option D fits a line that cuts the quantity axis.

questions.question: The supply of a good is Qs = -20 + 4P, a straight line that cuts the price axis. Using Es = (P/Q)(change in Q / change in P), the price elasticity of supply at P = N10 is
questions.explanation: At P = 10, Qs = -20 + 40 = 20 and the slope term is 4, so Es = (10/20) x 4 = 2.0, which is elastic; any straight-line supply curve that cuts the price axis is elastic. Option A uses P/Q = 0.5 but forgets to multiply by the slope of 4. Option C uses the slope alone without multiplying by P/Q, and option D would hold only for a line through the origin.

questions.question: The supply of a good is Qs = 20 + 2P, a straight line that cuts the quantity axis. Using Es = (P/Q)(change in Q / change in P), the price elasticity of supply at P = N10 is
questions.explanation: At P = 10, Qs = 20 + 20 = 40 and the slope term is 2, so Es = (10/40) x 2 = 0.5, which is inelastic; any straight-line supply curve that cuts the quantity axis is inelastic. Option A uses the slope of 2 alone without multiplying by P/Q. Option C is P/Q = 0.25 without the slope, and option B would hold only for a line through the origin.

questions.question: A firm's supply function is Qs = 100 + 6P - 2W, where W is the wage rate. If W rises from N20 to N30, the supply curve

options.a: shifts left by 20 units at every price
options.b: shifts right by 20 units at every price
options.c: does not shift; quantity supplied moves along the curve
options.d: shifts left by 60 units at every price

questions.explanation: The quantity supplied at each price changes by -2 x (30 - 20) = -20 units, so the whole supply curve shifts 20 units to the left. Option B has the wrong direction, since the wage coefficient is negative. Option D uses the price coefficient of 6 instead of the wage coefficient, and option C is wrong because the wage is a determinant other than the good's own price.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about supply elasticities is correct?

options.a: The price elasticity of supply is usually positive, while the elasticity of supply with respect to raw-input prices is usually negative
options.b: Both the price elasticity of supply and the elasticity with respect to input prices are usually negative
options.c: The price elasticity of supply is usually negative, while the elasticity of supply with respect to raw-input prices is usually positive
options.d: Both the price elasticity of supply and the elasticity with respect to input prices are usually positive

questions.explanation: A higher price of the good encourages more output, so price elasticity of supply is positive, whereas a higher price of inputs raises costs and reduces output, so that elasticity is negative. Option C swaps the two signs. Options D and B wrongly give both elasticities the same sign.

questions.question: For most manufactured products, the price elasticity of supply is

options.a: larger in the long run than in the short run, because firms need time to expand capacity
options.b: larger in the short run than in the long run, because firms run down stocks
options.c: the same in the short run and the long run
options.d: always zero in the long run

questions.explanation: In the short run firms face capacity limits, but with time they can build new plants and new firms can enter, so supply responds more to price in the long run. Option B reverses the usual pattern. Option C ignores capacity constraints, and option D describes perfectly inelastic supply, which is the opposite of what happens over time.

questions.question: Estimated price elasticities of total copper supply are 0.25 in the short run and 1.50 in the long run. If the price of copper rises by 10% and stays at the new level, the long-run increase in the quantity of copper supplied is about
questions.explanation: Price elasticity of supply is the % change in quantity supplied divided by the % change in price, so the long-run change is 1.50 x 10% = 15%. The figure 2.5% uses the short-run elasticity of 0.25, which describes the response before firms have time to expand capacity.

questions.question: For which of the following is the price elasticity of supply generally smaller in the long run than in the short run?

options.a: Secondary supply of a durable good, such as scrap metal
options.d: Primary supply of copper from mines

questions.explanation: Long-run supply is usually more elastic because firms can expand capacity, but secondary supply of a durable good like scrap metal is the exception: for secondary copper the elasticity falls from 0.43 in the short run to 0.31 in the long run. Primary copper from mines follows the normal pattern, with its elasticity rising from 0.20 to 1.60.

questions.question: Before any subsidy, sachet water producers in Lagos need a price of at least N60 per bag to supply 500 bags a day. The government then pays them a subsidy of N4 per bag. Other things equal, the lowest price buyers must now pay for producers to supply 500 bags a day is
questions.explanation: A per-unit subsidy shifts the supply curve down by the amount of the subsidy, so producers who still need N60 in total per bag now need only N60 - N4 = N56 from buyers. The figure N64 adds the subsidy instead of subtracting it, which is how a N4 per-unit tax would shift supply up.

questions.question: The supply of a good is Qs = -20 + 4P, where P is in naira. The government imposes a tax of N5 per unit, paid by sellers. Written in terms of the price buyers pay, the new supply equation is
questions.explanation: A per-unit tax shifts supply up by the tax, so sellers now receive only P - 5 of each price P that buyers pay: Qs = -20 + 4(P - 5) = -40 + 4P. The equation Qs = 4P comes from adding the tax to the price instead of subtracting it, which would wrongly make sellers more willing to supply.

questions.question: The elasticity of supply of bread with respect to the price of flour is -0.4 for bakeries in Surulere. If the price of flour rises by 10%, other things equal, the quantity of bread supplied will
questions.explanation: This elasticity is the % change in bread supplied divided by the % change in the flour price, so the change is -0.4 x 10% = -4%, a fall of about 4%. The negative sign is normal here, because dearer raw materials raise costs and reduce supply, so an answer of a 4% rise ignores the sign.

questions.question: The price elasticity of supply is best defined as the

options.a: percentage change in quantity supplied resulting from a 1 percent rise in input prices
options.b: change in quantity supplied resulting from a N1 increase in the price
options.c: percentage change in quantity demanded resulting from a 1 percent increase in price
options.d: percentage change in quantity supplied resulting from a 1 percent increase in price

questions.explanation: Elasticity of supply compares percentage changes, telling us by what percent quantity supplied changes when price rises by 1 percent. The change in quantity per N1 rise in price is the slope of the supply curve, which depends on the units used and is not the same thing as elasticity.

questions.question: A manufacturing firm in Ikeja finances its machines with bank loans. If the interest rate it pays on these loans rises sharply, other things equal, the firm's supply curve will

options.a: stay put, with a movement up along it

questions.explanation: Interest is part of a firm's cost of production, alongside wages and raw materials, so a higher interest rate raises costs and the firm offers less at each price, a leftward shift. A movement along the curve happens only when the good's own price changes, not when a cost changes.

questions.question: When the price of tomatoes at Mile 12 market rises sharply, the total quantity of tomatoes offered for sale rises. One reason the market supply curve slopes upward in this way is that

options.a: the cost of fertiliser to existing growers falls
options.b: consumers' incomes rise, so buyers want more tomatoes
options.c: the supply curve of tomatoes shifts to the right
options.d: higher-cost growers now find it worthwhile to enter the market

questions.explanation: At a higher price, existing growers can cover the extra cost of overtime or more workers, and growers whose costs were too high at the old price now find it profitable to sell, so quantity supplied rises along the curve. A fall in fertiliser costs is a different event: it is a non-price determinant that shifts the whole supply curve rather than explaining its upward slope.

questions.question: A decrease in supply when demand remains the same will cause equilibrium ______.

options.a: P and Q to both fall
options.b: P and Q to both rise
options.c: P to rise while Q falls
options.d: P to fall while Q rises

questions.explanation: A decrease in supply shifts the supply curve to the left; with demand unchanged, a shortage appears at the old price, so price rises and the quantity bought and sold falls. Option A (both fall) is what happens when demand decreases, and option B (both rise) is the result of an increase in demand. Option D describes an increase in supply.

questions.question: Any price below the equilibrium price will lead to ______ which is also referred to as ______.
questions.explanation: Below the equilibrium price, quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied, giving excess demand, which is also called a shortage. Options C and D refer to excess supply, which occurs above the equilibrium price and is called a surplus. Option A wrongly pairs excess demand with surplus.

questions.question: Given Qd = 300 - 2.5P and Qs = 200 + 1.5P, the equilibrium price and quantity are ______ and ______ respectively.
questions.explanation: At equilibrium Qd = Qs, so 300 - 2.5P = 200 + 1.5P, which gives 100 = 4P and P = 25. Substituting, Q = 300 - 2.5(25) = 237.5, and the supply side gives the same: 200 + 1.5(25) = 237.5. The other options do not make quantity demanded equal to quantity supplied; for example, at P = 20 demand is 250 but supply is only 230.

questions.question: The market equilibrium for a commodity is determined by

options.a: The market demand for the commodity
options.b: The market supply of the commodity
options.c: The balancing of the forces of demand and supply for the commodity

questions.explanation: Market equilibrium is reached at the price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, so it is set by the balancing of demand and supply together. Demand alone (option A) or supply alone (option B) cannot fix the price, which is like asking which blade of a pair of scissors does the cutting.

questions.question: At prices above the equilibrium price:

options.d: Any of the above is possible

questions.explanation: Above the equilibrium price, sellers want to sell more and buyers want to buy less, so quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded and there is a surplus. Options B and C describe a shortage, which happens below the equilibrium price.

questions.question: An increase in market supply, with demand remaining the same, causes:

options.c: Decrease in equilibrium price and increase in equilibrium quantity
options.d: Both equilibrium price and quantity rises

questions.explanation: A rightward shift of supply with demand unchanged creates a surplus at the old price, so price falls and buyers move down their demand curve to buy more. Option A has price moving the wrong way, and option D is what happens when demand, not supply, increases.

questions.question: An increase in market demand, with supply remaining the same, results in:

options.c: A decrease in equilibrium price and an increase in equilibrium quantity
options.d: A rise in both equilibrium price and quantity

questions.explanation: A rightward shift of demand with supply unchanged creates a shortage at the old price, so price is bid up and sellers move up their supply curve, raising quantity too. Option C pairs a fall in price with a rise in quantity, which happens when supply increases.

questions.question: A fall in market demand, with supply remaining the same, results in:

options.c: An increase in equilibrium price and a decrease in equilibrium quantity
options.d: A fall in both equilibrium price and quantity

questions.explanation: A leftward shift of demand with supply unchanged leaves a surplus at the old price, so price falls and sellers cut the quantity they supply, lowering both. Option C is the result of a decrease in supply, not of a fall in demand.

questions.question: Unusually hot weather shifts the demand curve for ice cream to the right. Why does the price of ice cream rise to a new market-clearing level?

options.a: The supply curve shifts to the left because sellers expect hot weather
options.b: Sellers raise the price, but the quantity sold must stay the same as before
options.c: At the old price quantity demanded now exceeds quantity supplied, and the shortage bids the price up until the two are equal again
options.d: At the old price quantity supplied now exceeds quantity demanded, and the surplus pushes the price up

questions.explanation: After demand shifts right, buyers want more ice cream than sellers offer at the old price, so there is a shortage. Competition among buyers pushes the price up, which raises quantity supplied along the supply curve and reduces quantity demanded until the market clears again at a higher price and a larger quantity. Option D describes a surplus, which would push price down, and option B is wrong because the new equilibrium quantity is larger.

questions.question: Margarine is a substitute for butter. Using supply and demand, how would an increase in the price of margarine affect the market for butter?

options.a: The price of butter rises and the quantity of butter bought and sold rises
options.b: The price of butter rises and the quantity of butter bought and sold falls
options.c: The price of butter falls and the quantity of butter bought and sold rises
options.d: The price of butter falls and the quantity of butter bought and sold falls

questions.explanation: Dearer margarine makes consumers switch to butter, so the demand curve for butter shifts to the right along an unchanged supply curve. A rightward demand shift raises both equilibrium price and equilibrium quantity. Option B is the result of a fall in supply, and option D is the result of a fall in demand.

questions.question: Milk is the main input used in producing butter. Using supply and demand, how would an increase in the price of milk affect the market for butter?

options.a: The price of butter rises and the quantity of butter bought and sold rises
options.b: The price of butter falls and the quantity of butter bought and sold falls
options.c: The price of butter falls and the quantity of butter bought and sold rises
options.d: The price of butter rises and the quantity of butter bought and sold falls

questions.explanation: A rise in the price of milk raises the cost of making butter, so the supply curve of butter shifts to the left while demand stays the same. At the old price there is now a shortage, so price rises and the quantity traded falls. Option A is what happens when demand increases, not when supply decreases.

questions.question: The copper market has supply Q = -9 + 9P and demand Q = 27 - 3P (Q in million metric tons per year, P in dollars per pound). A fall in production costs shifts the supply curve to the right by 40 percent, to Q = 1.4(-9 + 9P). What happens to the price of copper?

options.a: It falls from $3.00 to about $2.54 per pound
options.b: It falls from $3.00 to about $2.75 per pound
options.c: It rises from $3.00 to about $3.46 per pound
options.d: It falls from $3.00 to about $1.80 per pound

questions.explanation: Initially 27 - 3P = -9 + 9P gives 12P = 36, so P = $3.00. The new supply is Q = -12.6 + 12.6P, so 27 - 3P = -12.6 + 12.6P gives 15.6P = 39.6 and P = about $2.54 per pound. Option D wrongly cuts the price itself by 40 percent, and option C has price moving the wrong way, since more supply lowers price.

questions.question: The demand curve for a product is Q = 300 - 2P + 4I, where I is average income in thousands of dollars, and the supply curve is Q = 3P - 50. If I = 25, what are the market-clearing price and quantity?
questions.explanation: With I = 25, demand is Q = 300 - 2P + 100 = 400 - 2P. Setting 400 - 2P = 3P - 50 gives 5P = 450, so P = 90 and Q = 3(90) - 50 = 220. Option C leaves out the income term (350 = 5P), and option D is the answer for I = 50.

questions.question: The demand curve for a product is Q = 300 - 2P + 4I, where I is average income in thousands of dollars, and the supply curve is Q = 3P - 50. If I = 50, what are the market-clearing price and quantity?
questions.explanation: With I = 50, demand is Q = 300 - 2P + 200 = 500 - 2P. Setting 500 - 2P = 3P - 50 gives 5P = 550, so P = 110 and Q = 3(110) - 50 = 280. Option C is the equilibrium when I = 25, so it ignores the income rise that shifts demand to the right.

questions.question: The total demand for U.S. wheat is Q = 3244 - 283P and domestic supply is QS = 1944 + 207P (Q in million bushels, P in dollars per bushel). New export markets add 200 million bushels to demand at every price. What are the new free-market price and quantity?

options.a: P = about $3.06, Q = about 2578 million bushels
options.b: P = about $3.06, Q = about 2778 million bushels
options.c: P = about $2.24, Q = about 2409 million bushels
options.d: P = about $2.65, Q = about 2493 million bushels

questions.explanation: New demand is Q = 3444 - 283P. Setting 3444 - 283P = 1944 + 207P gives 490P = 1500, so P = about $3.06 and Q = 1944 + 207(3.06) = about 2578 million bushels. Option D is the old equilibrium before the extra demand, and option C subtracts the 200 instead of adding it.

questions.question: A vegetable fiber has a world price of $9 per pound, and unlimited imports are available at that price. U.S. supply and demand (million pounds) are: price $3, supply 2, demand 34; $6, supply 4, demand 28; $9, supply 6, demand 22; $12, supply 8, demand 16; $15, supply 10, demand 10; $18, supply 12, demand 4. In a free market, what will be the level of U.S. fiber imports?
questions.explanation: With unlimited imports at $9, the U.S. price is $9. At that price U.S. demand is 22 million pounds and U.S. supply is 6 million pounds, so imports fill the gap of 22 - 6 = 16 million pounds. Option B is domestic supply, option D is total demand, and option C would be correct only at the domestic equilibrium price of $15.

questions.question: Total demand for U.S. wheat is Q = 3244 - 283P, of which domestic demand is QD = 1700 - 107P; domestic supply is QS = 1944 + 207P (Q in million bushels, P in dollars per bushel). Export demand then falls by 40 percent at every price. What happens to the free-market price of wheat?

options.a: It falls from about $2.65 to about $1.63 per bushel
options.b: It stays at about $2.65 per bushel
options.c: It falls from about $2.65 to about $0.98 per bushel
options.d: It falls from about $2.65 to about $2.24 per bushel

questions.explanation: Export demand is total minus domestic: (3244 - 283P) - (1700 - 107P) = 1544 - 176P, and 60 percent of it is 926.4 - 105.6P. New total demand is 2626.4 - 212.6P, so 2626.4 - 212.6P = 1944 + 207P gives P = 682.4/419.6 = about $1.63, down from 1300/490 = about $2.65. Option B ignores the fall in export demand, which shifts total demand to the left and must lower the price.

questions.question: Rental demand in a city is QD = 160 - 8P and supply is QS = 70 + 7P, where Q is in tens of thousands of apartments and P is the average monthly rent in hundreds of dollars. What are the free-market rent and number of apartments?
questions.explanation: Setting 160 - 8P = 70 + 7P gives 15P = 90, so P = 6, which is $600 per month. Then Q = 160 - 8(6) = 112 tens of thousands, or 1,120,000 apartments. Option C forgets to convert the units, and option B uses the demand at a rent of $300 instead of the equilibrium.

questions.question: The copper market is in equilibrium at P = $3 per pound and Q = 18 million metric tons per year, with supply elasticity 1.5 and demand elasticity -0.5, giving supply Q = -9 + 9P and demand Q = 27 - 3P. If copper demand increases by 20 percent at every price, what is the new equilibrium price?
questions.explanation: New demand is 1.2(27 - 3P) = 32.4 - 3.6P. Setting 32.4 - 3.6P = -9 + 9P gives 12.6P = 41.4, so P = about $3.29, with Q = -9 + 9(3.29) = about 20.6 million tons. Option D raises the price itself by 20 percent, and option B is the price when supply also falls by 20 percent.

questions.question: The copper market is in equilibrium at P = $3 per pound and Q = 18 million metric tons per year, with supply elasticity 1.5 and demand elasticity -0.5, giving supply Q = -9 + 9P and demand Q = 27 - 3P. If copper demand increases by 20 percent and copper supply decreases by 20 percent at every price, what are the new equilibrium price and quantity?

options.a: P = about $3.67, Q = about 19.2 million tons
options.b: P = about $3.67, Q = about 24.0 million tons
options.c: P = about $3.29, Q = about 20.6 million tons

questions.explanation: New demand is 32.4 - 3.6P and new supply is 0.8(-9 + 9P) = -7.2 + 7.2P. Setting them equal gives 10.8P = 39.6, so P = about $3.67 and Q = -7.2 + 7.2(3.67) = about 19.2 million tons. Option C ignores the fall in supply, and option B works out quantity from the old supply curve.

questions.question: The world oil market is at P = $50 per barrel, with world demand of 35 billion barrels per year (bb/yr), competitive (non-OPEC) supply of 23 bb/yr and OPEC supply of 12 bb/yr. Short-run demand is D = 36.75 - 0.035P and short-run competitive supply is SC = 21.85 + 0.023P; long-run demand is D = 45.5 - 0.210P and long-run competitive supply is SC = 16.1 + 0.138P. OPEC then raises output by 2 bb/yr to 14 bb/yr. What is the new short-run price of oil?
questions.explanation: In the short run total supply is 21.85 + 0.023P + 14. Setting 36.75 - 0.035P = 35.85 + 0.023P gives 0.058P = 0.90, so P = about $15.52. Because short-run demand and supply are very inelastic, a small rise in output causes a big price fall. Option A is the long-run price.

questions.question: The world oil market is at P = $50 per barrel, with world demand of 35 billion barrels per year (bb/yr), competitive (non-OPEC) supply of 23 bb/yr and OPEC supply of 12 bb/yr. Short-run demand is D = 36.75 - 0.035P and short-run competitive supply is SC = 21.85 + 0.023P; long-run demand is D = 45.5 - 0.210P and long-run competitive supply is SC = 16.1 + 0.138P. OPEC then raises output by 2 bb/yr to 14 bb/yr. What is the new long-run price of oil?
questions.explanation: In the long run total supply is 16.1 + 0.138P + 14. Setting 45.5 - 0.210P = 30.1 + 0.138P gives 0.348P = 15.4, so P = about $44.25. Long-run demand and supply are more elastic, so the price falls far less than in the short run. Option C is the short-run price, and option A has price rising when supply has increased.

questions.question: The natural gas market (Q in trillion cubic feet, Tcf) has supply Q = 15.90 + 0.72PG + 0.05PO and demand Q = 0.02 - 1.8PG + 0.69PO, where PG is the price of gas ($ per thousand cubic feet) and PO is the price of oil ($ per barrel). If the gas market is unregulated and the price of oil rises from $50 to $100, what happens to the free-market price of gas?

options.b: It rises from about $6.40 to about $12.80
options.c: It rises from about $6.40 to about $19.10
options.d: It falls from about $6.40 to about $3.20

questions.explanation: With PO = 100, supply is 15.90 + 5.00 + 0.72PG = 20.90 + 0.72PG and demand is 0.02 + 69.00 - 1.8PG = 69.02 - 1.8PG. Setting them equal gives 2.52PG = 48.12, so PG = about $19.10. Oil is a substitute for gas, so dearer oil raises gas demand much more than gas supply; option B simply doubles the gas price, which the equations do not support.

questions.question: The price that equates the quantity supplied to the quantity demanded in a market is called the
questions.explanation: At the equilibrium or market-clearing price, the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer, so there is neither shortage nor surplus. A ceiling price (option C) and a support price (option B) are prices set by government, usually away from equilibrium. A reservation price (option A) is the most a buyer will pay or the least a seller will accept, not the price that clears the market.

questions.question: The tendency in a free market for price to change until the market clears is called the
questions.explanation: The market mechanism is the process by which shortages push prices up and surpluses push them down until quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. Option D is government interference with that process. Option C describes only how sellers respond to price, and option A is not the name of this process.

questions.question: A situation in which the quantity supplied exceeds the quantity demanded at the current price is called a
questions.explanation: A surplus or excess supply exists when sellers offer more than buyers want at the going price, which happens when price is above equilibrium. Option B is the opposite situation. Options D and C describe the point where the two quantities are equal.

questions.question: In a market, a shortage (excess demand) means that at the current price

options.a: quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded
options.b: both quantity demanded and quantity supplied are zero
options.d: quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied

questions.explanation: A shortage occurs when buyers want more than sellers are offering, which happens when price is below equilibrium. Option A describes a surplus. Option C describes equilibrium, and option B is not what a shortage means.

questions.question: If the current price in a competitive market is above the equilibrium price, what will happen?

options.a: A surplus exists, and the price will tend to fall towards equilibrium
options.b: A shortage exists, and the price will tend to fall towards equilibrium
options.c: A shortage exists, and the price will tend to rise further
options.d: A surplus exists, and the price will tend to rise further

questions.explanation: Above equilibrium, sellers offer more than buyers want, so unsold stock builds up and sellers cut prices until the market clears. Option C wrongly names the situation as a shortage. Option D has the right situation but the wrong direction, and option B gets the situation wrong.

questions.question: At a price below equilibrium in a competitive market, buyers who cannot get the good will

options.a: bid the price up, which reduces quantity demanded and raises quantity supplied until the market clears
options.b: force sellers to cut output, which removes the shortage
options.c: accept the shortage permanently, since price cannot change
options.d: push the price down, which raises quantity demanded further

questions.explanation: When there is a shortage, unsatisfied buyers offer more, so the price rises; along the way quantity demanded falls and quantity supplied rises until they are equal. Option C ignores the market mechanism in a free market. Option D moves price the wrong way and would widen the shortage, and option B would make the shortage worse, not remove it.

questions.question: Other things equal, an increase in demand with supply unchanged will cause equilibrium price and quantity to
questions.explanation: A rightward demand shift creates a shortage at the old price, so price is bid up and sellers move up their supply curve to a larger quantity; both price and quantity rise. Option B follows a fall in demand. Option A is the result of a fall in supply, and option D is the result of a rise in supply.

questions.question: Other things equal, an increase in supply with demand unchanged will cause the equilibrium price to

options.a: rise and the equilibrium quantity to fall
options.b: rise and the equilibrium quantity to rise
options.c: fall and the equilibrium quantity to fall
options.d: fall and the equilibrium quantity to rise

questions.explanation: A rightward supply shift creates a surplus at the old price, so price falls and buyers move down their demand curve to a larger quantity. Option B is the effect of a rise in demand. Option C follows a fall in demand, and option A follows a fall in supply.

questions.question: A pest destroys a large part of the tomato harvest in Kano, while demand for tomatoes is unchanged. The equilibrium price and quantity of tomatoes will
questions.explanation: The pest shifts supply left, so at the old price there is a shortage; price rises and buyers move up their demand curve to a smaller quantity. Option D is the result of a rise in demand. Option B follows a fall in demand, and option A follows a rise in supply.

questions.question: If demand and supply both increase at the same time, then

options.a: equilibrium price falls, but the change in equilibrium quantity is indeterminate
options.b: equilibrium quantity rises, but the change in equilibrium price is indeterminate
options.c: equilibrium price and quantity both definitely rise
options.d: equilibrium price rises, but the change in equilibrium quantity is indeterminate

questions.explanation: Both shifts push quantity up, so quantity certainly rises; but more demand pushes price up while more supply pushes it down, so the price change depends on which shift is bigger. Option D swaps which variable is certain. Option C wrongly treats the price rise as certain, and option A wrongly treats a price fall as certain.

questions.question: If demand increases while supply decreases, then

options.a: equilibrium quantity rises, but the change in equilibrium price is indeterminate
options.b: equilibrium price falls, but the change in equilibrium quantity is indeterminate
options.c: equilibrium price and quantity both definitely rise
options.d: equilibrium price rises, but the change in equilibrium quantity is indeterminate

questions.explanation: Both changes push price up, so price certainly rises; but more demand raises quantity while less supply lowers it, so the quantity change depends on the relative sizes of the shifts. Option A swaps which variable is certain. Option C wrongly treats the quantity rise as certain, and option B has price moving the wrong way.

questions.question: If demand decreases while supply increases, then

options.a: equilibrium price and quantity both definitely fall
options.b: equilibrium price falls, but the change in equilibrium quantity is indeterminate
options.c: equilibrium price rises, but the change in equilibrium quantity is indeterminate
options.d: equilibrium quantity falls, but the change in equilibrium price is indeterminate

questions.explanation: Both changes push price down, so price certainly falls; but lower demand reduces quantity while higher supply raises it, so the net effect on quantity is uncertain. Option D swaps which variable is certain. Option A wrongly treats the quantity fall as certain, and option C has price moving the wrong way.

questions.question: Which combination of changes will DEFINITELY reduce the equilibrium quantity, whatever the sizes of the shifts?

options.a: An increase in demand together with an increase in supply
options.b: An increase in demand together with a decrease in supply
options.c: A decrease in demand together with an increase in supply
options.d: A decrease in demand together with a decrease in supply

questions.explanation: When both demand and supply fall, each shift on its own lowers quantity, so quantity definitely falls, while the price change is uncertain. In options B and C the two shifts pull quantity in opposite directions, so the result depends on their sizes. Option A definitely raises quantity rather than reducing it.

questions.question: After a disaster, office space in a city was destroyed (supply fell), but many firms also moved away (demand fell). Rents actually fell. This shows that when demand and supply both fall,

options.b: the change in price depends on which shift is larger

questions.explanation: With both curves shifting left, quantity definitely falls but price can go either way; here the demand fall was larger than the supply fall, so rents dropped. Options D and A wrongly treat the price change as certain in one direction. Option C is wrong because two leftward shifts both reduce quantity.

questions.question: The simple supply-demand model of price determination assumes that the market is

options.b: an oligopoly in which a few firms agree on prices
options.c: roughly competitive, with buyers and sellers having little market power
options.d: a monopoly, with one seller setting the price

questions.explanation: The model works because each buyer and seller is a price taker, so price is set by the interaction of total demand and supply. Option D is excluded because a monopolist has no simple one-to-one relation between price and quantity supplied. Option A describes intervention, not a free market, and option B also involves market power.

questions.question: When the government imposes a specific (per-unit) tax of N10 on sellers of a good, the supply curve

options.a: shifts upward (to the left) by N10 at every quantity
options.b: does not move, but the demand curve shifts up by N10
options.c: becomes vertical at the old equilibrium quantity
options.d: shifts downward (to the right) by N10 at every quantity

questions.explanation: Sellers now need N10 more per unit to be willing to supply each quantity, so the supply curve moves up by exactly the tax at every quantity. Option D describes a per-unit subsidy. Option B is wrong for a tax collected from sellers, and option C has no basis.

questions.question: With a normal downward-sloping demand curve and upward-sloping supply curve, a per-unit tax on sellers will usually cause the price paid by buyers to

options.a: rise by exactly the amount of the tax, so buyers bear all of it
options.c: rise by less than the tax, so buyers and sellers share the burden
options.d: stay the same, so sellers bear all of the tax

questions.explanation: When neither curve is vertical or horizontal, the buyers' price rises by part of the tax and the sellers' net price falls by the rest, so the burden is shared. Option A happens only when demand is perfectly inelastic or supply perfectly elastic. Option D happens only when demand is perfectly elastic or supply perfectly inelastic, and option B has price moving the wrong way.

questions.question: The burden (incidence) of a per-unit tax falls more heavily on buyers when

options.b: demand is more elastic than supply
options.c: demand is more inelastic than supply

questions.explanation: The side of the market that is less able to respond to price changes bears more of a tax, so when demand is relatively inelastic, buyers pay most of it through a higher price. Option B puts more of the burden on sellers. Options A and D are cases where sellers bear the whole tax.

questions.question: If the demand for a good is perfectly inelastic and a per-unit tax is placed on sellers, then

options.a: buyers bear the whole tax, and the equilibrium quantity does not change
options.b: buyers and sellers share the tax equally, and quantity falls
options.c: sellers bear the whole tax, and the equilibrium quantity does not change
options.d: buyers bear the whole tax, and the equilibrium quantity falls sharply

questions.explanation: With a vertical demand curve, buyers keep buying the same quantity whatever the price, so price rises by the full tax and quantity stays the same. Option C is what happens when supply, not demand, is perfectly inelastic. Option B assumes equal slopes, and option D is wrong because a vertical demand fixes quantity.

questions.question: A per-unit subsidy paid to producers of a good will, other things equal,

options.a: shift the demand curve to the right, raising both price and quantity
options.b: shift the supply curve down (to the right), lowering the buyers' price and raising quantity
options.c: shift the supply curve up (to the left), raising the buyers' price and lowering quantity
options.d: leave price and quantity unchanged, since it only transfers money

questions.explanation: A subsidy lowers producers' effective cost per unit, so they will supply each quantity at a lower price; the supply curve moves down, buyers pay less and more is traded. Option C describes a per-unit tax. Option A confuses a producer subsidy with a demand change, and option D ignores the effect on supply.

questions.question: In a market, Qd = 100 - 2P and Qs = 20 + 2P. The equilibrium price is
questions.explanation: Setting Qd = Qs gives 100 - 2P = 20 + 2P, so 4P = 80 and P = N20 (and Q = 60). Option B adds the intercepts (120/4) instead of subtracting them. Option D divides 80 by 2 instead of by the combined slope of 4, and option C divides 100 by 4, ignoring the supply intercept.

questions.question: The market for a good has Qd = 240 - 4P and Qs = -60 + 6P. The equilibrium quantity is
questions.explanation: Solving 240 - 4P = -60 + 6P gives 10P = 300, so P = 30, and then Q = 240 - 4(30) = 120 units (check: -60 + 180 = 120). Option D is the equilibrium price, not the quantity. Option A uses only 6 x 30 and ignores the supply intercept, and option B is the value of 10P, the step before dividing by 10.

questions.question: For a good, Qd = 500 - 10P and Qs = -100 + 20P (equilibrium price N20). If the price is N25, the market has
questions.explanation: At P = 25, Qd = 500 - 250 = 250 and Qs = -100 + 500 = 400, so sellers offer 150 more than buyers want, a surplus. Option C gets the type wrong, since price is above equilibrium. Option D reports quantity demanded instead of the gap, and option B simply multiplies the 5-naira price gap by 10.

questions.question: With Qd = 240 - 4P and Qs = -60 + 6P, how large is the excess demand when the price is held at N15?
questions.explanation: At P = 15, Qd = 240 - 60 = 180 and Qs = -60 + 90 = 30, so excess demand is 180 - 30 = 150 units. Option A is quantity demanded alone and option C is quantity supplied alone. Option D adds the two quantities instead of subtracting them.

questions.question: The market for wheat in a year has supply QS = 1800 + 240P and demand QD = 3550 - 266P (quantities in millions of bushels, P in dollars per bushel). The equilibrium price, to two decimal places, is
questions.explanation: Setting supply equal to demand gives 1800 + 240P = 3550 - 266P, so 506P = 1750 and P = $3.46. Option B divides 1750 by the demand slope only and option A by the supply slope only. Option D adds the two intercepts instead of subtracting them.

questions.question: In a later year the wheat market has demand QD = 2900 - 125P and supply QS = 1460 + 115P (millions of bushels, P in dollars). The equilibrium quantity is
questions.explanation: Solving 1460 + 115P = 2900 - 125P gives 240P = 1440, so P = $6, and Q = 1460 + 115(6) = 2,150 million bushels. Option C is the demand intercept, the quantity at a zero price. Option A is the equilibrium price, and option D comes from wrongly using 125 instead of 115 when substituting into supply.

questions.question: A market starts with Qd = 100 - 2P and Qs = 20 + 2P, so P = N20 and Q = 60. Higher incomes shift demand to Qd = 120 - 2P. The new equilibrium is
questions.explanation: Solving 120 - 2P = 20 + 2P gives 4P = 100, so P = 25, and Q = 20 + 2(25) = 70; price and quantity both rise, as expected for an increase in demand. Option D keeps the old price, which would leave a shortage. Option B keeps the old quantity, and option C gets the price right but substitutes it wrongly.

questions.question: A market has Qd = 100 - 2P and Qs = 20 + 2P. A rise in input costs changes supply to Qs = 2P. The new equilibrium price and quantity are
questions.explanation: With Qs = 2P, setting 100 - 2P = 2P gives P = 25 and Q = 50, so price rises and quantity falls, as expected when supply decreases. Option B is what a supply increase would give. Option C keeps the old price, which would leave a shortage, and option A is the price at which nothing would be demanded.

questions.question: A market starts with Qd = 100 - 2P and Qs = 20 + 2P (P = N20, Q = 60). Demand then shifts to Qd = 130 - 2P and supply to Qs = 50 + 2P. The new equilibrium is
questions.explanation: Solving 130 - 2P = 50 + 2P gives 4P = 80, so P = 20, and Q = 50 + 40 = 90: quantity rises while price is unchanged because both curves shifted out by the same 30 units. Option B is the result of the demand shift alone, and option C the supply shift alone. Option A wrongly assumes nothing changes.

questions.question: In a market, Qd = a - 3P and Qs = 10 + 2P. If the equilibrium price is N8, the value of a is
questions.explanation: At P = 8 the quantity supplied is 10 + 2(8) = 26, and in equilibrium demand must equal 26, so a - 3(8) = 26 and a = 26 + 24 = 50. Option C is the equilibrium quantity, not the intercept. Option B adds only 8 instead of 3 x 8, and option D is just the slope term 3 x 8.

questions.question: A market has inverse demand P = 40 - 0.5Q and inverse supply P = 10 + Q. The equilibrium price and quantity are
questions.explanation: Setting 40 - 0.5Q = 10 + Q gives 1.5Q = 30, so Q = 20, and P = 10 + 20 = 30. Option B swaps price and quantity. Option A divides 30 by 2 instead of 1.5, and option D divides 30 by 0.5, ignoring the supply slope.

questions.question: Demand is Qd = 60 - 3P + 0.5I, where I is an income index, and supply is Qs = 4P. When I = 20, the equilibrium price and quantity are
questions.explanation: With I = 20, demand becomes Qd = 60 - 3P + 10 = 70 - 3P; setting 70 - 3P = 4P gives 7P = 70, so P = 10 and Q = 40. Option B leaves out the income term (60/7). Option A adds the full value of I (20) instead of 0.5I, and option D divides 70 by 5 using a wrong slope.

questions.question: Demand for a life-saving drug is fixed at Qd = 100 units whatever the price, and supply is Qs = -20 + 4P, so the equilibrium price is N30. A per-unit tax of N5 is imposed on sellers. The new price paid by buyers is
questions.explanation: The tax shifts supply to Qs = -20 + 4(P - 5); setting this equal to 100 gives 4P = 140, so P = N35 and buyers pay the whole N5 because demand is perfectly inelastic. Option C assumes sellers absorb the tax. Option D assumes the tax is split equally, and option B subtracts the tax instead of adding it.

questions.question: In a market, Qd = 100 - 2P and Qs = 20 + 2P (equilibrium P = N20, Q = 60). A per-unit tax of N6 is imposed on sellers, so supply becomes Qs = 20 + 2(P - 6). The new price paid by buyers is
questions.explanation: Setting 100 - 2P = 20 + 2(P - 6) gives 100 - 2P = 8 + 2P, so 4P = 92 and buyers pay N23; sellers keep 23 - 6 = N17 and the equal slopes split the tax N3 each. Option C assumes buyers pay the whole tax. Option A ignores the tax, and option B is the sellers' net price, not the buyers' price.

questions.question: A market has Qd = 120 - 2P and Qs = -30 + 3P, so the equilibrium price is N30. A per-unit tax of N5 is placed on sellers. After the tax, the net price received by sellers is
questions.explanation: With the tax, -30 + 3(P - 5) = 120 - 2P gives 5P = 165, so buyers pay N33 and sellers keep 33 - 5 = N28; buyers bear N3 and sellers N2 of the tax because demand is steeper relative to supply here. Option B is the buyers' price. Option D assumes sellers bear the whole tax, and option C ignores the tax.

questions.question: In a market with Qd = 120 - 2P and Qs = -30 + 3P, a per-unit tax of N5 on sellers raises the buyers' price to N33. What is the total tax revenue collected by the government?
questions.explanation: After the tax, quantity is Qd = 120 - 2(33) = 54 units, so revenue = tax per unit x quantity = 5 x 54 = N270. Option C uses the old quantity of 60. Option A multiplies the buyers' price by 5, and option D is buyers' spending (33 x 54), not tax revenue.

questions.question: A market has Qd = 120 - 2P and Qs = -30 + 3P (equilibrium P = N30). The government pays producers a subsidy of N5 per unit, so supply becomes Qs = -30 + 3(P + 5). The new price paid by buyers is
questions.explanation: Setting 120 - 2P = -30 + 3(P + 5) gives 120 - 2P = -15 + 3P, so 5P = 135 and buyers pay N27, while sellers receive 27 + 5 = N32. Option D assumes buyers get the whole subsidy. Option C is the sellers' price including the subsidy, and option A ignores the subsidy.

questions.question: In a market with Qd = 120 - 2P and Qs = -30 + 3P, a producer subsidy of N5 per unit lowers the buyers' price to N27. What is the total cost of the subsidy to the government?
