questions.explanation: After the subsidy, quantity is 120 - 2(27) = 66 units, so the cost = subsidy per unit x quantity = 5 x 66 = N330. Option C uses the old quantity of 60. Option B multiplies the buyers' price by 5, and option A is buyers' spending (27 x 66), not the subsidy bill.

questions.question: Copper supply is Q = -9 + 9P and, after a fall in demand, copper demand is Q = 12.15 - 1.35P (Q in million metric tons, P in dollars per pound). The new equilibrium price, to two decimal places, is
questions.explanation: Setting -9 + 9P = 12.15 - 1.35P gives 10.35P = 21.15, so P = $2.04. Option B was the price before demand fell. Option A subtracts 9 from 12.15 instead of adding it, and option D divides 21.15 by the supply slope of 9 alone.

questions.question: In a market with Qd = 100 - 2P and Qs = 20 + 2P, the government fixes the price at N10. At this price there is
questions.explanation: At P = 10, Qd = 100 - 20 = 80 and Qs = 20 + 20 = 40, so buyers want 40 more units than are offered, a shortage of 40. Option A gets the size right but the type wrong, since price is below equilibrium. Option C reports quantity demanded instead of the gap, and option B has neither the type nor the size right.

questions.question: Natural-gas supply is Q = 15.90 + 0.72PG + 0.05PO and demand is Q = 0.02 - 1.8PG + 0.69PO, where PG is the gas price and PO = $50 is the oil price. If PG is held at a ceiling of $3.00, excess demand is approximately
questions.explanation: At PG = 3 and PO = 50, quantity supplied is 15.90 + 2.16 + 2.50 = 20.56 Tcf and quantity demanded is 0.02 - 5.40 + 34.50 = 29.12 Tcf, so excess demand is 29.12 - 20.56 = 8.56 Tcf. Options A and C are quantity supplied and quantity demanded on their own, not the gap. Option D leaves out the oil-price term in the supply equation.

questions.question: If government imposes a rent ceiling below equilibrium rent, it will lead to: ______.
questions.explanation: A rent ceiling below equilibrium holds rent at a level where more people want housing than landlords are willing to supply. Quantity demanded rises while quantity supplied falls, creating a shortage of housing. Option A, a surplus, happens with a price floor above equilibrium, and option D is wrong because a lower rent reduces landlords' willingness to supply.

questions.question: When rent is artificially lowered below equilibrium, quantity demanded of hostel accommodation will: ______.
questions.explanation: When rent is held below equilibrium, accommodation becomes cheaper, so by the law of demand more students want hostel space and quantity demanded increases. At the same time landlords supply less, which creates a shortage. Option A describes what happens to quantity supplied, not quantity demanded.

questions.question: If the Lagos State Government were to impose rent control on students' housing around university vicinities, landlords are likely to: ______.
questions.explanation: Rent control holds rent below the market level, so renting out rooms becomes less profitable and landlords offer fewer rooms or convert them to other uses. Quantity supplied therefore falls, which worsens the housing shortage. Options A and D are wrong because a lower controlled rent gives landlords less reason to supply more, and option B ignores how supply responds to price.

questions.question: The government fixes the prices of beef and chicken below their market-clearing levels, creating shortages. What will happen to the price of pork, a substitute that is not regulated?

options.a: It will fall, because pork producers move into beef and chicken production
options.b: It will rise, because consumers who cannot buy enough beef and chicken increase their demand for pork
options.c: It will not change, because pork is not regulated
options.d: It will fall, because the price controls lower meat prices generally

questions.explanation: With ceilings below equilibrium, quantity demanded of beef and chicken exceeds quantity supplied, and the size of each shortage depends on how far the ceiling is below equilibrium and on the elasticities of demand and supply. Consumers who are rationed out switch to pork, a substitute, so the demand for pork shifts right and its price rises. Option C is wrong because a change in the market for substitutes shifts pork demand even though pork itself is not controlled.

questions.question: Market rents for two-bedroom apartments in a college town are $700 per month and are expected to rise to $900 within a year. The city council caps rents at $700. Will this policy benefit all students?

options.a: No; every student must now pay more than the market rent
options.b: Yes; every student pays less rent than the market rate
options.c: Yes; the cap increases the number of apartments available
options.d: No; students who obtain apartments at $700 gain, but others cannot find apartments because the cap creates a shortage

questions.explanation: Once demand rises so that the market rent would be $900, the $700 cap acts as a price ceiling below equilibrium, so quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied. Students who secure an apartment pay less and gain, but those left out are worse off. Option B ignores the shortage, and option C is wrong because a lower rent reduces, not increases, the quantity of apartments landlords supply.

questions.question: Suppose the demand for natural gas is perfectly inelastic. If the government sets a ceiling on the price of natural gas below the market-clearing price, what is the effect?

options.a: Quantity demanded is unchanged, quantity supplied falls, and the shortage equals the fall in quantity supplied
options.b: Quantity demanded falls and the market ends up in surplus
options.c: Quantity demanded rises and quantity supplied falls, so the shortage is larger than with normal demand
options.d: There is no effect, because buyers do not respond to price

questions.explanation: With perfectly inelastic (vertical) demand, buyers want the same quantity whatever the price, so the ceiling does not change quantity demanded. Producers, however, supply less at the lower price, so the shortage is exactly the cut in quantity supplied. Option C is wrong because quantity demanded cannot rise when demand is perfectly inelastic, and option D ignores the response of sellers.

questions.question: In a competitive market, the quantities demanded and supplied (millions per year) are: at $60, demand 22 and supply 14; at $80, demand 20 and supply 16; at $100, demand 18 and supply 18; at $120, demand 16 and supply 20. If the government sets a price ceiling of $80, will there be a shortage, and how large?

options.a: Yes, a shortage of 2 million units
options.b: Yes, a shortage of 6 million units
options.c: Yes, a shortage of 4 million units
options.d: No, there will be no shortage

questions.explanation: Equilibrium is at $100, where 18 million are demanded and supplied, so a $80 ceiling is binding. At $80, quantity demanded is 20 million but quantity supplied is only 16 million, giving a shortage of 20 - 16 = 4 million. Option A compares demand at $80 with the old equilibrium quantity, and option D wrongly treats the ceiling as non-binding.

questions.question: Total demand for U.S. wheat is Q = 3244 - 283P, of which domestic demand is QD = 1700 - 107P; domestic supply is QS = 1944 + 207P (Q in million bushels, P in dollars per bushel). Export demand then falls by 40 percent at every price. How much wheat must the government buy to raise the price to $3.50 per bushel, and what will this cost?

options.a: About 786 million bushels, costing about $2.75 billion
options.b: About 415 million bushels, costing about $1.45 billion
options.c: About 786 million bushels, costing about $1.28 billion
options.d: About 2669 million bushels, costing about $9.34 billion

questions.explanation: After the drop, demand is 2626.4 - 212.6P. At $3.50, supply is 1944 + 207(3.5) = 2668.5 and private demand is 2626.4 - 212.6(3.5) = 1882.3, so the government must buy 2668.5 - 1882.3 = about 786 million bushels at $3.50, costing about $2.75 billion. Option B uses the demand before export demand fell, and option C values the purchase at the free-market price of $1.63 instead of $3.50.

questions.question: The natural gas market (Q in trillion cubic feet, Tcf) has supply Q = 15.90 + 0.72PG + 0.05PO and demand Q = 0.02 - 1.8PG + 0.69PO, where PG is the price of gas ($ per thousand cubic feet) and PO is the price of oil ($ per barrel). With PO = $50, how much excess demand would there be if the price of gas were regulated at $4.50?

options.c: Zero, because $4.50 is above the free-market price

questions.explanation: With PO = 50, supply is 18.40 + 0.72PG and demand is 34.52 - 1.8PG (free-market PG = 16.12/2.52 = about $6.40). At $4.50, supply is 18.40 + 3.24 = 21.64 and demand is 34.52 - 8.10 = 26.42, so excess demand is 26.42 - 21.64 = 4.78 Tcf. Option D is the excess demand at a regulated price of $3.00, and option C is wrong because $4.50 is below the free-market price.

questions.question: In economics, the model that explains recurring fluctuations of price and output in markets where producers decide current output on the basis of the previous period's price is called the
questions.explanation: The cobweb model shows how a lag between the production decision and the sale of output can make price and quantity swing around equilibrium, tracing a cobweb-like pattern on the supply and demand diagram. Option B and option D are macroeconomic models of investment and income, while option C explains price rigidity in oligopoly.

questions.question: In the basic cobweb model, the quantity supplied in period t depends on the

options.c: price expected in period t+1 under perfect foresight

questions.explanation: Producers in the cobweb model base this period's output on last period's price, because output must be planned before the current price is known. Option A is what determines quantity demanded, not quantity supplied, and option C contradicts the model, which assumes producers simply expect last period's price to continue.

questions.question: The main reason the cobweb model uses a lagged supply function is that

options.a: production takes time, so output must be decided before the selling price is known
options.b: consumers respond to price changes only after a delay
options.c: government fixes the price at the start of every season
options.d: producers hold large stocks that they release slowly

questions.explanation: In many agricultural markets there is a gestation period between planting and harvest, so the amount offered for sale this season was fixed by decisions made earlier at an earlier price. Option B is wrong because demand responds to the current price in the model, and option D is wrong because the model assumes output is perishable and sold in the period it is produced.

questions.question: Tomato prices were very high in one season, so many farmers in Kano planted more tomatoes. The next season there was a glut and prices crashed, so farmers planted less, and prices rose sharply again the season after. This pattern is best explained by the
questions.explanation: The alternating high and low prices come from farmers reacting to last season's price, which is exactly the lagged-supply mechanism of the cobweb model. Option C involves a government-imposed maximum price, which is absent here, and option B relates to labour supply at high wages, not crop cycles.

questions.question: In the cobweb model, with price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis, the fluctuations in price and output become smaller each period (convergent cobweb) when

options.a: the supply curve is flatter than the demand curve
options.c: the supply curve is steeper than the demand curve
options.d: the supply and demand curves have the same absolute slope

questions.explanation: When supply is steeper than demand, producers respond only weakly to last period's price, so each overshoot is smaller than the one before and price converges to equilibrium. Option A gives an explosive (divergent) cobweb, and option D gives a continuous oscillation of constant size.

questions.question: In the cobweb model, the oscillations of price and output become larger and larger (divergent or explosive cobweb) when, at equilibrium,

options.a: supply and demand are equally elastic (in absolute value)
options.b: supply is more elastic than demand (in absolute value)
options.c: demand is more elastic than supply (in absolute value)
options.d: demand is perfectly elastic and supply is perfectly inelastic

questions.explanation: If supply is more responsive than demand, a small price change triggers a large output response, which then needs an even bigger price change to clear the market, so the swings grow. Option C is the condition for a convergent cobweb, and option A is the condition for a continuous (constant-amplitude) cobweb.

questions.question: In the cobweb model, price and output oscillate around equilibrium with a constant amplitude, neither growing nor dying out, when

options.a: the supply and demand curves have equal slopes in absolute value
options.b: the supply curve is steeper than the demand curve
options.c: the demand curve is perfectly elastic
options.d: the supply curve is flatter than the demand curve

questions.explanation: With equal absolute slopes, every overshoot is exactly as large as the previous one, so the cycle repeats forever around equilibrium. Option B gives a convergent (damped) cobweb, while option D gives a divergent (explosive) one.

questions.question: In the cobweb model, a situation in which price and output move further away from equilibrium in each successive period is described as
questions.explanation: A divergent cobweb is one where the deviations from equilibrium grow each period, so the market never settles. Option D describes deviations that shrink over time, option A describes deviations of constant size, and option B is the opposite of what is happening.

questions.question: In the cobweb model with demand Qd(t) = a - bP(t) and supply Qs(t) = c + dP(t-1), where a, b, c and d are positive constants, the price path converges to equilibrium if
questions.explanation: Each period's price deviation equals -(d/b) times the previous one, so deviations shrink only when d/b is less than 1, that is d < b. Option C makes the deviations grow (divergent), option D makes them constant (continuous oscillation), and option A only ensures a positive equilibrium, not stability.

questions.question: In a cobweb market, demand is Qd(t) = 100 - 2P(t) and supply is Qs(t) = 10 + P(t-1), with P in naira. The long-run equilibrium price, where P(t) = P(t-1), is
questions.explanation: At equilibrium the price is the same in every period, so 100 - 2P = 10 + P, giving 3P = 90 and P = N30. Option B comes from dividing 90 by (2 - 1) instead of (2 + 1), and option A comes from adding 10 to 100 instead of subtracting it.

questions.question: In a cobweb market, demand is Qd(t) = 100 - 2P(t) and supply is Qs(t) = 10 + P(t-1). If the price in period 0 is N36, what is the market-clearing price in period 1?
questions.explanation: Farmers supply 10 + 36 = 46 units in period 1, and price must fall until buyers take all 46 units: 100 - 2P = 46, so P = 54/2 = N27. Option B is the quantity supplied, not the price, and option D forgets to divide by 2.

questions.question: In a cobweb market, demand is Qd(t) = 100 - 2P(t) and supply is Qs(t) = 10 + P(t-1). The price in period 0 is N36 and the price in period 1 is N27. What is the market-clearing price in period 2?
questions.explanation: In period 2 farmers supply 10 + 27 = 37 units, and buyers absorb them when 100 - 2P = 37, so P = 63/2 = N31.50. Option D is the quantity supplied rather than the price, and option A simply repeats the period 1 price.

questions.question: In a cobweb market, demand is Qd(t) = 60 - P(t) and supply is Qs(t) = 2P(t-1). Starting away from equilibrium, the price path will be

options.a: a smooth movement to equilibrium without any oscillation
options.b: divergent, because supply responds more strongly to price than demand does
options.c: a continuous oscillation, because both curves have the same slope
options.d: convergent, because demand responds more strongly to price than supply does

questions.explanation: Here d = 2 and b = 1, so each price deviation is -(2/1) = -2 times the previous one, and the swings double in size every period. Option D would need d < b, option C would need d = b, and option A never happens in the cobweb because the factor -(d/b) is negative, so price always alternates above and below equilibrium.

questions.question: In a cobweb market, demand is Qd(t) = 90 - 3P(t) and supply is Qs(t) = 3P(t-1) - 30. The equilibrium price is N20. If the market starts at a price different from N20, price will

options.a: oscillate around N20 with a constant amplitude
options.b: stay at the starting price forever
options.d: move further and further away from N20

questions.explanation: Demand and supply have the same price coefficient (3), so the ratio d/b equals 1 and each deviation is exactly reversed in the next period, giving a continuous cycle of constant size. Option C would require d < b and option D would require d > b.

questions.question: Which of the following markets is most likely to show cobweb-type price fluctuations?

options.a: Electricity sold at a tariff fixed by a regulator
options.b: Recharge cards, whose supply can be increased within hours
options.c: Bread from a bakery that adjusts output every morning
options.d: Yam, where planting decisions are made many months before harvest

questions.explanation: Cobweb cycles need a production lag, which is typical of crops and livestock like yam, where output is fixed long before the selling price is known. Options B and C can adjust supply almost immediately to current price, and option A has a regulated price that does not respond to market conditions.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an assumption of the basic cobweb model?

options.a: Output produced in a period is sold in that period at whatever price clears the market
options.b: Quantity demanded depends on the current period's price
options.c: Quantity supplied depends on the previous period's price
options.d: Producers correctly forecast next period's market price

questions.explanation: The cobweb model assumes producers naively expect last period's price to continue, so they do not correctly forecast the next price; that is why they keep overshooting. Options C, B and A are genuine assumptions of the model: lagged supply, current-price demand and no storage of output.

questions.question: A legal maximum price, set by government below the market-clearing price, is called a
questions.explanation: A price ceiling is the highest price sellers are legally allowed to charge, and it only has an effect when it is set below equilibrium. Option A and option D are minimum prices set above equilibrium, while option C is the market-clearing price itself.

questions.question: When government imposes a price ceiling below the equilibrium price, the market will experience

options.a: a shortage, because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
options.b: no change in quantity, only a lower price
options.c: a surplus, because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
options.d: an increase in the quantity supplied

questions.explanation: At a price below equilibrium buyers want more than before while sellers offer less, so excess demand appears. Option C is the effect of a binding price floor, and option D is wrong because a lower price moves sellers down their supply curve, reducing the quantity supplied.

questions.question: Government sets a maximum price of N900 for a bag of cement whose equilibrium price is N800. The most likely effect is that

options.a: a black market for cement develops
options.b: the ceiling has no effect and the market stays at equilibrium

questions.explanation: A ceiling above the equilibrium price is non-binding: sellers can still charge the market price of N800, which is legal, so nothing changes. Options D and A only arise when the ceiling is set below equilibrium, and option C is the effect of a binding floor.

questions.question: After a maximum pump price for petrol is set below the market-clearing level, long queues form at filling stations and some people resell petrol in jerrycans at far higher prices by the roadside. The roadside trade is an example of
questions.explanation: A black market is illegal trading at prices above the legal ceiling, which arises because some buyers are willing to pay more than the controlled price for the scarce good. Option B is a minimum price, and option D is wrong because the controlled market does not clear: there are queues.

questions.question: When a binding price ceiling creates a shortage, which of the following is NOT a way the limited quantity may be allocated?

options.c: Queuing on a first-come, first-served basis
options.d: Letting the price rise until quantity demanded equals quantity supplied

questions.explanation: Under a binding ceiling the price cannot legally rise to clear the market, so the price mechanism is exactly what is NOT available. Options C, A and B are genuine non-price rationing methods that replace the price mechanism when there is a shortage.

questions.question: The demand for a good is Qd = 200 - 4P and the supply is Qs = -40 + 2P, with P in naira. If government sets a price ceiling of N30, the resulting shortage is
questions.explanation: At N30, quantity demanded is 200 - 4(30) = 80 and quantity supplied is -40 + 2(30) = 20, so the shortage is 80 - 20 = 60 units. Option C is only the quantity demanded, option B is only the quantity supplied, and option A is the equilibrium quantity.

questions.question: The demand for a good is Qd = 200 - 4P and the supply is Qs = -40 + 2P. If government sets a price ceiling of N30, the quantity actually bought and sold in the legal market is
questions.explanation: Trade cannot exceed what sellers are willing to offer, so with a ceiling the quantity traded is the quantity supplied, -40 + 2(30) = 20 units. Option A is what buyers want but cannot get, option D is the equilibrium quantity that would be traded without the ceiling, and option C is the shortage.

questions.question: The demand for a good is Qd = 200 - 4P and the supply is Qs = -40 + 2P. A ceiling of N30 limits supply to 20 units. The highest price buyers would be willing to pay for those 20 units on a black market is
questions.explanation: Buyers' willingness to pay for the 20th unit is found from the demand curve: 20 = 200 - 4P, so P = 180/4 = N45. Option D is the legal ceiling, option A is the free-market equilibrium price, and option C is the price at which quantity demanded falls to zero.

questions.question: In a market, demand is Qd = 120 - 2P and supply is Qs = 3P - 30, with P in naira. The equilibrium price is N30. If government imposes a price ceiling of N25, the shortage is
questions.explanation: At N25, quantity demanded is 120 - 50 = 70 and quantity supplied is 75 - 30 = 45, so excess demand is 70 - 45 = 25 units. Option C and option B are just the quantities demanded and supplied, and option A is the equilibrium quantity.

questions.question: Which statement about a binding price ceiling is correct?

options.a: All consumers gain and producers are unaffected
options.b: Nobody gains, because quantity traded stays the same
options.c: Producers gain because they sell more at the controlled price
options.d: Consumers who can still buy the good gain, producers lose, and consumers who are rationed out lose

questions.explanation: Buyers who obtain the good pay less, but sellers receive a lower price on fewer units, and buyers who cannot obtain it are worse off. Option A ignores the rationed-out consumers and the producers, option C is wrong because sellers actually sell less, and option B is wrong because the quantity traded falls.

questions.question: A state government fixes maximum rents in Lagos well below the market level. Which outcome is most likely over time?

options.a: A surplus of empty apartments as landlords build more
options.b: A shortage of rental apartments, with long searches and some landlords collecting illegal extra payments
options.c: No change, since housing demand is fixed
options.d: Rents and the number of apartments both rise

questions.explanation: A rent ceiling below equilibrium lowers the quantity of housing supplied and raises the quantity demanded, so tenants face a shortage, and side payments act as a hidden black market. Option A is the effect of a price floor, option D contradicts the legal maximum, and option C is wrong because demand still responds to price.

questions.question: A legal minimum price, set by government above the market-clearing price, is called a
questions.explanation: A price floor is the lowest price at which a good may legally be sold, and it is effective only when it is set above equilibrium. Option C is a maximum price set below equilibrium, option A is the market-clearing price, and option B is the illegal price that arises under a ceiling.

questions.question: A binding price floor set above the equilibrium price leads to

options.a: a surplus, because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
options.b: the market clearing at a higher quantity
options.c: a rise in the quantity demanded
options.d: a shortage, because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied

questions.explanation: At a price above equilibrium sellers want to sell more and buyers want to buy less, so unsold output (excess supply) appears. Option D is the effect of a binding ceiling, and options C and B are wrong because a higher price reduces the quantity demanded.

questions.question: For a price control to change the market outcome, a price ceiling must be set ___ the equilibrium price and a price floor must be set ___ the equilibrium price.
questions.explanation: A maximum price only binds if it stops the price reaching equilibrium from above, so it must lie below equilibrium, while a minimum price binds only if it lies above equilibrium. Option C reverses the two, and those controls would simply be ignored by the market.

questions.question: A national minimum wage set above the equilibrium wage in a competitive labour market will most likely cause

options.a: higher employment, because workers earn more
options.c: a shortage of workers, because firms want to hire more
options.d: unemployment, because more people want to work than firms want to hire

questions.explanation: A minimum wage is a price floor in the labour market, so at a wage above equilibrium the quantity of labour supplied exceeds the quantity demanded, which is unemployment. Option C would follow from a wage set below equilibrium, and option A is wrong because firms hire fewer workers at a higher wage.

questions.question: Government guarantees cocoa farmers a price above the market-clearing price and promises to keep the market price at that level. To do this, government must

options.a: buy and store the surplus that private buyers will not take
options.b: tax cocoa farmers to reduce their output
options.c: impose a maximum price on cocoa
options.d: sell cocoa from its own stocks to raise supply

questions.explanation: At a guaranteed price above equilibrium farmers produce more than private buyers want, so the price can only be held up if government buys the excess supply. Option D would push the price down, option C is a ceiling, which is the opposite policy, and option B would hurt rather than support farmers.

questions.question: The demand for a good is Qd = 200 - 4P and the supply is Qs = -40 + 2P, with P in naira. If government sets a price floor of N45, the surplus is
questions.explanation: At N45, quantity supplied is -40 + 2(45) = 50 and quantity demanded is 200 - 4(45) = 20, so excess supply is 50 - 20 = 30 units. Option C is just the quantity supplied, option D is the quantity demanded, and option A adds them instead of subtracting.

questions.question: Demand is Qd = 200 - 4P and supply is Qs = -40 + 2P. Government sets a guaranteed price of N45 and buys all the unsold output at that price. How much does government spend?
questions.explanation: The surplus at N45 is 50 - 20 = 30 units, and buying them at N45 each costs 30 x 45 = N1,350. Option D values all 50 units supplied, option B values only the 20 units bought by consumers, and option A wrongly uses the equilibrium price of N40.

questions.question: In a market, demand is Qd = 120 - 2P and supply is Qs = 3P - 30, with P in naira. If government imposes a price floor of N40, the surplus is
questions.explanation: At N40, quantity supplied is 3(40) - 30 = 90 and quantity demanded is 120 - 2(40) = 40, giving a surplus of 90 - 40 = 50 units. Options D and B are only one side of the market, and option A is the equilibrium quantity at N30.

questions.question: In a labour market, labour demand is Ld = 500 - 10W and labour supply is Ls = 20W - 100, where W is the daily wage in naira. If a minimum wage of N25 is imposed, the resulting unemployment is
questions.explanation: At W = 25, firms want 500 - 250 = 250 workers while 20(25) - 100 = 400 people want jobs, so 400 - 250 = 150 are unemployed. Option B is the number willing to work, option A is the number hired, and option D is the equilibrium employment at a wage of N20.

questions.question: In a labour market, labour demand is Ld = 500 - 10W and labour supply is Ls = 20W - 100. The equilibrium wage is N20. If a minimum wage of N25 is imposed, how many workers are actually employed?
questions.explanation: Employment is set by the short side of the market, which is labour demand: 500 - 10(25) = 250 workers. Option C is employment at the old equilibrium, option D is the number of people who want work, and option B is the unemployment created.

questions.question: The net loss of total (consumer plus producer) surplus that results when a market is prevented from reaching its competitive equilibrium is called
questions.explanation: Deadweight loss is surplus that disappears altogether because some mutually beneficial trades no longer take place; nobody receives it. Options D and B are the gains that buyers and sellers do receive from trade, and option A is a shortage of quantity, not a loss of welfare.

questions.question: A binding price ceiling creates a deadweight loss mainly because

options.a: some units that buyers value above their cost of production are no longer produced and traded
options.b: quantity demanded rises above its equilibrium level
options.c: consumers pay a lower price than before
options.d: producers transfer part of their surplus to consumers

questions.explanation: The ceiling cuts the quantity traded below equilibrium, so trades that would have created value for both sides are lost, and that lost value is the deadweight loss. Options C and D describe a transfer from producers to consumers, which is a redistribution rather than a loss to society, and option B is a shortage effect, not the reason surplus is lost.

questions.question: Which of the following does NOT create a deadweight loss?

options.a: A competitive market left free to reach its equilibrium
options.c: A binding price ceiling on rented housing
options.d: A binding minimum price for maize

questions.explanation: A free competitive equilibrium already exploits all mutually beneficial trades, so total surplus is maximised and there is no deadweight loss. Options C, D and B are all binding price controls that change the quantity traded away from equilibrium and so cause market distortions.

questions.question: Zero price elasticity means ______.
questions.explanation: A price elasticity of zero means quantity demanded does not change at all when price changes, so demand is perfectly inelastic and the demand curve is vertical. Option B, inelastic demand, means elasticity is between 0 and 1, so quantity still responds a little. Option A, perfectly elastic, is the opposite extreme with an infinite elasticity and a horizontal curve.

questions.question: When goods have income elasticity between 0 and 1, they are better described as: ______
questions.explanation: An income elasticity between 0 and 1 means demand rises with income but by a smaller percentage than income, which is the mark of a necessity such as basic food items. Option C, luxury goods, have income elasticity greater than 1, and option D, inferior goods, have negative income elasticity. Option B, Giffen goods, are a special type of inferior good.

questions.question: Closeup and Pepsodent are two common brands of toothpaste on the campus of University of Lagos. Using the elasticity construct, these products are best described as: ______.
questions.explanation: Closeup and Pepsodent serve the same purpose, so if the price of one rises, many students will switch to the other, giving a positive cross-price elasticity of demand. Goods with a positive cross elasticity are substitutes. Option A, complementary goods, are used together and have a negative cross elasticity, like toothpaste and toothbrushes, and option D, independent goods, have a cross elasticity of zero.

questions.question: For normal goods, income elasticity of demand is: ______
questions.explanation: For a normal good, demand rises when income rises, so income and quantity demanded move in the same direction and income elasticity is positive. Option D, negative income elasticity, is the mark of an inferior good, and option C, zero, means demand does not respond to income at all.

questions.question: When crude oil prices increase due to restricted supply routes, the percentage decrease in quantity demanded is: ______.

options.a: Greater than the percentage increase in price
options.b: Equal to the percentage increase in price
options.d: Less than the percentage increase in price

questions.explanation: Crude oil has inelastic demand because it is essential and has few quick substitutes, and inelastic demand means the percentage fall in quantity demanded is smaller than the percentage rise in price. Option A describes elastic demand, and option B describes unit elastic demand. Option C is wrong because quantity demanded still responds to price, only weakly.

questions.question: An increase in the price of Dettol Antiseptic Soap leads consumers to switch to Dudu Osun. This indicates: ______
questions.explanation: When a rise in the price of Dettol soap causes consumers to buy more Dudu Osun, the price of one good and the quantity demanded of the other move in the same direction. That gives a positive cross-price elasticity, which shows the two soaps are substitutes. Option D, perfect complementarity, would give a negative cross elasticity, and options A and B are about income changes, not price changes of another good.

questions.question: Inferior goods are characterized by: ______
questions.explanation: An inferior good is one whose demand falls when income rises, so income and quantity demanded move in opposite directions and income elasticity is negative. Option A, positive income elasticity, belongs to normal goods, and option B, zero, means demand does not respond to income at all.

questions.question: Crude oil remains essential for transport and industry despite price hikes caused by geopolitical disruptions. This indicates that crude oil is: ______

options.c: A Giffen good with elastic demand

questions.explanation: Crude oil is essential for transport and industry, so people keep buying it even when the price rises sharply. A good that is needed regardless of price is a necessity with inelastic demand. Option A is wrong because luxuries are things people cut back on easily, and option C is wrong because a Giffen good is a rare inferior good and does not have elastic demand.

questions.question: If the price of Indomie increases and the demand for Chikki Noodles rises, the cross-price elasticity of demand is: ______.
questions.explanation: Cross-price elasticity compares the change in demand for one good with the change in price of another. Here the price of Indomie rises and demand for Chikki Noodles also rises, so both move in the same direction and the cross elasticity is positive, showing they are substitutes. Option A, negative, would mean the goods are complements, and option B, zero, would mean they are unrelated.

questions.question: A good with income elasticity greater than 1 is classified as ______.
questions.explanation: An income elasticity greater than 1 means demand rises by a bigger percentage than income, which is the mark of a luxury good. Option C, necessity goods, have income elasticity between 0 and 1, and option A, inferior goods, have negative income elasticity. Option D, complementary goods, are defined by cross-price elasticity, not income elasticity.

questions.question: If the income elasticity of a commodity is negative, the commodity is:
questions.explanation: A negative income elasticity means demand falls as income rises, which defines an inferior good. Options A and B, normal and luxury goods, both have positive income elasticity. Option C, a substitute good, is defined by a positive cross-price elasticity, not by income elasticity.

questions.question: In the short run after a major supply disruption like the Strait of Hormuz closure, the demand for crude oil is: ______.

options.a: Inelastic due to lack of immediate substitutes
options.b: More elastic due to availability of substitutes
options.d: Unit elastic due to proportional adjustments

questions.explanation: Immediately after a major supply disruption, users of crude oil cannot quickly switch to other fuels or change their vehicles and machines, so quantity demanded falls very little even as the price jumps. Demand is therefore inelastic due to the lack of immediate substitutes. Option B describes the longer run, when substitutes become available, and option C, perfectly elastic, would mean consumers stop buying completely after any price rise.

questions.question: For complementary goods, the cross elasticity of demand is:
questions.explanation: Complements are used together, so a rise in the price of one reduces the quantity demanded of the other, giving a negative cross elasticity. A positive cross elasticity (option A) belongs to substitutes, while zero (option C) means the goods are unrelated.

questions.question: The relationship between the price of one commodity and the demand for another commodity is measured by:
questions.explanation: Cross elasticity of demand measures how the quantity demanded of one good responds to a change in the price of another good. Price elasticity (option A) looks at a good's own price, and income elasticity (option B) looks at changes in income.

questions.question: For luxury goods, the income elasticity of demand will be:
questions.explanation: For a luxury, quantity demanded rises proportionately more than income, so the income elasticity is greater than one. A value between zero and one (option A) describes a necessity.

questions.question: If the percentage increase in the quantity demanded of a commodity is smaller than the percentage fall in its price, the coefficient of price elasticity is:
questions.explanation: Price elasticity equals the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price, so a smaller percentage change in quantity than in price gives a coefficient below one (inelastic demand). A coefficient greater than one (option A) would need the quantity response to be the larger of the two.

questions.question: A fall in the price of a commodity whose demand curve is a rectangular hyperbola causes total expenditure on the commodity to:
questions.explanation: A demand curve shaped like a rectangular hyperbola has P x Q constant at every point, which means elasticity is one throughout. Because spending equals P x Q, a fall in price leaves total expenditure unchanged, so options A and B are wrong.

questions.question: If the quantity demanded remains unchanged as the price of a commodity falls, the coefficient of price elasticity of demand is:
questions.explanation: If quantity demanded does not respond at all when price changes, the percentage change in quantity is zero, so the elasticity coefficient is zero (perfectly inelastic demand). Option C, smaller than one, fits inelastic demand where quantity still responds a little.

questions.question: An increase in the price of a commodity whose demand is inelastic causes consumers' total expenditure on the commodity to:
questions.explanation: When demand is inelastic, quantity falls by a smaller percentage than price rises, so the higher price outweighs the lower quantity and total expenditure (P x Q) increases. Option C holds only for unit elastic demand, and option B holds when demand is elastic.

questions.question: A negative income elasticity of demand for a commodity indicates that, as income falls, the amount of the commodity purchased:
questions.explanation: A negative income elasticity means income and quantity bought move in opposite directions, so when income falls the amount purchased rises, as with an inferior good. Option B would be the case for a positive income elasticity.

questions.question: If the amount of the commodity purchased remains unchanged when the price of another commodity changes, the cross elasticity of demand between them will be:
questions.explanation: If the purchase of one good does not change at all when another good's price changes, the numerator of the cross elasticity is zero, so the cross elasticity is zero and the goods are unrelated. Positive (option A) would indicate substitutes and negative (option B) complements.

questions.question: If the income elasticity of demand for a commodity is found to be 0.4, the commodity is a:
questions.explanation: An income elasticity of 0.4 is positive but less than one, so demand rises with income but more slowly, which is the definition of a necessity. A luxury (option A) needs an income elasticity above one, and a Giffen good (option C) is an inferior good with negative income elasticity.

questions.question: The elasticity of supply for a positively sloped straight-line supply curve that intersects the price axis is:
questions.explanation: Write the line as Q = k + mP; if it cuts the price axis, k is negative, so elasticity = mP/(k + mP) is greater than one at every point. In other words, quantity supplied always changes by a bigger percentage than price, so supply is elastic. Unit elasticity (option B) applies only to a line through the origin, and option D is wrong because elasticity changes along such a line.

questions.question: If a positively sloped linear supply curve crosses the quantity axis, the elasticity of supply is:
questions.explanation: When a straight-line supply curve starts on the quantity axis, some quantity is supplied even at a zero price, so the percentage change in quantity is always smaller than the percentage change in price and supply is inelastic. Option B describes a line cutting the price axis, and option C a line through the origin.

questions.question: If a positively sloped linear supply curve passes through the origin, the elasticity of supply is:
questions.explanation: Any straight-line supply curve through the origin has Q proportional to P, so a given percentage change in price causes the same percentage change in quantity and elasticity equals one at every point, whatever the slope. Options A and B describe lines that cut the quantity and price axes respectively.

questions.question: A horizontal supply curve, parallel to the quantity axis, represents:
questions.explanation: A horizontal supply curve means sellers will supply any quantity at that single price but nothing below it, so elasticity of supply is infinite (perfectly elastic). A vertical supply curve would be perfectly inelastic (option D).

questions.question: Which of the following elasticities measures a movement along a demand curve rather than a shift of the curve?
questions.explanation: Price elasticity of demand measures the response of quantity demanded to the good's own price, which is a movement along a given demand curve. Income elasticity (option B) and cross elasticity (option C) measure responses to income and to other goods' prices, which shift the demand curve.

questions.question: In the case of substitutes, the cross elasticity of demand is:
questions.explanation: Substitutes replace each other, so a rise in the price of one raises demand for the other, which makes the cross elasticity positive. A negative cross elasticity (option B) is the sign for complements, and zero (option A) means the goods are unrelated.

questions.question: If a fall in the price of a commodity causes total expenditure on it to decrease, the coefficient of price elasticity of demand is:
questions.explanation: If total expenditure falls when price falls, quantity rose by a smaller percentage than price fell, which means demand is inelastic with a coefficient less than one. A coefficient greater than one (option B) would make spending rise after a price cut, and one (option A) would leave it unchanged.

questions.question: If a small change in price leads to an infinitely large change in quantity demanded, demand is:
questions.explanation: When even a tiny price change causes an infinitely large change in quantity demanded, elasticity is infinite and demand is perfectly elastic, shown by a horizontal demand curve. Perfectly inelastic demand (option B) is the opposite case, where quantity does not respond at all and the curve is vertical.

questions.question: When the demand curve is a rectangular hyperbola, the price elasticity of demand is:
questions.explanation: On a rectangular hyperbola P x Q is constant, so every percentage fall in price is matched by an equal percentage rise in quantity, giving price elasticity equal to one at every point. Zero (option A) and infinity (option D) are the vertical and horizontal demand curve cases.

questions.question: If a 3-percent increase in the price of corn flakes causes a 6-percent decline in the quantity demanded, what is the price elasticity of demand?
questions.explanation: Price elasticity of demand = percentage change in quantity demanded / percentage change in price = -6% / 3% = -2.0, so demand is elastic. Option A divides the figures the wrong way round (3/6), option B subtracts them, and option D multiplies them.

questions.question: Why is the long-run price elasticity of supply of many goods larger than the short-run elasticity?

options.a: Production costs are always fixed in the long run
options.b: In the long run consumers become more sensitive to price
options.c: In the short run firms can easily build new plants, but in the long run they cannot
options.d: In the short run firms are limited by existing capacity, while in the long run they can expand capacity and new firms can enter

questions.explanation: In the short run a firm can raise output only by using its existing plant more intensively, so quantity supplied responds little to price. Given time, firms can build new capacity and new producers can enter, so the supply response to a price change becomes larger. Option B is about demand, not supply, and option A is wrong because in the long run all costs are variable.

questions.question: Televisions are durable goods. How does the price elasticity of demand for televisions in the short run compare with that in the long run?

options.a: It is the same in the short run and the long run, because televisions are durable
options.b: It is larger in the short run, because consumers can delay or bring forward replacing their existing sets
options.c: It is larger in the long run, because consumers take time to change their habits
options.d: It is zero in the short run, because people never change their purchase plans quickly

questions.explanation: For a durable good, a price rise mainly makes people postpone replacing the set they already own, so purchases drop sharply at first. Over time old sets wear out and must be replaced, so the long-run response is smaller than the short-run one. Option C is the pattern for non-durable goods such as paper towels, where habits adjust slowly.

questions.question: Paper towels are a non-durable good. Would you expect the price elasticity of demand for paper towels to be larger in the short run or in the long run?

options.a: Larger in the short run, because paper towels are a necessity
options.b: The same in both periods, because paper towels are cheap
options.c: Larger in the short run, because consumers can postpone replacing their stock
options.d: Larger in the long run, because consumers need time to change habits and find substitutes

questions.explanation: For most non-durable goods, people adjust slowly to a price change: it takes time to change habits and switch to alternatives such as cloth towels, so the quantity response grows over time and demand is more elastic in the long run. Option C describes durable goods, where postponing replacement creates a large short-run response.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct?

options.a: The supply of apartments is more elastic in the short run than in the long run
options.b: The supply of apartments is more inelastic in the short run than in the long run
options.c: The cross-price elasticity of demand is always positive
options.d: The elasticity of demand is the same as the slope of the demand curve

questions.explanation: In the short run the stock of apartments is fixed by what has already been built, so quantity supplied hardly responds to rent, while in the long run new apartments can be built. Option D is false because elasticity is the slope multiplied by P/Q, so it changes along a straight-line demand curve even though the slope does not. Option C is false because cross-price elasticity is negative for complements.

questions.question: A university doubled its real tuition over 15 years, yet the number and quality of applicants did not fall. An official concludes that demand for admission is completely price inelastic. What is the best response?

options.a: Accept the argument: tuition is a necessity, so its demand must be perfectly inelastic
options.b: Reject the argument: rising tuition proves that demand is perfectly elastic
options.c: Reject the argument: the observed points are different equilibria, and the demand curve itself has probably shifted rightward over time
options.d: Accept the argument: unchanged applications at a higher price prove a vertical demand curve

questions.explanation: The official sees only price-quantity points from different years, not a single demand curve. If demand rose over the period (for example, because the value of a degree grew), price could double without applications falling, even if demand at any moment is quite price sensitive. Option D assumes the demand curve stayed fixed, and option B draws an equally unsupported conclusion.

questions.question: The demand curve for a product is Q = 10 - 2P + PS, where P is the price of the product and PS is the price of a substitute good. PS = $2.00 and P = $1.00. What are the price elasticity of demand and the cross-price elasticity of demand?
questions.explanation: First find quantity: Q = 10 - 2(1) + 2 = 10. Price elasticity = (dQ/dP)(P/Q) = -2 x 1/10 = -0.2, and cross-price elasticity = (dQ/dPS)(PS/Q) = 1 x 2/10 = 0.2. Option A reports the slopes without multiplying by price over quantity, and option D wrongly uses Q = 8 by leaving out the substitute's price.

questions.question: The demand curve for a product is Q = 10 - 2P + PS, where P is the price of the product and PS is the price of a substitute good. PS = $2.00 and P = $2.00. What are the price elasticity of demand and the cross-price elasticity of demand?
questions.explanation: Quantity is now Q = 10 - 2(2) + 2 = 8. Price elasticity = -2 x 2/8 = -0.5, and cross-price elasticity = 1 x 2/8 = 0.25. Option B wrongly keeps the old quantity of 10, and option D gives only the slopes of the demand equation.

questions.question: In a competitive market, the quantities demanded and supplied (millions per year) are: at $60, demand 22 and supply 14; at $80, demand 20 and supply 16; at $100, demand 18 and supply 18; at $120, demand 16 and supply 20. What is the price elasticity of demand at a price of $80?
questions.explanation: Demand falls by 2 million for every $20 rise in price, so DeltaQ/DeltaP = -2/20 = -0.1. At $80, elasticity = (DeltaQ/DeltaP)(P/Q) = -0.1 x 80/20 = -0.40. Option D gives only the slope, option C inverts the ratio, and option A is the elasticity at $100 (-0.1 x 100/18).

questions.question: A vegetable fiber has a world price of $9 per pound, and unlimited imports are available at that price. U.S. supply and demand (million pounds) are: price $3, supply 2, demand 34; $6, supply 4, demand 28; $9, supply 6, demand 22; $12, supply 8, demand 16; $15, supply 10, demand 10; $18, supply 12, demand 4. What is the price elasticity of demand at a price of $9?
questions.explanation: The table gives the straight-line demand Q = 40 - 2P, so DeltaQ/DeltaP = -2. At $9, Q = 22, so elasticity = -2 x 9/22 = about -0.82. Option D inverts the ratio (22/18), option B is the elasticity at $12 (-2 x 12/16), and option A is just the slope.

questions.question: Americans bought 15.75 billion packs of cigarettes at an average price of $5.00 per pack. The price elasticity of demand is -0.4 and the price elasticity of supply is 0.5. What linear demand curve, Q = a - bP, is consistent with these figures?
questions.explanation: From elasticity = -b(P/Q), we get b = 0.4 x 15.75/5 = 1.26. Then a = Q + bP = 15.75 + 1.26 x 5 = 22.05, so Q = 22.05 - 1.26P. Option D uses the elasticity itself as the slope, and option A subtracts bP from Q instead of adding it.

questions.question: In the copper market the equilibrium price is $3 per pound and the equilibrium quantity is 18 million metric tons per year. If the price elasticity of demand is -0.75, what linear demand curve, Q = a - bP, is consistent with these figures?
questions.explanation: From elasticity = -b(P/Q), b = 0.75 x 18/3 = 4.5. Then a = 18 + 4.5 x 3 = 31.5, so Q = 31.5 - 4.5P. Option D is the demand curve for an elasticity of -0.5, and option C uses the elasticity itself as the slope.

questions.question: Instant coffee: Year 1 price $10.35/lb with sales 75 million lbs; Year 2 price $10.48/lb with sales 70 million lbs. Roasted coffee: Year 1 price $4.11/lb with sales 820 million lbs; Year 2 price $3.76/lb with sales 850 million lbs. Using the arc (midpoint) formula, what is the short-run price elasticity of demand for roasted coffee?
questions.explanation: Arc elasticity = (DeltaQ / average Q) / (DeltaP / average P) = (30/835) / (-0.35/3.935) = 0.0359 / -0.0889 = about -0.40, so demand for roasted coffee is inelastic. Option C turns the ratio upside down, option A is just DeltaQ/DeltaP (30/-0.35), and option B is the elasticity for instant coffee.

questions.question: Instant coffee: Year 1 price $10.35/lb with sales 75 million lbs; Year 2 price $10.48/lb with sales 70 million lbs. Roasted coffee: Year 1 price $4.11/lb with sales 820 million lbs; Year 2 price $3.76/lb with sales 850 million lbs. Using the arc (midpoint) formula, what is the short-run price elasticity of demand for instant coffee?
questions.explanation: Arc elasticity = (DeltaQ / average Q) / (DeltaP / average P) = (-5/72.5) / (0.13/10.415) = -0.0690 / 0.0125 = about -5.53, so instant coffee has much more elastic demand than roasted coffee. Option A turns the ratio upside down, option C is just DeltaQ/DeltaP (-5/0.13), and option D is the elasticity for roasted coffee.

questions.question: In economics, the percentage change in one variable that results from a 1 percent increase in another variable is called
questions.explanation: Elasticity measures responsiveness in percentage terms, so it does not depend on the units in which quantities and prices are measured. Option A is the absolute change in one variable per unit change in another, which does depend on units, and option D relates to indifference curves, not responsiveness.

questions.question: The percentage change in the quantity demanded of a good resulting from a 1 percent increase in its own price is the
questions.explanation: Price elasticity of demand links the quantity demanded of a good to its own price. Option C uses income instead of price, option D uses the price of another good, and option A concerns quantity supplied rather than quantity demanded.

questions.question: Which of the following is the point formula for the price elasticity of demand, Ep?
questions.explanation: Elasticity is (dQ/Q) divided by (dP/P), which rearranges to (P/Q) times dQ/dP. Option A inverts the ratio of price to quantity, option C uses the slope of the demand curve drawn with price on the vertical axis instead of dQ/dP, and option B is just the slope term without converting to percentages.

questions.question: Demand for a good is described as price elastic when the absolute value of its price elasticity is
questions.explanation: Elastic demand means quantity changes by a larger percentage than price, so the magnitude of the elasticity exceeds 1. Option D describes inelastic demand, option C unitary elasticity, and option A perfectly inelastic demand.

questions.question: If the price elasticity of demand for salt is -0.1, demand for salt is
questions.explanation: An elasticity of magnitude 0.1 is less than 1, so a 1 percent price rise reduces quantity demanded by only 0.1 percent, which is inelastic. Option A needs a magnitude above 1, option D needs exactly 1, and option C would require an infinite elasticity.

questions.question: A horizontal demand curve at a single price represents demand that is
questions.explanation: With a horizontal demand curve, consumers buy as much as they can get at that price but nothing at any higher price, so the elasticity is infinite. Option C is shown by a vertical demand curve, and options D and A have finite elasticities on a downward-sloping curve.

questions.question: When consumers buy a fixed quantity of a good regardless of its price, the demand curve is

options.a: upward sloping, and demand is elastic
options.b: horizontal, and demand is infinitely elastic
options.c: downward sloping, and demand is unitary elastic
options.d: vertical, and demand is completely inelastic

questions.explanation: A fixed quantity at every price gives a vertical demand curve with an elasticity of zero, called completely inelastic demand. Option B describes infinitely elastic demand, and option A is impossible for a normal demand curve, which slopes downward.

questions.question: If the demand for a good is price elastic, a reduction in its price will
questions.explanation: With elastic demand, quantity rises by a larger percentage than price falls, so price times quantity goes up. Option B is what happens when demand is inelastic, option A applies to unitary elasticity, and option D contradicts the law of demand.

questions.question: When the price elasticity of demand is exactly -1, a small change in price will

options.d: reduce quantity demanded by more than the price change

questions.explanation: At unitary elasticity the percentage change in quantity exactly offsets the percentage change in price, so total revenue stays the same. Options A and B require inelastic or elastic demand depending on the direction of the price change, and option D describes elastic demand.

questions.question: The price elasticity of demand for a good is likely to be high when

options.a: the good has many close substitutes
options.b: the good has no close substitutes
options.c: consumers are given very little time to adjust
options.d: the good takes a tiny share of the consumer's income

questions.explanation: When close substitutes exist, buyers can easily switch away after a price rise, so quantity demanded falls a lot. Options B, D and C all make demand less elastic, because buyers either cannot switch, hardly notice the price change, or have not had time to change their habits.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a determinant of the price elasticity of demand for a good?

options.a: The proportion of income spent on the good
options.b: The production technology used by firms making the good
options.c: The length of time allowed for adjustment

questions.explanation: Production technology affects how easily firms can supply the good, which belongs to the elasticity of supply, not demand. Options D, A and C are genuine determinants of the price elasticity of demand: substitutes, budget share and time.

questions.question: For a non-durable good such as petrol, the price elasticity of demand is usually

options.a: larger in magnitude in the short run than in the long run
options.b: the same in the short run and long run
options.c: larger in magnitude in the long run than in the short run

questions.explanation: Over a longer period consumers can change habits and replace the cars and equipment that use petrol, so the quantity demanded responds more strongly. Option A applies to durable goods such as cars, and option D contradicts the fact that demand becomes more responsive over time.

questions.question: For durable goods such as cars and refrigerators, demand is typically more price elastic in the short run than in the long run because

options.a: the existing stock is large relative to annual purchases, so buyers can postpone replacement
options.b: firms cannot change the supply of durables in the long run
options.d: consumers spend only a small share of income on durables

questions.explanation: A price rise lets owners keep their old cars longer, causing a big short-run drop in new purchases, though in the long run the stock must still be replaced. Option C is false and would make demand less elastic, option D is also false, and option B is about supply, not demand.

questions.question: Along a straight-line demand curve Q = a - bP, which statement is correct?

options.a: The price elasticity equals the slope at every point
options.b: The price elasticity is constant but the slope changes
options.c: The slope and the price elasticity are both constant
options.d: The slope is constant but the price elasticity changes from point to point

questions.explanation: The term dQ/dP = -b is fixed, but elasticity also depends on P/Q, which rises as we move up the curve, so elasticity varies. Option C confuses slope with elasticity, option B reverses them, and option A ignores the P/Q factor.

questions.question: On a straight-line demand curve, demand is price elastic

options.a: above the midpoint, towards the price axis
options.c: at every point, because the slope is constant
options.d: below the midpoint, towards the quantity axis

questions.explanation: Near the price axis quantity is small and price is high, so P/Q is large and the elasticity exceeds 1 in magnitude; it equals 1 at the midpoint and falls towards 0 at the quantity axis. Option D is the inelastic section, option B is where elasticity is exactly unitary, and option C confuses constant slope with constant elasticity.

questions.question: Two demand curves pass through the same price-quantity point. At that point, the steeper curve (price on the vertical axis) is

options.a: less elastic than the flatter curve
options.b: more elastic than the flatter curve
options.c: equally elastic as the flatter curve

questions.explanation: At a common point P/Q is the same, so elasticity depends only on dQ/dP, which is smaller in magnitude for the steeper curve. Option B reverses the relationship, and option D describes a horizontal, not a steep, curve.

questions.question: The price elasticity of demand calculated over a range of prices, using average price and average quantity, is called the
questions.explanation: Arc elasticity measures responsiveness between two points on the demand curve, using the averages so the answer is the same whether price rises or falls. Option A is the elasticity at one particular point, and options B and D involve another good's price and income respectively.

questions.question: For a straight-line demand curve, which statement about the arc (midpoint) elasticity of demand between two prices is correct?

options.a: It depends on whether price rises or falls between the two points
options.b: It lies somewhere between the point elasticities at the lower and higher prices
options.c: It is always larger in magnitude than both point elasticities
options.d: It is always exactly halfway between the two point elasticities

questions.explanation: Using average price and quantity gives a value between the two point elasticities, but not necessarily exactly halfway. Option D is too strong, option C is false, and option A is exactly the problem the midpoint formula is designed to avoid.

questions.question: As workers in Ibadan get pay rises, many buy less garri and more rice and meat. In this case, garri is

options.a: a normal good with positive income elasticity
options.b: a luxury good with income elasticity above 1
options.c: a complement of rice with negative cross-price elasticity
options.d: an inferior good with negative income elasticity

questions.explanation: Buying less of a good as income rises means its income elasticity is negative, so garri is an inferior good here. Options A and B would require demand to rise with income, and option C confuses income elasticity with the response to another good's price.

questions.question: If the cross-price elasticity of demand between two goods is positive, the goods are
questions.explanation: A positive cross elasticity means a rise in the price of one good increases demand for the other, as buyers switch, which defines substitutes. Option C has a negative cross elasticity, option B has a cross elasticity of zero, and option D is about income, not other prices.

questions.question: Cars and petrol are used together. The cross-price elasticity of demand for cars with respect to the price of petrol is expected to be

options.d: greater than 1, because cars are luxuries

questions.explanation: A rise in the price of petrol makes running a car more expensive, so fewer cars are demanded, giving a negative cross elasticity, the mark of complements. Option C would apply to goods that replace each other, and option D mixes up cross elasticity with income elasticity.

questions.question: The price elasticity of supply measures the percentage change in quantity supplied resulting from a 1 percent increase in price, and it is usually

options.a: negative, because higher prices reduce output
options.b: positive, because higher prices encourage firms to produce more
options.c: zero, because supply never responds to price
options.d: equal to the price elasticity of demand

questions.explanation: Supply curves usually slope upward, so price and quantity supplied move in the same direction and the elasticity is positive. Option A describes the sign of price elasticity of demand, and option D has no basis since supply and demand elasticities are generally different.

questions.question: For most manufactured goods, the price elasticity of supply is

options.b: the same in the short run and long run
options.c: greater in the long run than in the short run
options.d: greater in the short run than in the long run

questions.explanation: In the short run firms face capacity limits, but in the long run they can build new plants and new firms can enter, so supply responds more to price. Option D is true only for special cases like recycled scrap metal, and option A contradicts the upward-sloping supply curve.

questions.question: In the short run, the number of rental flats in a city cannot change quickly whatever happens to rent. The short-run supply of rental flats is therefore

options.b: more elastic than in the long run

questions.explanation: If quantity supplied cannot change at all in response to rent, the supply curve is vertical and the elasticity is zero. Option D is a horizontal supply curve, and option B is wrong because building new flats over time makes long-run supply more elastic.

questions.question: The price of a crate of eggs rises from N100 to N110 and the quantity demanded falls from 500 to 450 crates. Using the point formula E = (dQ/Q)/(dP/P) with the initial price and quantity, the price elasticity of demand is
questions.explanation: The percentage change in quantity is -50/500 = -10 percent and the percentage change in price is 10/100 = 10 percent, so E = -10/10 = -1.00, which is unit elastic. Option C, -0.10, is only the proportional change in quantity and has not been divided by the change in price. Option B, -10.00, is the percentage change in quantity left undivided as well.

questions.question: The price of a loaf of bread rises from N200 to N250 and the quantity demanded falls from 100 to 80 loaves. Using the arc (midpoint) formula E = (dQ/dP) x (average P / average Q), the price elasticity of demand is
questions.explanation: The change in quantity is -20 and the change in price is 50, with average price 225 and average quantity 90, so E = (-20/50)(225/90) = -0.4 x 2.5 = -1.00. Option A uses the initial values (-20 percent / 25 percent) and option B uses the new values (-25 percent / 20 percent), which is why the midpoint formula is preferred.

questions.question: When the price of a bag of sachet water rises from N40 to N60, the quantity demanded falls from 1,000 to 600 bags. Using the arc (midpoint) formula E = (dQ/dP) x (average P / average Q), the price elasticity of demand is
questions.explanation: The changes are dQ = -400 and dP = 20, with averages 800 and 50, so E = (-400/20)(50/800) = -20 x 0.0625 = -1.25. Option C uses initial values (-40 percent / 50 percent), option D uses new values, and option A is just dQ/dP without the price-quantity ratio.

questions.question: The demand for a good is Q = 100 - 4P. Using the point formula E = (dQ/dP)(P/Q), the price elasticity of demand at P = N10 is
questions.explanation: At P = 10, Q = 100 - 40 = 60, and dQ/dP = -4, so E = -4 x (10/60) = -0.67, which is inelastic. Option D is only the slope term dQ/dP, option C inverts the ratio, and option B is simply 1/(-4), the slope of the curve with price on the vertical axis.

questions.question: The demand for a good is Q = 100 - 4P. Using the point formula E = (dQ/dP)(P/Q), at P = N20 demand is
questions.explanation: At P = 20, Q = 100 - 80 = 20, so E = -4 x (20/20) = -4.00, whose magnitude exceeds 1. Option C inverts the calculation, and option A applies only at the midpoint of the curve, where P = 12.50.

questions.question: The demand for a good is Q = 100 - 4P. Using the point formula E = (dQ/dP)(P/Q), at what price is demand unitary elastic?
questions.explanation: Set -4P/(100 - 4P) = -1, so 4P = 100 - 4P and P = 12.50, which is the midpoint of the linear demand curve. Option B is the price intercept where Q = 0 and elasticity is infinite, option A is the quantity at the midpoint, and option C is half the correct price.

questions.question: The demand for a good is Q = 60 - 3P. Using the point formula E = (dQ/dP)(P/Q), the price elasticity of demand at P = N5 is
questions.explanation: At P = 5, Q = 60 - 15 = 45, so E = -3 x (5/45) = -0.33, which is inelastic. Option B is only the slope term dQ/dP and option D is only the ratio P/Q (5/45); the elasticity needs the two multiplied together. Option A is far too large for a point this close to the quantity axis, where demand is inelastic.

questions.question: The inverse demand curve for a good is P = 50 - 0.5Q. Using the point formula E = (dQ/dP)(P/Q), the price elasticity of demand at P = N30 is
questions.explanation: Rewriting gives Q = 100 - 2P, so dQ/dP = -2; at P = 30, Q = 40 and E = -2 x (30/40) = -1.50. Option D wrongly uses dP/dQ = -0.5 in place of dQ/dP, option A inverts the answer, and option B is just dQ/dP.

questions.question: A seller faces demand Q = 200 - 5P. Using the point formula E = (dQ/dP)(P/Q) and the rule that total revenue is maximised where demand is unitary elastic, the revenue-maximising price is
questions.explanation: Unitary elasticity requires 5P = 200 - 5P, so P = 20 and Q = 100, giving revenue of N2,000. Option B is the price intercept where nothing is sold, option D is the quantity at the revenue-maximising point, and option C is half the correct price.

questions.question: A trader cuts the price of a phone case from N100 to N80, and sales rise from 50 to 70 cases. Using the arc (midpoint) formula E = (dQ/dP) x (average P / average Q), which statement is correct?

options.a: E = -1.50, demand is elastic and total revenue falls by N600
options.b: E = -1.00, demand is unitary elastic and total revenue is unchanged
options.c: E = -0.67, demand is inelastic and total revenue falls by N600
options.d: E = -1.50, demand is elastic and total revenue rises by N600

questions.explanation: With dQ = 20, dP = -20, average P = 90 and average Q = 60, E = (20/-20)(90/60) = -1.50, and revenue rises from N5,000 to N5,600. Option C inverts the elasticity and gets the revenue direction wrong, and option A forgets that a price cut raises revenue when demand is elastic.

questions.question: The price of a paint bucket of garri rises from N500 to N600 and the quantity demanded falls from 200 to 180 buckets. Using the point formula E = (dQ/Q)/(dP/P), using the initial price and quantity, the price elasticity of demand is
questions.explanation: Quantity falls by 20/200 = 10 percent while price rises by 100/500 = 20 percent, so E = -10/20 = -0.50, which is inelastic; total revenue rises from N100,000 to N108,000. Option C inverts the ratio, and options A and B report only one of the percentage changes as a decimal.

questions.question: The price elasticity of demand for kerosene is -0.4. Using E = (percentage change in Q)/(percentage change in P), a 10 percent rise in the price of kerosene will change the quantity demanded by
questions.explanation: Rearranging gives percentage change in Q = E x percentage change in P = -0.4 x 10 = -4 percent. Option B divides 10 by 0.4 instead of multiplying, and options D and A misplace the decimal point.

questions.question: The price of a life-saving drug rises by 30 percent but the quantity demanded does not change at all. Using E = (percentage change in Q)/(percentage change in P), the price elasticity of demand is
questions.explanation: With no change in quantity, the numerator is 0 and E = 0/30 = 0, which is completely inelastic demand shown by a vertical demand curve. Option C is unitary elasticity, and option B belongs to a horizontal, perfectly elastic demand curve.

questions.question: In a market, demand is Qd = 120 - 2P and supply is Qs = 3P - 30. Using the point formula E = (dQ/dP)(P/Q) at the equilibrium point, the price elasticity of demand is
questions.explanation: Equilibrium is where 120 - 2P = 3P - 30, so P = 30 and Q = 60; then ED = -2 x (30/60) = -1.00, which is unit elastic. Option A is only the slope dQ/dP = -2, option D uses Q/P = 2 instead of P/Q = 0.5, and option C is just the reciprocal of the slope (1/-2).

questions.question: In a market, demand is Qd = 120 - 2P and supply is Qs = 3P - 30. Using the point formula E = (dQ/dP)(P/Q) at the equilibrium point, the price elasticity of supply is
questions.explanation: At equilibrium P = 30 and Q = 60, and dQs/dP = 3, so ES = 3 x (30/60) = 1.50. Option A is just the supply coefficient, option D inverts the answer, and option B uses Q/P instead of P/Q.

questions.question: At the equilibrium price of N20 per unit, 100 units of a good are sold, and the point price elasticity of demand there is -0.5. If demand is linear, Q = a - bP, and the point formula ED = -b(P/Q) holds, the value of b is
questions.explanation: From -0.5 = -b(20/100) we get b = 0.5 x 5 = 2.5, and then a = 100 + 2.5 x 20 = 150, so demand is Q = 150 - 2.5P. Option C multiplies 0.5 by 20, option A is 0.5 x (20/100), which forgets to divide, and option B ignores the 0.5.

questions.question: When a household's monthly income rises from N100,000 to N120,000, its monthly purchases of restaurant meals rise from 50 to 65. Using the point formula EI = (dQ/Q)/(dI/I) with initial values, the income elasticity and type of good are

options.a: 1.50; a normal good and a luxury
options.b: 0.67; a normal good and a necessity
options.d: 0.30; a normal good and a necessity

questions.explanation: Quantity rises 15/50 = 30 percent and income rises 20,000/100,000 = 20 percent, so EI = 30/20 = 1.50, which is positive and above 1, so a luxury. Option B inverts the ratio, option C gets the right number but wrongly treats a positive value as inferior, and option D reports only the quantity change.

questions.question: When a family's income rises from N200,000 to N250,000 a month, its purchases of a cheap brand of rice fall from 40 to 38 bags a year. Using the point formula EI = (dQ/Q)/(dI/I) with initial values, the income elasticity is
questions.explanation: Quantity falls by 2/40 = 5 percent and income rises by 50,000/200,000 = 25 percent, so EI = -5/25 = -0.20, a negative value that marks an inferior good. Option B drops the minus sign, option A inverts the ratio, and option C reports only the quantity change.

questions.question: When average income in a town rises from N100,000 to N140,000, the quantity of bread bought per household rises from 20 to 24 loaves a month. Using the arc (midpoint) formula EI = (dQ/dI) x (average I / average Q), the income elasticity is
questions.explanation: With dQ = 4, dI = 40,000, average Q = 22 and average I = 120,000, EI = (4/22)/(40,000/120,000) = 0.18/0.33 = 0.55, so bread is a necessity. Option C uses initial values (20 percent / 40 percent), option A inverts the answer, and option B is only the percentage change in quantity.

questions.question: The income elasticity of demand for air travel is 1.2. Using EI = (percentage change in Q)/(percentage change in income), a 5 percent rise in income will increase the quantity of air travel demanded by
questions.explanation: Rearranging gives percentage change in Q = 1.2 x 5 = 6 percent. Option A divides 5 by 1.2 instead of multiplying, option D just repeats the elasticity, and option C divides 1.2 by 5.

questions.question: When the price of a bottle of Coke rises from N200 to N240, the quantity of Pepsi demanded rises from 500 to 550 bottles. Using the point formula Exy = (dQx/Qx)/(dPy/Py) with initial values, the cross-price elasticity and relationship are
questions.explanation: Pepsi quantity rises 50/500 = 10 percent while Coke price rises 40/200 = 20 percent, so Exy = 10/20 = +0.50, and a positive sign means substitutes. Option B gets the sign wrong, option A inverts the ratio and misreads the sign, and option C has the right number but the wrong relationship.

questions.question: When the price of petrol rises from N600 to N720 per litre, the number of cars bought in a city falls from 1,000 to 900. Using the point formula Exy = (dQx/Qx)/(dPy/Py) with initial values, the cross-price elasticity of demand for cars with respect to the petrol price is
questions.explanation: Car purchases fall 100/1,000 = 10 percent while petrol price rises 120/600 = 20 percent, so Exy = -10/20 = -0.50, showing the goods are complements. Option D drops the negative sign, option A inverts the ratio, and option C reports only the change in quantity.
