questions.question: When the price of printers rises from N50,000 to N70,000, the quantity of ink cartridges demanded falls from 300 to 240. Using the arc (midpoint) formula Exy = (dQx/dPy) x (average Py / average Qx), the cross-price elasticity is
questions.explanation: With dQx = -60, dPy = 20,000, average Qx = 270 and average Py = 60,000, Exy = (-60/270)/(20,000/60,000) = -0.22/0.33 = -0.67, so printers and cartridges are complements. Option D uses initial values, option B drops the sign, and option C inverts the ratio.

questions.question: The cross-price elasticity of demand for chicken with respect to the price of beef is 0.8. Using Exy = (percentage change in Qx)/(percentage change in Py), a 15 percent rise in the price of beef will change the quantity of chicken demanded by
questions.explanation: Percentage change in chicken demanded = 0.8 x 15 = +12 percent, and the positive cross elasticity means beef and chicken are substitutes. Option B has the wrong sign, option D divides 15 by 0.8, and option A just repeats the elasticity.

questions.question: When the price of tomatoes rises from N50 to N60 per kg, the quantity supplied rises from 200 kg to 260 kg. Using the point formula Es = (dQ/Q)/(dP/P) with initial values, the price elasticity of supply is
questions.explanation: Quantity supplied rises 60/200 = 30 percent while price rises 10/50 = 20 percent, so Es = 30/20 = 1.50, which is elastic supply. Option A inverts the ratio, option B uses absolute changes 60/10 without converting to percentages, and option D reports only the quantity change.

questions.question: When the price of a carton of fish rises from N10,000 to N14,000, the quantity supplied rises from 100 to 120 cartons. Using the arc (midpoint) formula Es = (dQ/dP) x (average P / average Q), the price elasticity of supply is
questions.explanation: With dQ = 20, dP = 4,000, average Q = 110 and average P = 12,000, Es = (20/110)/(4,000/12,000) = 0.18/0.33 = 0.55, so supply is inelastic. Option A uses initial values (20 percent / 40 percent), option C inverts the answer, and option D is only the percentage change in quantity.

questions.question: The supply of a good is Qs = -20 + 4P. Using the point formula Es = (dQ/dP)(P/Q), the price elasticity of supply at P = N10 is
questions.explanation: At P = 10, Qs = -20 + 40 = 20 and dQ/dP = 4, so Es = 4 x (10/20) = 2.00. Option B is only the slope term, option D inverts the answer, and option C would hold only for a straight-line supply curve through the origin.

questions.question: The price elasticity of supply of maize is 0.5. Using Es = (percentage change in Qs)/(percentage change in P), a 20 percent rise in the price of maize will raise the quantity supplied by
questions.explanation: Percentage change in quantity supplied = 0.5 x 20 = 10 percent, so supply is inelastic. Option B divides 20 by 0.5 instead of multiplying, option D assumes unit elasticity, and option C simply repeats the elasticity.

questions.question: The marginal product of labor is equal to

options.a: the additional labor required to produce one more unit of output.
options.b: average product when average product is at a minimum.
options.c: the additional output produced by hiring one more unit of labor.
options.d: the slope of a ray drawn from the origin to a point on the total product curve.

questions.explanation: The marginal product of labour is the extra output produced when one more unit of labour is employed, holding other inputs fixed: MPL = change in TP / change in L. Option A turns the ratio upside down (labour per unit of output), and option D describes the average product, which is the slope of a ray from the origin to the TP curve.

questions.question: The average product of labor is equal to

options.a: the additional labor required to produce one more unit of output.
options.b: marginal product when average product is at a minimum.
options.c: the additional output produced by hiring one more unit of labor.
options.d: the slope of a ray drawn from the origin to a point on the total product curve.

questions.explanation: Average product of labour is TP/L, and that is exactly the slope of a straight line (ray) drawn from the origin to a point on the TP curve. Option C is the definition of marginal product, and option B is wrong because MP equals AP where AP is at its maximum, not its minimum.

questions.question: The output elasticity of labor is

options.a: equal to one at the level of output where average product is at a maximum.
options.b: the percentage change in labor required to produce one more unit of output.
options.c: equal to the ratio of total product to the quantity of labor employed.
options.d: a measure of the percentage change in output that can result when the quantity of labor is held constant.

questions.explanation: Output elasticity of labour is the percentage change in output divided by the percentage change in labour, which simplifies to MP/AP. Where AP is at its maximum, MP = AP, so the elasticity equals one. Option C describes average product itself, and option D is impossible because output cannot be changed by labour if labour is held constant.

questions.question: The point of inflection on the total product curve corresponds to the level of output where

options.b: average product is at a maximum.
options.c: marginal product is at a maximum.
options.d: All of the above are correct.

questions.explanation: At the point of inflection the TP curve stops rising at an increasing rate and starts rising at a decreasing rate, so its slope, the marginal product, is at its maximum there. Options A and B are wrong because AP reaches its maximum, and Stage II begins, at a larger output where MP falls to meet AP, so D is also wrong.

questions.question: The law of diminishing returns

options.a: is reflected in the negatively sloped portion of the marginal product curve.
options.b: is the result of specialization and division of labor.
options.c: applies in both the short run and the long run.
options.d: All of the above are correct.

questions.explanation: The law of diminishing returns says that as more of a variable input is added to fixed inputs, marginal product eventually falls, which is the downward-sloping part of the MP curve. Option B is wrong because specialisation and division of labour explain rising returns, not diminishing ones, and option C is wrong because the law needs at least one fixed input, so it is a short-run law only.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a production function?

options.a: An equation, table or graph showing the maximum output that can be produced from different combinations of inputs, given technology
options.b: A graph showing all combinations of two inputs that cost the same amount
options.c: A list of the prices the firm pays for each of its inputs
options.d: A schedule showing the total cost of producing each level of output

questions.explanation: A production function is a purely technical relationship: it shows the maximum output obtainable from each combination of inputs with the existing technology. Options D and C bring in costs and prices, which belong to cost analysis, and option B describes an isocost line, not a production function.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes a fixed input?

options.a: An input whose price never changes
options.b: An input whose quantity cannot be changed within the period under consideration (the short run)
options.c: An input that can never be changed, even in the long run
options.d: An input whose quantity rises and falls directly with output

questions.explanation: A fixed input, such as factory buildings, cannot be varied within the short run, but it can be changed in the long run. Option C is wrong because in the long run all inputs become variable, option D describes a variable input, and option A confuses a fixed quantity with a fixed price.

questions.question: The output elasticity of an input is equal to

options.a: the marginal product of the input multiplied by its price
options.b: the average product of the input divided by its marginal product
options.c: the marginal product of the input divided by its average product
options.d: the change in output divided by the change in the input

questions.explanation: Output elasticity is (% change in Q)/(% change in L) = (change in Q / change in L) x (L/Q), which is MP x 1/AP = MP/AP. Option B is the inverse, and option D is just the marginal product, which ignores the percentage form.

questions.question: The law of diminishing returns is

options.a: the same thing as decreasing returns to scale
options.b: a short-run concept, because it requires at least one input to be fixed
options.c: a long-run concept, because all inputs are varied together
options.d: a law that applies only when all inputs are increased in the same proportion

questions.explanation: Diminishing returns arise because more and more of a variable input is combined with a fixed input, so the law belongs to the short run. Options C and D describe changing all inputs together, which is about returns to scale, and option A confuses diminishing returns to a factor with decreasing returns to scale.

questions.question: When the marginal product of a variable input is less than its average product, the average product is
questions.explanation: Whenever the marginal unit adds less than the current average, it pulls the average down, so AP is falling when MP < AP. Option D applies when MP > AP, and option C applies only at the single point where MP = AP.

questions.question: Stage II of production begins and ends, respectively, where

options.a: total product is at a maximum, and marginal product is at a maximum
options.b: average product equals zero, and total product is at a maximum
options.c: average product is at a maximum, and marginal product equals zero
options.d: marginal product is at a maximum, and average product equals zero

questions.explanation: Stage II starts where AP reaches its peak (where MP = AP) and ends where MP falls to zero, which is also where TP is at its maximum. Option D is wrong because MP peaks earlier, inside Stage I, and option A gets the end of the stage confused with its start.

questions.question: The marginal product of labour curve shows the change in total product resulting from a:

options.a: One-unit increase in the quantity of a particular resource used, letting other resources vary.
options.b: One-unit increase in the quantity of a particular resource used, holding constant other resources.
options.c: Change in the cost of a variable resource.
options.d: Change in the cost of a fixed resource.

questions.explanation: Marginal product measures the extra output from adding one more unit of an input while all other inputs are held constant. Option A is wrong because letting other inputs vary would mix in their contribution. Options C and D are about costs, not physical output.

questions.question: When the total product curve is falling, the:

options.a: Marginal product of labor is zero.
options.b: Marginal product of labor is negative.
options.c: Average product of labor is increasing.
options.d: Average product of labor must be negative .

questions.explanation: Marginal product is the change in total product from one more unit of labour. If total product is falling, each extra worker reduces output, so marginal product is negative. Option A is true only at the very top of the total product curve, and option D is wrong because average product stays positive as long as total product is positive.

questions.question: When marginal product reaches its maximum, what can be said of total product?

options.a: Total product must be at its maximum
options.b: Total product starts to decline even if marginal product is positive
options.c: Total product is increasing if marginal product is still positive

questions.explanation: When marginal product reaches its maximum, it is still positive, so total product is still rising, and in fact rising at its fastest rate (the inflection point of the TP curve). Option A is wrong because TP is at its maximum only when MP falls to zero, and option D is wrong for the same reason.

questions.question: Which of the following statements best describes the general form of a production function: (i) It is a purely technological relationship between quantities of input and quantities of output. (ii) It represents the technology of an organisation, sector of an economy. iii) Prices of inputs or of the output do not enter into the production function. (iv) It is a flow concept describing the transformation of inputs into output per unit of time.
questions.explanation: A production function is a purely technical relationship showing the maximum output obtainable from given inputs with a given state of technology. It can describe a firm, an industry or a whole economy, it contains no prices, and it is a flow measured per period of time. All four statements are therefore correct, so options A, B and C each leave out a true statement.

questions.question: Which of the following statements describes the presence of diminishing returns. Holding at least one factor constant .......

options.a: The marginal product of a factor is positive and rising.
options.b: The marginal product of a factor is positive but falling.
options.c: The marginal product of a factor is falling and negative.
options.d: The marginal product of a factor is constant.

questions.explanation: Diminishing returns describes the stage where each extra unit of the variable factor still adds to output, but by less and less, so marginal product is positive but falling. Option A describes increasing returns, and option D constant returns. Option C goes beyond diminishing returns to negative returns, where adding the factor actually reduces total output.

questions.question: A basic distinction between the long run and the short run is that

options.a: If a firm produces no output in the long run it still incurs a cost, while in the short run a firm incurs a cost only if it produces output.
options.b: The opportunity costs of production are constant in the short run, while the opportunity costs of production are variable in the long run.
options.c: In the long run some inputs are fixed, while in the short run all inputs are variable.
options.d: In the short run complete adjustment of all inputs is impossible, while in the long run all inputs can be adjusted.

questions.explanation: The short run is a period in which at least one input cannot be changed, while in the long run the firm has enough time to adjust every input. Option C has this backwards, and option A is also reversed, since fixed costs that must be paid even at zero output exist only in the short run.

questions.question: Whenever marginal product is positive but declining with increasing use of an input,

options.a: Total product is declining as input increases.
options.b: Average product is declining as input use increases
options.c: Marginal product is greater than average product
options.d: Total product is increasing at a decreasing rate as input use increases.

questions.explanation: As long as marginal product is positive, each extra unit of input still adds to total product, so TP keeps rising; if MP is falling, each addition is smaller, so TP rises at a decreasing rate. Option B is not always true, because average product keeps rising while MP is still above AP, and option C is not guaranteed either.

questions.question: When average product is at a maximum, marginal product is
questions.explanation: Marginal product cuts average product at the highest point of the AP curve. While MP is above AP it pulls AP up, and once MP falls below AP it pulls AP down, so at the peak MP = AP. Option A is wrong because MP is zero where total product, not average product, is at a maximum, and option B is wrong because MP is already falling at that point.

questions.question: Whenever average product is declining, with increases in input usage,

options.a: Marginal product is less than average product
options.b: Total product is declining with increases in input
options.c: Total product is increasing with increases in input
options.d: Marginal product is greater than average product

questions.explanation: An average falls only when the marginal addition is below it, so whenever average product is declining, marginal product must be less than average product. Option B is not necessarily true: total product keeps rising after AP starts falling, as long as MP is still positive. Option D describes the stage when AP is rising.

questions.question: The total product curve may initially show output increasing at an increasing rate as more labour is hired because of the:

options.a: Declining quality of the labor force.

questions.explanation: In the early stage of production, adding workers allows better division of labour and fuller use of the fixed input, so each extra worker adds more than the previous one. This rising marginal physical product makes total product grow at an increasing rate. Option C, diminishing marginal returns, explains the later stage when TP grows at a decreasing rate.

questions.question: When both average and total product are greater than zero, and marginal product equals average product, then total product:
questions.explanation: Marginal product equals average product at the maximum point of the AP curve. At that point MP is still positive (because AP is positive), so total product is positive and still rising. Option A is wrong because TP is at its maximum only where MP = 0, which comes later.

questions.question: The law of diminishing marginal returns is encountered as increasing amounts of labour are hired because:

options.a: As production rises, the additional labor hired is less and less skilled.
options.b: Experienced workers are hired before the less skilled.
options.c: Each extra worker hired decreases the amounts of land and capital per worker, so the work place becomes more congested and managerial control becomes more difficult.
options.d: As more and more is produced, selling it requires cutting prices.

questions.explanation: Diminishing returns arise because the other inputs are fixed: each extra worker has less land and capital to work with, so the work place becomes crowded and harder to manage, and each addition to output gets smaller. Options A and B are wrong because the law assumes all units of labour are equally skilled, and option D is about selling prices, not physical output.

questions.question: In production theory, the short run is best defined as a period in which

options.a: the firm operates for less than one calendar year
options.b: technology changes while all inputs stay fixed
options.c: at least one factor of production is fixed in quantity
options.d: all factors of production can be varied

questions.explanation: The short run is defined by how flexible inputs are, not by calendar time: it is any period in which at least one input, such as plant or machinery, cannot be changed. Option D describes the long run, and Option A is wrong because the short run is not a set number of months; its length depends on how quickly the firm can change its fixed inputs.

questions.question: A bakery in Yaba can hire extra bakers within a week, but it would take more than a year to build and equip a new bakery hall. In the short run, the bakery hall is an example of a
questions.explanation: An input whose quantity cannot be changed within the period being considered is a fixed input, and the bakery hall fits this because it takes over a year to change, so C is right. Option B describes the bakers, who can be added quickly, and Option A refers to goods such as flour that are used up in making the bread.

questions.question: Which of the following is most likely to be a variable input in the short run for a garri-processing factory in Ogun State?

options.b: The land on which the factory stands

questions.explanation: A variable input is one the firm can increase or reduce quickly as it changes output, and the daily purchase of cassava tubers fits this, so D is correct. Options C, A and B are buildings, installed machinery and land, which cannot be changed quickly and are therefore fixed inputs in the short run.

questions.question: The change in total product resulting from employing one additional unit of a variable input, with all other inputs held constant, is called the
questions.explanation: Marginal product measures the extra output from one more unit of the variable input, MP = change in TP / change in L, so D is right. Option B is output per unit of input (TP/L), and Option C is the rate at which one input can replace another while output stays the same, which is an isoquant idea, not a single-input one.

questions.question: The average product of labour (APL) is calculated as

options.a: total product divided by the number of units of labour
options.b: change in total product divided by change in labour
options.c: number of units of labour divided by total product
options.d: total product multiplied by the number of units of labour

questions.explanation: Average product is output per unit of the variable input, APL = TP/L, so A is correct. Option B is the formula for marginal product, and Option C turns the ratio upside down, giving labour per unit of output instead of output per worker.

questions.question: When the marginal product of labour is greater than the average product of labour, the average product of labour is
questions.explanation: If the extra output from the next worker is above the current average, adding that worker pulls the average up, so AP is rising and B is right. Option C happens when MP is below AP, and Option A happens only at the point where MP exactly equals AP.

questions.question: Total product of a variable input reaches its maximum when the marginal product of that input is
questions.explanation: TP keeps rising as long as MP is positive and starts falling once MP turns negative, so TP peaks exactly where MP = 0 and B is right. Option D marks the point of inflection of TP, where diminishing marginal returns begin, and Option A marks the maximum of AP, not of TP.

questions.question: A cocoa farmer in Ondo keeps adding workers to the same plot until an extra worker actually causes total output to fall. The marginal product of that extra worker is
questions.explanation: Marginal product is the change in total output from one more worker, so if output falls the change is below zero and MP is negative, making D correct. Option B would mean output stayed exactly the same, and Option C would mean output still rose, only by less than before.

questions.question: The law of diminishing marginal returns states that as more units of a variable input are added to a fixed input, with technology unchanged,

options.b: the marginal product of the variable input eventually declines
options.c: the average cost of production always falls
options.d: output increases in the same proportion as the input

questions.explanation: The law says that beyond some point each extra unit of the variable input adds less to output than the one before, because it has less of the fixed input to work with, so B is right. Option A is wrong because TP falls only if MP becomes negative and need not reach zero, and Option D describes a constant marginal product, which is the opposite of what the law predicts.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an assumption of the law of variable proportions?

options.a: At least one input is held fixed
options.b: Units of the variable input are homogeneous
options.c: The state of technology is given
options.d: All inputs are increased in the same proportion

questions.explanation: The law of variable proportions is a short-run law in which only one input changes while others stay fixed, so increasing all inputs in the same proportion is not one of its assumptions; that is returns to scale, and D is the answer. Options C, A and B are genuine assumptions: given technology, at least one fixed factor and identical units of the variable factor.

questions.question: In the three stages of production, Stage I extends from the origin to the point where

options.a: the average product of the variable input is at its maximum
options.b: total product is at its maximum
options.c: the marginal product of the variable input becomes zero
options.d: the marginal product of the variable input is at its maximum

questions.explanation: Stage I is the range over which average product is rising, so it ends where AP reaches its peak and MP = AP, making A correct. Option D is a point inside Stage I where diminishing marginal returns begin, while Options B and C mark the end of Stage II, where MP = 0 and TP is at its maximum.

questions.question: Stage III of production is the range in which

options.a: the marginal product exceeds the average product
options.b: the average product of the variable input is rising
options.c: total product is rising at an increasing rate
options.d: the marginal product of the variable input is negative

questions.explanation: Stage III begins once MP falls below zero, so each extra unit of the variable input reduces total output; D is correct. Options B and A describe Stage I, where AP is still rising because MP is above it, and Option C describes the early part of Stage I where MP is rising.

questions.question: A rational producer will choose to operate in which stage of production?

options.a: Stage I, where AP is rising
options.b: Stage III, where MP is negative
options.c: Stage II, between maximum AP and zero MP
options.d: At the point where MP is at its maximum

questions.explanation: Stage II is the economic region: AP is falling but MP is still positive, so extra units still add to output, and C is correct. Option A is irrational because output per unit of input can still be raised by using more of the variable input, Option B is irrational because extra units cut output, and Option D lies inside Stage I.

questions.question: A firm would never knowingly operate in Stage III because in that stage

options.a: the marginal product of the variable input is at its maximum
options.b: the average product of the variable input is still rising
options.c: adding more of the variable input reduces total output
options.d: the fixed input is being under-used

questions.explanation: In Stage III the marginal product of the variable input is negative, so the firm would pay for extra units that actually lower output; C is correct. Option B describes Stage I, Option A is a point inside Stage I, and Option D is also a Stage I feature, since in Stage III the fixed input is overcrowded rather than under-used.

questions.question: Stage I of production is considered irrational for a producer mainly because

options.a: average product of the variable input is still rising, so using more of it raises output per unit
options.b: the marginal product of the variable input is negative
options.d: the variable input is used too intensively relative to the fixed input

questions.explanation: In Stage I the average product of the variable input is still rising, so the firm can raise output per unit of that input by using more of it, and stopping there wastes the fixed input; A is right. Options B and C describe Stage III, and Option D is the problem of Stage III too, where the fixed input is overcrowded.

questions.question: Over the range where the marginal product of labour is rising, the total product curve is
questions.explanation: Rising MP means each extra worker adds more output than the last, so TP climbs more and more steeply, which is C. Option D applies once MP is falling but still positive, Option A applies only when MP is negative, and Option B applies only where MP is zero.

questions.question: On a total product curve, the marginal product at any point is measured by

options.a: the slope of a straight line from the origin to that point
options.b: the slope of the TP curve at that point
options.c: the area under the TP curve up to that point
options.d: the height of the TP curve at that point

questions.explanation: MP is the change in TP per unit change in input, which is the slope of the TP curve at that point, so B is correct. Option A measures average product, because the slope of a ray from the origin equals TP/L, and Option D is simply total product itself.

questions.question: The main difference between the law of variable proportions and returns to scale is that

options.a: the former applies to the long run, while the latter applies to the short run
options.b: the former assumes changing technology, while the latter assumes fixed technology
options.c: the former varies one input with others fixed, while the latter varies all inputs in the same proportion
options.d: the former concerns costs, while the latter concerns revenue

questions.explanation: The law of variable proportions is a short-run law about changing one input while others stay fixed, whereas returns to scale is a long-run idea about changing all inputs together in the same proportion, so C is right. Option A reverses the time periods, and Option B is wrong because both concepts assume a given technology.

questions.question: Diminishing marginal returns to a variable input set in at the point where

options.a: the total product curve reaches its maximum
options.b: the marginal product curve reaches its maximum
options.d: the average product curve reaches its maximum

questions.explanation: Marginal returns start to diminish as soon as MP stops rising, which is at the peak of the MP curve and the point of inflection of the TP curve, so B is correct. Option D comes later and marks the start of Stage II, while Options A and C both mark the end of Stage II.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT true of Stage II of production?

options.a: The average product of the variable input is rising
options.b: The marginal product of the variable input is below its average product
options.d: The marginal product of the variable input is positive

questions.explanation: In Stage II average product is falling, because it begins at the peak of AP, so the statement that AP is rising is false and A is the answer. Options D, B and C are all true of Stage II: MP is positive but below AP, so TP is still increasing, only at a decreasing rate.

questions.question: A poultry farm in Abeokuta has a fixed number of pens and records the following total product (TP, crates of eggs per week) as it hires more workers (L): L = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8; TP = 10, 24, 42, 57, 66, 72, 72, 68. What is the marginal product of the 3rd worker?
questions.explanation: Marginal product is the change in TP when one more worker is hired: MP of the 3rd worker = 42 - 24 = 18 crates, so B is correct. Option D is the average product of 3 workers (42/3), Option A is the total product of 3 workers, and Option C is the total product of 2 workers.

questions.question: A poultry farm in Abeokuta has a fixed number of pens and records the following total product (TP, crates of eggs per week) as it hires more workers (L): L = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8; TP = 10, 24, 42, 57, 66, 72, 72, 68. What is the average product of labour when 5 workers are employed?
questions.explanation: Average product is TP divided by the number of workers: 66 / 5 = 13.20 crates per worker, so B is right. Option D is the marginal product of the 5th worker (66 - 57), Option A is total product, and Option C is the average product of 4 workers.

questions.question: A poultry farm in Abeokuta has a fixed number of pens and records the following total product (TP, crates of eggs per week) as it hires more workers (L): L = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8; TP = 10, 24, 42, 57, 66, 72, 72, 68. Diminishing marginal returns to labour begin with the hiring of which worker?
questions.explanation: The marginal products are 10, 14, 18, 15, 9, 6, 0 and -4, so MP rises up to the 3rd worker and first falls with the 4th worker (from 18 to 15), making A correct. Option C is the worker with the highest MP, not the first with a lower MP, and Option B is where MP reaches zero, which is much later.

questions.question: A poultry farm in Abeokuta has a fixed number of pens and records the following total product (TP, crates of eggs per week) as it hires more workers (L): L = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8; TP = 10, 24, 42, 57, 66, 72, 72, 68. At what level of employment is the average product of labour at its maximum?
questions.explanation: The average products are 10, 12, 14, 14.25, 13.2, 12, about 10.29 and 8.5, so AP peaks at 14.25 with 4 workers, and A is right. Option B is where MP peaks (18), and Options D and C are where TP reaches its maximum of 72, not where output per worker is highest.

questions.question: A poultry farm in Abeokuta has a fixed number of pens and records the following total product (TP, crates of eggs per week) as it hires more workers (L): L = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8; TP = 10, 24, 42, 57, 66, 72, 72, 68. What is the marginal product of the 8th worker?
questions.explanation: MP of the 8th worker = 68 - 72 = -4 crates: hiring this worker actually lowers output, so C is correct and the farm is in Stage III. Option D is the MP of the 7th worker, Option A is the average product of 8 workers (68/8), and Option B is total product.

questions.question: A poultry farm in Abeokuta has a fixed number of pens and records the following total product (TP, crates of eggs per week) as it hires more workers (L): L = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8; TP = 10, 24, 42, 57, 66, 72, 72, 68. Within what range of employment is the farm in Stage II, the rational stage of production?
questions.explanation: Stage II runs from the point of maximum AP (4 workers, AP = 14.25) to the point where MP becomes zero (the 7th worker, MP = 0), so B is right. Option D is Stage I, where AP is still rising, Option A covers the move into Stage III, where the 8th worker has a negative MP, and Option C starts too early, at the peak of MP.

questions.question: A tailoring shop in Aba finds that the average product of 5 tailors is 20 shirts per day and the average product of 6 tailors is 19 shirts per day. What is the marginal product of the 6th tailor?
questions.explanation: First find total products: TP(5) = 5 x 20 = 100 and TP(6) = 6 x 19 = 114, so MP of the 6th tailor = 114 - 100 = 14 shirts, and A is correct. Option D wrongly subtracts the two averages, Option C is the average product of 6 tailors, and Option B is the total product of 6 tailors.

questions.question: On a rice farm in Ebonyi the average product of 4 workers is 25 bags. If the 5th worker has a marginal product of 15 bags, what is the total product of 5 workers?
questions.explanation: TP of 4 workers = 4 x 25 = 100 bags; adding the 5th worker's MP gives 100 + 15 = 115 bags, so A is right. Option B simply adds AP and MP, Option D wrongly multiplies AP of 25 by 5 workers, and Option C is the new average product (115/5).

questions.question: A firm's short-run production function is Q = 10L - L^2, where L is labour. At what level of labour is total product at its maximum?
questions.explanation: MP = dQ/dL = 10 - 2L, and TP is maximised where MP = 0, giving 10 - 2L = 0 and L = 5, so B is correct. Option A is where output falls back to zero (10L = L^2), and Option D is the maximum output itself (25), not the labour input.

questions.question: A firm's short-run production function is Q = 10L - L^2. What is the maximum output the firm can produce?
questions.explanation: MP = 10 - 2L equals zero at L = 5, so maximum output is Q = 10(5) - 5^2 = 50 - 25 = 25, and D is right. Option B forgets to subtract L^2, Option A is output at L = 4 (or L = 6), and Option C is the labour input at the maximum rather than the output.

questions.question: For the production function Q = 10L - L^2, what is the marginal product of labour when L = 3?
questions.explanation: MP = dQ/dL = 10 - 2L, so at L = 3, MP = 10 - 6 = 4, and D is correct. Option A is the average product (Q/L = 10 - L = 7), Option B is total output at L = 3 (30 - 9 = 21), and Option C is MP at L = 2.

questions.question: For the production function Q = 10L - L^2, what is the average product of labour when L = 4?
questions.explanation: AP = Q/L = (10L - L^2)/L = 10 - L, so at L = 4, AP = 6, and C is right. Option B is the marginal product at L = 4 (10 - 2L = 2), Option D is total output at L = 4 (40 - 16 = 24), and Option A would follow from wrongly using AP = 10 - L/2.

questions.question: A firm's short-run production function is Q = 6L^2 - 0.2L^3, where L is labour. At what level of labour is the marginal product of labour at its maximum?
questions.explanation: MP = dQ/dL = 12L - 0.6L^2, and MP is at its peak where dMP/dL = 12 - 1.2L = 0, giving L = 10, so C is correct. Option B is where AP is maximised, Option A is where MP = 0 and TP is maximised, and Option D is where output falls back to zero.

questions.question: A firm's short-run production function is Q = 6L^2 - 0.2L^3, where L is labour. At what level of labour is the average product of labour at its maximum?
questions.explanation: AP = Q/L = 6L - 0.2L^2, which peaks where dAP/dL = 6 - 0.4L = 0, giving L = 15; at that point AP = MP = 45, as the theory predicts, so B is right. Option D is where MP is maximised, and Option C is where MP becomes zero.

questions.question: A firm's short-run production function is Q = 6L^2 - 0.2L^3, where L is labour. At what level of labour is total product at its maximum?
questions.explanation: TP is maximised where MP = 12L - 0.6L^2 = 0, that is L(12 - 0.6L) = 0, giving L = 20, so A is correct. Option B is the peak of MP and Option C is the peak of AP, both of which come before the peak of TP, while Option D is where output has fallen back to zero.

questions.question: A firm's short-run production function is Q = 6L^2 - 0.2L^3, where L is labour. What is the maximum total product the firm can obtain?
questions.explanation: TP peaks where MP = 12L - 0.6L^2 = 0, at L = 20, so Q = 6(400) - 0.2(8,000) = 2,400 - 1,600 = 800, and B is right. Option D is output at L = 15, where AP (not TP) is maximised, while Options C and A are just the separate terms 0.2L^3 and 6L^2 at L = 20.

questions.question: A firm's short-run production function is Q = 6L^2 - 0.2L^3, where L is labour. What is the maximum value of the average product of labour?
questions.explanation: AP = 6L - 0.2L^2 is maximised at L = 15, giving AP = 90 - 45 = 45, so D is correct. Option B is the maximum marginal product (at L = 10), Option A is AP at L = 10, and Option C is total product at L = 15 rather than output per worker.

questions.question: A firm's short-run production function is Q = 6L^2 - 0.2L^3, where L is labour. Over what range of labour input is the firm in Stage II of production?
questions.explanation: Stage II begins at the maximum of AP (L = 15) and ends where MP = 0 (L = 20), so D is right. Options B and A wrongly start the stage at the peak of MP (L = 10), which is inside Stage I, and Option C is Stage III, where MP is negative.

questions.question: A firm's short-run production function is Q = 6L^2 - 0.2L^3, where L is labour. What is the marginal product of labour when L = 5?
questions.explanation: MP = dQ/dL = 12L - 0.6L^2, so at L = 5, MP = 60 - 15 = 45, and C is correct. Option B is the average product (6L - 0.2L^2 = 25), Option A is total output (150 - 25 = 125), and Option D forgets the second term of the MP function.

questions.question: A block-making yard in Ibadan produces 40 blocks per hour with 4 workers and 52 blocks per hour with 5 workers. What is the marginal product of the 5th worker?
questions.explanation: MP is the change in total product from the extra worker: 52 - 40 = 12 blocks, so C is right. Option D is the average product of 5 workers (52/5), Option B is the average product of 4 workers (40/4), and Option A is total product, not the addition to it.

questions.question: A palm-oil mill increases its workers from 5 to 7 and daily output rises from 100 to 130 litres. What is the marginal product per additional worker over this range?
questions.explanation: MP = change in TP / change in L = (130 - 100) / (7 - 5) = 30/2 = 15 litres per worker, so D is correct. Option C forgets to divide by the 2 extra workers, Option B is the average product of 7 workers (130/7), and Option A is the average product of 5 workers.

questions.question: Eight labourers on a tomato farm in Kano harvest 96 baskets in a day. What is the average product of labour?
questions.explanation: Average product = TP / L = 96 / 8 = 12 baskets per labourer, so D is right. Option A multiplies instead of dividing, Option B divides labour by output, and Option C wrongly divides by 7 instead of 8.

questions.question: A firm's production function is Q = 30L - 1.5L^2. What is the maximum output the firm can produce?
questions.explanation: MP = 30 - 3L equals zero at L = 10, so maximum output is 30(10) - 1.5(100) = 300 - 150 = 150, and A is correct. Option B forgets to subtract 1.5L^2, Option D is output at L = 5, and Option C is the labour input at which output is maximised.

questions.question: In a cassava mill the average product of labour is currently 30 kg per worker. The next worker hired has a marginal product of 24 kg. When that worker is hired, the average product of labour will
questions.explanation: When marginal product is below average product, adding that unit pulls the average down, just as a low score lowers a class average, so with MP = 24 below AP = 30 the AP falls and C is right. Option B would require MP above 30, and Option D would require MP exactly equal to 30.

questions.question: A bakery's 3 workers produce 45 loaves per hour. A 4th worker adds 9 loaves. What is the average product of labour with 4 workers?
questions.explanation: TP with 4 workers = 45 + 9 = 54 loaves, so AP = 54/4 = 13.50 loaves per worker, and B is correct. Option A is the marginal product of the 4th worker, Option C is the average product of 3 workers (45/3), and Option D is total product rather than output per worker.

questions.question: An isoquant that is

options.a: further from the origin represents greater output.
options.b: flatter represents the trade-offs between inputs that are poor substitutes.
options.c: negatively sloped represents input combinations associated with Stage I of production.
options.d: All of the above are correct.

questions.explanation: Each isoquant shows one level of output, and an isoquant further from the origin contains more of at least one input, so it represents a higher output. Option B is wrong because poor substitutes give a sharply curved, nearly L-shaped isoquant, not one that simply looks flatter, and option C is wrong because the negatively sloped part of an isoquant is the economic region (Stage II), not Stage I. Since B and C are false, D is false too.

questions.question: The absolute value of the slope of a convex isoquant

options.a: is equal to the marginal rate of technical substitution.
options.b: is equal to the ratio of the marginal products of the two inputs.
options.d: All of the above are correct.

questions.explanation: The absolute slope of an isoquant is the marginal rate of technical substitution, and MRTS of L for K = MPL/MPK. Because isoquants are convex, this MRTS falls as we move down the curve from left to right (diminishing MRTS). All three statements are true, so D is correct.

questions.question: The combination of inputs is optimal

options.a: at points of tangency between isoquants and isocosts.
options.b: if the marginal revenue product is equal to the marginal resource cost for all inputs.
options.c: if the marginal rate of technical substitution between every pair of inputs is equal to the ratio of the prices of those inputs.
options.d: All of the above are correct.

questions.explanation: The least-cost (optimal) input combination is where an isoquant is tangent to an isocost line, which means MRTS = w/r, the ratio of input prices. Hiring each input until its marginal revenue product equals its price also gives MPL/MPK = w/r, so it satisfies the same condition. Because A, B and C all describe the optimum, D is correct.

questions.question: An isocost line will be shifted further away from the origin

options.a: if the prices of both inputs increase.
options.c: if there is an advance in technology.
options.d: All of the above are correct.

questions.explanation: The isocost line is C = wL + rK, so a higher total cost outlay at the same input prices moves it parallel and further from the origin. Option A does the opposite: higher input prices let the same money buy less, so the line shifts toward the origin. Option C is wrong because better technology shifts the isoquants, not the isocost line, so D is also wrong.

questions.question: If isoquants are plotted on a graph with capital measured on the vertical axis and labor on the horizontal axis, then an increase in the wage rate will cause the isocost line

options.a: to become steeper and the optimal quantity of labor will decrease.
options.b: to become steeper and the optimal quantity of labor will increase.
options.c: to become flatter and the optimal quantity of labor will decrease.
options.d: to become flatter and the optimal quantity of labor will increase.

questions.explanation: With capital on the vertical axis and labour on the horizontal axis, the isocost slope is -w/r, so a higher wage makes the line steeper. Labour has become relatively dearer, so the cost-minimising firm substitutes capital for labour and uses less labour. Options C and D get the slope wrong, and option B gets the direction of substitution wrong.

questions.question: A line that connects all points where the marginal rate of technical substitution is equal to the ratio of input prices is called the
questions.explanation: The expansion path joins the tangency points between isoquants and isocost lines as output or outlay grows, and at each of those points MRTS = w/r. Option D, the isocost line, shows combinations with the same total cost, and option B, the TP curve, relates output to one variable input, so neither links all the tangency points.

questions.question: Suppose that three isoquants that represent 10, 20, and 30 units of output are plotted on a graph and a straight line is drawn from the origin through the isoquants. If the portion of the line between the isoquants that represent 10 and 20 units of output is longer than the portion of the line between the isoquants that represent 20 and 30 units of output, then the firm represented by these isoquants

options.b: is experiencing increasing returns to scale.
options.c: is experiencing decreasing returns to scale.
options.d: will maximize profits by producing 10 units of output.

questions.explanation: Each step from 10 to 20 and from 20 to 30 units adds the same 10 units of output. If the second step needs a shorter distance along the ray, it needs a smaller increase in inputs, so output is growing faster than inputs, which is increasing returns to scale. Option C would apply if the isoquants were getting further apart, and options A and D are not shown by isoquant spacing at all.

questions.question: If the output elasticities of all inputs used by a firm are summed together, then the total

options.a: will be greater than one if returns to scale are decreasing.
options.b: will be equal to one if returns to scale are constant.
options.c: will be less than one if returns to scale are increasing.
options.d: All of the above are correct.

questions.explanation: When the output elasticities of all inputs are added, the sum tells us returns to scale: greater than one means increasing, equal to one means constant, and less than one means decreasing returns. Options A and C reverse the signs of the inequalities, so they are false, which also rules out D.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a characteristic of production technologies that can be described by the Cobb-Douglas production function?

options.a: The marginal product of an input divided by the average product of that input is constant.
options.b: The exponents will sum to one if returns to scale are constant.
options.c: Linear regression can be used to estimate the parameters of the function.
options.d: All of the above are characteristics of the Cobb-Douglas production function.

questions.explanation: In a Cobb-Douglas function Q = A L^a K^b, MP/AP for each input equals its exponent, which is a constant; the exponents sum to one under constant returns to scale; and taking logs gives log Q = log A + a log L + b log K, which can be estimated by linear regression. Since A, B and C are all genuine characteristics, D is correct.

questions.question: If the marginal product of labor is 2, the marginal product of capital is 4, the wage rate is $3, the rental price of capital is $6, and the price of output is $1.50, then the firm should

options.a: Increase output by hiring more labor, more capital, or both.
options.b: Hold output constant, but hire more labor and less capital.
options.c: Decrease output by reducing the quantity of capital, reducing the number of units of labor, or both.
options.d: None of the above is correct.

questions.explanation: Check the cost-minimising rule first: MPL/w = 2/3 = 0.667 and MPK/r = 4/6 = 0.667, so the input mix is already correct and option B is wrong. Then check output: the value of each extra unit is MPL x P = 2 x 1.50 = 3 = w and MPK x P = 4 x 1.50 = 6 = r, so expanding or cutting output would not raise profit, which rules out A and C. The firm is already at its best position, so D is correct.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the long run in production is correct?

options.c: At least one input is fixed

questions.explanation: The long run is a period long enough for the firm to change the quantities of all its inputs, including plant and machinery. Option C describes the short run, where at least one input is fixed, and options A and B are even more restrictive, so they cannot describe the long run.

questions.question: Returns to scale describe how output responds when

options.a: one input is varied while the others are held fixed in the short run
options.b: output is held constant and one input is substituted for another
options.c: the price of one input changes
options.d: all inputs are changed in the same proportion in the long run

questions.explanation: Scale refers to the size of the whole operation, so returns to scale are a long-run idea measured by changing all inputs in the same proportion. Option A describes returns to a variable factor (the law of variable proportions), which is a short-run idea, and option B describes substitution along an isoquant.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about short-run and long-run decisions of a firm is correct?

options.a: The firm plans in the long run and operates in the short run
options.b: The firm both plans and operates only in the long run
options.c: The firm plans in the short run and operates in the long run
options.d: The firm's planning horizon is unrelated to the long run

questions.explanation: When a firm plans, it can still choose any plant size, so planning takes place in the long run; once a plant is built, day-to-day production happens with that fixed plant, which is the short run. Option C reverses this, and option B ignores that actual production always takes place with some inputs fixed.

questions.question: An isoquant shows

options.a: all combinations of two goods that give the consumer the same satisfaction
options.b: the maximum output obtainable from one variable input
options.c: all combinations of two inputs that produce the same level of output
options.d: all combinations of two inputs that have the same total cost

questions.explanation: Iso means equal and quant means quantity, so an isoquant joins all input combinations that yield the same output. Option D is an isocost line, option A is an indifference curve from consumer theory, and option B describes the short-run total product curve.

questions.question: Ridge lines drawn on an isoquant map

options.a: join points of equal total cost
options.b: separate the economic region of production (Stage II) from the uneconomic regions (Stages I and III)
options.c: join all points where isoquants are tangent to isocost lines
options.d: show the maximum output the firm can produce

questions.explanation: Ridge lines pass through the points where isoquants turn backward (where an input's MP becomes zero), so outside them the isoquants slope upward and one input has negative MP. A rational firm only operates between the ridge lines, in Stage II. Option C describes the expansion path and option A an isocost line.

questions.question: The marginal rate of technical substitution of labour for capital measures

options.a: the extra output obtained from one more unit of labour
options.b: the number of units of labour needed to produce one more unit of output
options.c: the number of units of capital that can be given up when one more unit of labour is added, with output held constant
options.d: the ratio of the price of labour to the price of capital

questions.explanation: MRTS is the rate at which one input can be swapped for another while staying on the same isoquant, so output does not change. Option A is the marginal product of labour, and option D is the slope of the isocost line, which equals the MRTS only at the least-cost point.

questions.question: The closer an isoquant is to a straight line, the closer the two inputs are to being
questions.explanation: A straight-line isoquant has a constant MRTS, meaning one input can always replace the other at the same rate, which is the case of perfect substitutes. Option D is wrong because perfect complements give L-shaped (right-angled) isoquants, the opposite of a straight line.

questions.question: An isocost line shows

options.a: the combination of inputs that maximises output
options.b: the total cost of producing each level of output
options.c: all combinations of inputs that produce the same output
options.d: all combinations of inputs that have the same total cost

questions.explanation: An isocost line, C = wL + rK, gives every combination of labour and capital the firm can buy with a given outlay at given input prices. Option C describes an isoquant, and option A is only the single tangency point between an isocost line and the highest isoquant.

questions.question: With capital on the vertical axis and labour on the horizontal axis, the absolute value of the slope of the isocost line equals

options.a: the ratio of the marginal product of labour to the marginal product of capital at every point
options.b: the ratio of the price of capital to the wage rate (r/w)
options.c: the total cost divided by the wage rate
options.d: the ratio of the wage rate to the price of capital (w/r)

questions.explanation: From C = wL + rK, K = C/r - (w/r)L, so the slope is -w/r. Option B inverts the ratio, option A is the slope of an isoquant, which equals w/r only at the tangency point, and option C is the horizontal intercept, not the slope.

questions.question: If two isocost lines are parallel, then

options.a: the one closer to the origin represents a higher total cost
options.b: they represent the same level of output
options.c: they have the same total cost but different input prices
options.d: they have the same input price ratio, and the one further from the origin represents a higher total cost

questions.explanation: Parallel lines have equal slopes, and the slope of an isocost is w/r, so the input price ratio is the same; the outer line lets the firm buy more of both inputs, so it reflects a bigger outlay. Option A reverses this, and option B confuses isocosts with isoquants.

questions.question: If a firm is minimising the total cost of producing a given level of output, then it is also

options.a: producing where MRTS is greater than the input price ratio
options.d: maximising the output that can be produced at that level of total cost

questions.explanation: Both problems lead to the same tangency of an isoquant with an isocost line, where MRTS = w/r, so the least-cost point for an output is also the maximum-output point for that cost. Option A is wrong because at the optimum MRTS equals, not exceeds, the price ratio, and option B is wrong because a rational firm operates between the ridge lines.

questions.question: Which of the following is true of every point on a firm's expansion path?

options.a: It lies on a straight line through the origin for every production function
options.b: It is an input combination that minimises the cost of producing that level of output
options.c: It is a point where the marginal products of both inputs are zero
options.d: It is an input combination that maximises the firm's profit

questions.explanation: The expansion path joins the tangency points of isoquants and isocosts, so every point on it is the least-cost way to produce its output. Option D is wrong because only one point on the path gives maximum profit, and option A is wrong because the path is a straight line through the origin only for special production functions, not for all.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about a firm's expansion path is correct?

options.a: A profit-maximising firm may operate anywhere off its expansion path
options.b: A profit-maximising firm must be on its expansion path, but being on the path does not by itself guarantee maximum profit
options.c: The expansion path shows combinations of output and price
options.d: Any point on the expansion path gives the firm maximum profit

questions.explanation: To maximise profit a firm must produce its chosen output at least cost, so it must be on the expansion path. But the path has a least-cost point for every output, and only one of those outputs maximises profit. Option D wrongly treats all least-cost points as profit-maximising, and option A ignores that any point off the path wastes money.

questions.question: If a firm is experiencing increasing returns to scale, then doubling output will require

options.a: less than a doubling of all inputs
options.c: more than a doubling of all inputs
options.d: exactly a doubling of all inputs

questions.explanation: Under increasing returns to scale, output rises proportionately more than inputs, so less than double the inputs is enough to double output. Option C describes decreasing returns to scale, and option D describes constant returns to scale.

questions.question: Decreasing returns to scale are mainly attributed to

options.a: the use of more specialised machinery
options.b: increased specialisation and division of labour
options.c: the indivisibility of some inputs at low output
options.d: managerial difficulties in coordinating and controlling a very large operation

questions.explanation: As a firm becomes very large, management finds it harder to coordinate, communicate and control, so output grows less than proportionately with inputs. Options B, A and C are the classic causes of increasing returns to scale, not decreasing returns.

questions.question: One reason that a firm may experience decreasing returns to scale is that greater levels of output can result in

options.b: an increase in meetings and paperwork.
options.c: smaller inventories per unit of output.
options.d: All of the above are correct.

questions.explanation: Decreasing returns to scale happen when output grows by a smaller proportion than inputs, and a common cause is that a very large firm becomes hard to manage, with more meetings, paperwork and layers of coordination. Option A, greater division of labour, is actually a source of increasing returns to scale, and option C, smaller inventories per unit, lowers cost per unit rather than raising it. So D cannot be correct either.

questions.question: If all resources used in the production of a product are increased by 20 percent and output increases by 20 percent, then there must be:
questions.explanation: Constant returns to scale means output changes in exactly the same proportion as all inputs. A 20 percent rise in every input giving a 20 percent rise in output fits that exactly. Option A would need output to rise by more than 20 percent, and option B by less than 20 percent.

questions.question: Which of the following statements describes increasing returns to scale:

options.a: Doubling the inputs used leads to double the output.
options.b: Increasing the inputs by 50% leads to a 25% increase in output.
options.c: Increasing inputs by 1/4 leads to an increase in output of 1/3.

questions.explanation: Increasing returns to scale means output rises by a larger proportion than inputs. In option C, inputs rise by 1/4 (25 percent) and output by 1/3 (about 33.3 percent), so output grows faster than inputs. Option A shows constant returns to scale, and option B (25 percent output for 50 percent more inputs) shows decreasing returns to scale.

questions.question: In production theory, a curve showing all the combinations of two inputs that produce the same level of output is called
questions.explanation: An isoquant (meaning 'equal quantity') joins all input combinations that yield the same output, so B is correct. Option D joins input combinations with the same total cost, and Option A is the consumer-theory curve joining bundles of goods that give equal satisfaction.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a property of normal isoquants in the economic region?

options.a: They are concave to the origin
options.c: They slope downward from left to right
options.d: Higher isoquants represent higher levels of output

questions.explanation: Normal isoquants are convex, not concave, to the origin because the MRTS diminishes as one input replaces another, so A is the answer. Options C, B and D are genuine properties: isoquants slope downward, never cross, and lie further from the origin for larger outputs.

questions.question: Normal isoquants are convex to the origin because of

options.b: the straight-line shape of the isocost line
options.d: a diminishing marginal rate of technical substitution

questions.explanation: As a firm substitutes labour for capital along an isoquant, it can give up less and less capital for each extra unit of labour, and this diminishing MRTS makes the curve bow in toward the origin; D is correct. Option A concerns what happens when all inputs are scaled up and so moves between isoquants, while Options C and B describe the isocost line, not the isoquant.

questions.question: Two isoquants of the same firm cannot intersect because

options.a: the inputs would then be perfect complements
options.b: the input combination at the crossing point would be producing two different levels of output
options.c: the isocost line would become vertical
options.d: returns to scale would then be constant

questions.explanation: Each isoquant stands for one output level, so a crossing point would mean the same quantities of labour and capital give two different maximum outputs, which is a contradiction; B is right. Option A concerns the shape of an isoquant (L-shaped), not whether two can cross, and Options C and D have nothing to do with intersection.

questions.question: The marginal rate of technical substitution of labour for capital (MRTS of L for K) is equal to
questions.explanation: Along an isoquant the output lost from giving up capital equals the output gained from extra labour, so -dK/dL = MPL/MPK, making D correct. Option C is the inverse, which is the MRTS of capital for labour, and Option B uses average products, which do not measure the trade-off at the margin.

questions.question: Diminishing MRTS means that as a firm substitutes labour for capital along an isoquant,

options.a: it gives up successively larger amounts of capital for each extra unit of labour
options.b: the cost of production falls continuously
options.c: it gives up successively smaller amounts of capital for each extra unit of labour
options.d: output falls by smaller and smaller amounts

questions.explanation: As labour becomes plentiful and capital scarce, each extra worker can replace less and less capital, so the firm gives up ever smaller amounts of capital per unit of labour; C is right. Option A would be an increasing MRTS, which would make the isoquant concave, and Option D is wrong because output is constant along an isoquant.

questions.question: If labour and capital are perfect substitutes in production, the isoquants are

options.c: smooth curves convex to the origin

questions.explanation: With perfect substitutes one input can always replace the other at a constant rate, so the MRTS is constant and the isoquant is a straight downward-sloping line, making A correct. Option B is the case of perfect complements (fixed proportions), and Option C is the normal case where substitution is possible but imperfect.

questions.question: A transport company in Lagos needs exactly one driver for each bus, and extra drivers without buses (or extra buses without drivers) add nothing to output. Its isoquants are

options.a: smooth curves convex to the origin

questions.explanation: When inputs must be combined in fixed proportions there is no substitution between them, so each isoquant has a right-angle corner at the required ratio, making C right. Option B is the perfect-substitutes case, and Option A is the normal case where labour and capital can partly replace each other.

questions.question: If a firm's total outlay on inputs rises while the wage rate and the rental rate of capital stay the same, its isocost line

options.a: shifts outward parallel to the original line
options.b: pivots inward on the labour axis

questions.explanation: The slope -w/r is unchanged because input prices have not changed, but both intercepts (C/w and C/r) increase, so the line shifts out parallel to itself and A is right. Options C and D would require a change in the relative price of labour, and Option B would follow from a rise in the wage rate.

questions.question: Labour is on the horizontal axis. If the wage rate rises while the rental rate of capital and the total outlay stay the same, the isocost line

options.a: pivots inward on the labour axis and becomes flatter
options.b: pivots outward on the capital axis
options.d: pivots inward on the labour axis and becomes steeper

questions.explanation: The capital intercept C/r is unchanged, but the labour intercept C/w falls, so the line swings inward along the labour axis; since the slope w/r has risen in size, it becomes steeper, which is D. Option A gets the direction of the slope wrong, Option C describes an increase in outlay, and Option B would need a fall in the price of capital.

questions.question: A firm using labour and capital is at its least-cost combination (producer equilibrium) where

options.b: MRTS of L for K = r/w
options.d: MRTS of L for K = w/r

questions.explanation: At equilibrium the rate at which the firm can technically swap capital for labour (MRTS = MPL/MPK) equals the rate at which the market lets it swap them (w/r), so D is correct. Option B inverts the price ratio, and Option C would hold only in the special case where the two inputs have equal prices.

questions.question: The least-cost condition for a firm using labour (L) and capital (K) can also be written as

options.d: MPL x w = MPK x r

questions.explanation: Rearranging MPL/MPK = w/r gives MPL/w = MPK/r: the last naira spent on each input must add the same amount of output, so A is right. Option C puts each input's marginal product over the wrong price, and Option B uses average rather than marginal products.

questions.question: On an isoquant-isocost diagram, the producer's equilibrium occurs where

options.a: the isoquant is tangent to the isocost line
options.b: the isoquant cuts the isocost line at two points
options.c: the isoquant meets a ridge line
options.d: the isocost line meets the capital axis

questions.explanation: At the tangency point the slope of the isoquant (MRTS) equals the slope of the isocost line (w/r), so the firm gets the highest output for its outlay or the lowest cost for its output, and A is correct. Option B means the firm could reach a higher isoquant at the same cost, and Option C marks the edge of the economic region, not equilibrium.

questions.question: A cement plant in Ewekoro doubles all of its inputs and its output more than doubles. The plant is experiencing
questions.explanation: When output rises by a larger proportion than all inputs, the firm has increasing returns to scale, so D is correct. Option B would mean output exactly doubles, Option C would mean it rises by less than double, and Option A is a short-run idea about adding one input to fixed inputs.

questions.question: Which of the following is a common reason for increasing returns to scale?

options.a: The fixity of one input in the short run
options.b: Greater specialisation and division of labour
options.c: Difficulties of coordinating a very large organisation
options.d: A rise in the wage rate

questions.explanation: As a firm grows it can split work into specialised tasks and use large, indivisible machines efficiently, which raises output more than proportionately, so B is right. Option C is a cause of decreasing returns to scale, and Option A is the basis of diminishing returns in the short run, not a scale effect.

questions.question: The expansion path of a firm is

options.a: the path of output as one input is increased with others fixed
options.b: the line joining points where isoquants become positively sloped
options.c: the line joining least-cost input combinations as outlay rises, with input prices constant
options.d: a curve joining input combinations that give equal output

questions.explanation: As the firm's budget rises with w and r unchanged, each new isocost line touches a higher isoquant, and the expansion path joins these tangency points, so C is right. Option B describes a ridge line, Option D is an isoquant, and Option A is the short-run total product curve.

questions.question: Wages in a Kano textile factory rise sharply while the rental cost of machines stays the same. To produce the same output at least cost, the factory will

options.a: cut both inputs in the same proportion
options.b: keep the same mix of labour and capital
options.c: use more capital and less labour
options.d: use more labour and less capital

questions.explanation: A higher w/r makes the isocost line steeper, so the new tangency on the same isoquant is at a point with more capital and less labour: the firm substitutes the relatively cheaper input for the dearer one, and C is correct. Option D is the opposite of what happens, and Option B ignores that the least-cost mix depends on relative input prices.

questions.question: On an isoquant map, ridge lines join the points where

options.a: the MRTS equals the input price ratio
options.b: isoquants are tangent to isocost lines
options.c: the marginal product of one of the inputs is zero
options.d: output doubles when all inputs double

questions.explanation: Ridge lines pass through the points where an isoquant turns vertical or horizontal, that is where the MP of capital or of labour falls to zero, so C is right. Options B and A describe the points of producer equilibrium that make up the expansion path, and Option D describes constant returns to scale.

questions.question: A rational firm will operate only in the region between the ridge lines because outside them

options.a: returns to scale are always increasing
options.b: the marginal product of one input is negative, so the isoquants slope upward

questions.explanation: Beyond a ridge line, adding more of one input lowers output, so more of both inputs would be needed to keep output constant and the isoquant slopes upward; no cost-minimising firm would pay for such inputs, so B is correct. Option D is wrong because the isocost line always slopes downward, and Option A has no connection to the ridge lines.

questions.question: If the last naira spent on labour adds more to output than the last naira spent on capital, a cost-minimising firm should

options.a: employ more capital and less labour
options.b: employ more labour and less capital

questions.explanation: Here MPL/w is greater than MPK/r, so shifting spending from capital to labour raises output at the same cost; the firm should keep doing this until the two ratios are equal, making B right. Option A moves in the wrong direction, and Option D is correct only when MPL/w = MPK/r.

questions.question: Returns to scale is a long-run concept because

options.a: it concerns only the fixed input
options.b: it requires all inputs to be variable
options.c: it applies only when technology changes
options.d: it is measured over a period of more than five years

questions.explanation: To change the scale of production, every input, including plant and machinery, must be variable, and that is possible only in the long run, so B is correct. Option C is wrong because returns to scale assume a given technology, and Option D is wrong because the long run is defined by input flexibility, not a fixed number of years.

questions.question: A poultry farm in Ogun has a budget of N12,000 per day to spend on labour and capital. The wage rate is N400 per worker-day and the rental rate of capital is N600 per machine-day. What is the maximum quantity of labour it can hire if it uses no capital?
questions.explanation: With K = 0 the whole budget goes on labour, so L = C/w = 12,000/400 = 30 worker-days, which is the labour intercept of the isocost line; B is correct. Option C divides by the price of capital and is the capital intercept, and Option A wrongly divides by the sum of the two prices.

questions.question: A firm's isocost line is drawn with capital (K) on the vertical axis and labour (L) on the horizontal axis. The wage rate is N400 and the rental rate of capital is N600. What is the slope of the isocost line?
questions.explanation: The isocost line K = C/r - (w/r)L has slope -w/r = -400/600 = -2/3, so D is right. Option A inverts the ratio (-r/w), option B subtracts the prices instead of dividing them, and option C has the wrong sign, since an isocost line always slopes downward.

questions.question: A firm spends N20,000 on labour (L) and capital (K). The wage rate is N500 and the rental rate of capital is N1,000. Which equation gives its isocost line with K on the vertical axis?
questions.explanation: From 20,000 = 500L + 1,000K, dividing by 1,000 gives K = 20 - 0.5L: the intercept is C/r = 20 and the slope is -w/r = -0.5, so D is correct. Option B uses the labour intercept (C/w = 40) and the inverted slope, while Options A and C each get one of the two parts wrong.

questions.question: At a firm's current input mix, the marginal product of labour is 12 units and the marginal product of capital is 4 units. What is the MRTS of labour for capital?
questions.explanation: MRTS of L for K = MPL/MPK = 12/4 = 3, meaning one extra unit of labour can replace 3 units of capital with output unchanged, so B is right. Option D is MPK/MPL, Option A multiplies the marginal products, and Option C subtracts them.

questions.question: A printing firm in Surulere has MPL = 10 copies and MPK = 40 copies. The wage is N200 per hour and the rental rate of a machine is N400 per hour. To minimise cost for its current output, the firm should

options.a: use more capital and less labour
options.b: keep its current input mix, as it is already in equilibrium
options.c: use more labour and less capital

questions.explanation: Compare output per naira: MPL/w = 10/200 = 0.05 while MPK/r = 40/400 = 0.1, so a naira spent on capital adds twice as much output as a naira on labour; the firm should switch towards capital, making A correct. Option C moves the wrong way, and Option B is wrong because the two ratios are not equal.

questions.question: A firm has the production function Q = K^0.5 L^0.5. The wage rate is N20, the rental rate of capital is N80 and the firm's budget is N1,600. How many units of labour will it employ at the least-cost (output-maximising) combination?
questions.explanation: Here MRTS = MPL/MPK = K/L; setting it equal to w/r = 20/80 gives K = L/4. Substituting into 20L + 80K = 1,600 gives 20L + 20L = 1,600, so L = 40 and C is correct. Option D is the capital used, Option A spends the whole budget on labour (1,600/20), and Option B is the output produced.

questions.question: A firm has the production function Q = K^0.5 L^0.5. The wage rate is N20, the rental rate of capital is N80 and the firm's budget is N1,600. How many units of capital will it employ at the least-cost (output-maximising) combination?
questions.explanation: Equilibrium requires K/L = w/r = 1/4, and the budget 20L + 80K = 1,600 then gives L = 40 and K = 10, so B is right. Option C is the labour used, Option D spends the whole budget on capital (1,600/80), and Option A would follow from wrongly halving L/4 again.

questions.question: A firm has the production function Q = K^0.5 L^0.5. The wage rate is N20, the rental rate of capital is N80 and the firm's budget is N1,600. What is the maximum output it can produce?
questions.explanation: At the optimum L = 40 and K = 10 (from K/L = w/r = 1/4 and the budget), so Q = 10^0.5 x 40^0.5 = sqrt(400) = 20, and A is correct. Option B forgets to take the square root of K x L, while Options D and C come from using wrong input quantities instead of the tangency point.

questions.question: For the production function Q = 10K^0.3 L^0.7, returns to scale are

options.a: decreasing, because each exponent is less than 1
options.b: increasing, because the constant 10 is greater than 1

questions.explanation: For a Cobb-Douglas function Q = A K^a L^b, returns to scale depend on a + b: here 0.3 + 0.7 = 1, so doubling both inputs exactly doubles output, which is D. Option B is wrong because A only scales the level of output, Option A confuses exponents below 1 (diminishing marginal products) with returns to scale, and Option C compares the exponents instead of adding them.

questions.question: For the production function Q = 2K^0.6 L^0.7, returns to scale are

options.b: constant, because the constant 2 doubles output
options.c: decreasing, because each exponent is less than 1
options.d: constant, because the function is of Cobb-Douglas form

questions.explanation: The sum of the exponents is 0.6 + 0.7 = 1.3, which is greater than 1, so scaling both inputs by any factor raises output by a larger proportion; A is correct. Option D is wrong because a Cobb-Douglas function shows constant returns only when the exponents sum to 1, and Option C confuses diminishing marginal products with returns to scale.

questions.question: Which of the following production functions exhibits decreasing returns to scale?
questions.explanation: Returns to scale in a Cobb-Douglas function depend on the sum of the exponents: 0.4 + 0.5 = 0.9 < 1, so A has decreasing returns. Options B and C both sum to exactly 1 (constant returns), whatever the constant in front, and Option D sums to 1.3 (increasing returns).

questions.question: For the production function Q = K^0.5 L^0.5, what is the MRTS of labour for capital when L = 9 and K = 36?
questions.explanation: MPL = 0.5K^0.5 L^-0.5 and MPK = 0.5K^-0.5 L^0.5, so MRTS = MPL/MPK = K/L = 36/9 = 4, and B is correct. Option C is L/K, which is the MRTS of capital for labour, Option A is output (sqrt(324) = 18), and Option D is the square root of the answer.
